description:
What it is: SMBus timeout and PEC unit: Monitors SMBus transactions for SCL-low timeouts and computes the CRC-8 packet error code over transferred bytes, keeping a low-time counter, a timeout flag and a PEC accumulator register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module smbus_pec_mon: an SMBus monitor for a 128-bit SoC prototyping bus bridge. It tracks SCL-low timeouts and folds 128-bit transfer words into a CRC-8 PEC (poly 0x07). Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (all state holds when en=0), scl_low, wvalid, wdata[127:0]. Every register below updates only when en=1.

State registers:
- low_cnt[5:0]: counts consecutive scl_low cycles and clears when SCL goes high. It saturates at TMAX=50.
- timeout_flag (1 bit): set when low_cnt==TMAX-1 && scl_low.
- before_to (1 bit): reset to 1 and cleared the first time timeout_flag rises. This is the scope register.
- wbuf[127:0]: latched input word.
- pend (1 bit): set on wvalid, cleared on fold. It feeds the PEC path.
- pend_cnt (1 bit): a duplicate pending flag, set and cleared identically to pend. It feeds the count path.
- pec_acc[7:0]: PEC accumulator. When pend=1 it takes pec_acc <= crc8_128(pec_acc, wbuf).
- wcnt[6:0]: folded-word counter, incremented mod 128 when pend_cnt=1. An increment always changes its value.
- pec_snap[7:0]: precedence shadow. When pend_cnt=1 it takes pec_snap <= crc8_128(pec_acc, wbuf), recording the PEC value produced by the most recent counted fold.

Relation R (holds by construction): pend == pend_cnt && pec_snap == pec_acc.

Property P (precedence, before-timeout scope, $stable style). P captures that a PEC change must be preceded by, and coincide with, a counted word fold:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff(!rst_n) before_to && $past(before_to) && $stable(wcnt) |-> $stable(pec_acc));
In words: if the word counter did not move, the PEC accumulator did not move either. Antecedents are before_to and $past(before_to).

P is true on reachable states. pec_acc changes only when pend=1, and by R pend_cnt=1 at the same moment, so wcnt changes too. Therefore $stable(wcnt) implies no fold, which implies $stable(pec_acc).

Counter-example to induction (P holds, R is violated):
- State: before_to=1, timeout_flag=0, low_cnt=0, pend=1, pend_cnt=0, pec_acc=8'h00, wbuf=128'h1, pec_snap=8'h00, wcnt=7'd5.
- This satisfies P now, and it violates R because pend != pend_cnt.
- With en=0 the state is frozen for any number of cycles. Every register is $stable, so P holds vacuously, and a k-induction run of any depth fails to reach a contradiction.
- On the first cycle with en=1 and scl_low=0, pec_acc becomes crc8(0x00, 128'h1)=0x07 while wcnt stays 5. Then $stable(wcnt) holds but pec_acc changed, which violates P while before_to is still 1.

Supplying R as a lemma excludes the pend/pend_cnt mismatch, and P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Elliptic-curve point adder/doubler: Performs point addition and doubling in projective or Jacobian coordinates by sequencing field multiplications and additions, holding the X, Y, Z coordinate registers of the operands and temporaries.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module ec_jdbl_seq: a 32-bit Jacobian point-doubling/addition sequencer. It has a 16-entry x 32-bit register file `rf[0:15]`. Entries 0-2 hold X1,Y1,Z1, entries 3-5 hold X2,Y2,Z2, and entries 6-15 hold temporaries. Field arithmetic is modulo p = 2^32-5.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), arm, start, clr, sel_add (add vs double), and wr_addr/wr_data (operand load while not running).

State registers:
- armed (1)
- started (1)
- done (1)
- pre_clr (1): starts at 1, cleared the first cycle en && clr.
- step [31:0]: micro-op index; 0 means not running.
- acc [31:0]: field multiply/add result.
- rf (16 x 32)

Behaviour when en is high:
- arm sets armed.
- If start && armed && step==0, then step<=1 and started<=1.
- While step != 0, each cycle performs micro-op number step from a fixed 11-op schedule, for example T6=Y1*Y1, T7=X1*T6, T8=X1*X1 and so on. Each op reads two rf entries, writes acc into a temporary, and does step<=step+1.
- When step==11, it writes back X3,Y3,Z3 into rf[0..2], sets done<=1 and step<=0.
- clr clears armed, started and done but deliberately leaves step and rf alone (soft clear of handshake flags only). Thus after a clr a run already in progress can finish with started=0. This is why the property is scoped before the first clr.

Relation R (holds by construction while pre_clr):
- (step != 0) -> (started && armed)
- started -> armed
- done -> started

Property P (Chain Precedence arm -> start -> finish, scope before clr; pre_clr listed in antecedents):
  always @(*) assert (!pre_clr || !done || (started && armed));

Counterexample-to-induction state:
- pre_clr=1, armed=1, started=0, done=0, step=10, en=0.
- P holds because done=0.
- R is violated because step != 0 while started=0.
- With en low the state is frozen indefinitely, so arbitrarily long stuttering prefixes all satisfy P. Plain k-induction therefore cannot exclude it for any k.

On the next en=1 cycle with clr=0:
- step goes 10 -> 11.
- One more cycle sets done=1 with started=0, violating P.

Supplying R as a lemma makes P 1-inductive. step==0 is guaranteed whenever started is 0, so done can only be set after the start event, which itself required armed.

What it is: Edge detector: Flags rising or falling transitions by comparing a signal with its value stored in a delay flop.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module cdc_line_edge_fifo: a USB-CDC style line-state change capturer. A 128-bit status word (DTR/RTS/break bits for all channels, packed) arrives each cycle on din[127:0]. A delay flop holds the previous word. A word-level change is flagged combinationally: edge_seen = en & (din != prev). Each change pushes the new word into a 16-entry 128-bit capture FIFO, which the host-side logic drains with rd_en. Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle when low: every register holds), din[127:0], rd_en, cfg_set (host SET_CONFIGURATION event). Outputs: dout[127:0], full, empty.

State registers: prev[127:0] (delay flop); mem[0:15][127:0]; wr_ptr[3:0]; rd_ptr[3:0]; count[4:0]; full (1b) and empty (1b), both registered and updated from count_next; armed (1b), sticky. On en: prev<=din. push=edge_seen&!full, pop=rd_en&!empty. count_next=count+push-pop. full<=(count_next==16), empty<=(count_next==0). armed<=armed|cfg_set, and it is never cleared after reset. Reset: count=0, empty=1, full=0, armed=0, prev=0.

Relation R (holds by construction): full==(count==16) && empty==(count==0) && count==({1'b0,wr_ptr}-{1'b0,rd_ptr}) mod 32 with count<=16.

Property P (absence, after Q, $rose style): assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff(!rst_n) (armed && $rose(edge_seen)) |-> !(full && empty)). In words: once the host has configured the device, whenever a line-state change edge rises, the FIFO is never flagged full and empty at the same time.

Why P needs R: full and empty are separate registers that are written only from count. Without R, k-induction may start from an unreachable state in which both flags are high. P alone does not rule that state out, because P only constrains cycles where edge_seen rises.

CTI state: armed=1, full=1, empty=1, count=5, wr_ptr=5, rd_ptr=0, prev=X. This state violates R because full=1 while count!=16, and empty=1 while count!=0.
- It satisfies P while en=0, since edge_seen=0 means there is no rise.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0, because every register holds. This defeats any finite k.
- Next step: en=1 with din!=prev makes edge_seen rise from 0 to 1. In that same cycle full&&empty is still 1, so P is violated.

With R supplied, full&&empty would require count==16 and count==0 simultaneously, which is impossible. P then becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: LSSD shift-register latch: A level-sensitive scan design latch pair in which an L1 latch with separate system and scan clocks feeds an L2 latch, and each latch keeps one bit.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
GPU core scan-dump unit built from LSSD L1/L2 latch pairs. A debug host requests a scan dump of a 2-entry, 64-bit warp-register snapshot. Each bit position is an LSSD pair: an L1 latch with a system clock and a scan A-clock feeds an L2 latch clocked by B. The latches are modeled as registers updated on internal A/B pulse phases.

State (all held when en=0):
- l1[0:1], l2[0:1]: 64-bit each, the latch pairs.
- busy: 1 bit.
- ph: 1 bit; 0 means an A pulse is due, 1 means a B pulse is due.
- sc: 7-bit shift count.
- cd: 8-bit countdown.

Behaviour when en=1:
- Idle, !scan_req: system capture into l1 is allowed and B copies l1 into l2. busy, sc, ph and cd are unchanged.
- Accept, !busy && scan_req: busy<=1, cd<=128, sc<=0, ph<=0.
- While busy, every cycle cd<=cd-1.
- When busy and ph==0 (A pulse): l1[i] <= {l2[i][62:0], scan_in_i}, where entry 1's scan_in is entry 0's l2 MSB and entry 0's is tdi. ph<=1.
- When busy and ph==1 (B pulse): l2<=l1, ph<=0, sc<=sc+1.
- Completion is triggered by the shift counter, not the countdown: when busy && ph==1 && sc==63, busy<=0 and sc<=0. cd decrements on that cycle as usual, from 1 to 0.
- tdo = l2[1][63].

Relation R (by construction):
- busy -> (cd == 128 - 2*sc - ph) && sc <= 63
- !busy -> (cd == 0 && sc == 0 && ph == 0)

Property P (global, two assertions, no arming):
- A1 (bounded response, safety form): busy -> cd != 0. The countdown never expires while the dump is outstanding.
- A2: !busy -> cd == 0. An idle unit never holds a stale countdown.

Neither assertion is inductive alone:
- A1 counterexample: busy=1, cd=1, sc=10, ph=0 satisfies A1 and A2 but violates R. One enabled cycle gives busy=1, cd=0, which violates A1.
- A2 counterexample: busy=1, cd=5, sc=63, ph=1 satisfies A1, and A2 vacuously, but violates R. It steps to busy=0, cd=4, which violates A2.

Either state can be held indefinitely with en=0, since all registers freeze. Adding R closes both assertions:
- Under R, busy && sc==63 && ph==1 forces cd==1, so completion lands exactly on cd==0.
- Under R, any other busy state has cd >= 2, so cd-1 stays nonzero.
- Idle with cd==0 is preserved, and accept loads cd=128 with sc=0, ph=0, which re-establishes R.

k = 128 cycles is the response bound.

What it is: Binary encoder: Converts an asserted input line into its binary index, combinationally.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module mips_wb_scoreboard: a writeback drain unit themed on the MIPS hazard detection unit. A 16-line combinational priority encoder turns pending load-destination lines into a 4-bit register index. It retires one index per cycle into writeback, and a countdown guarantees that the drain finishes.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, all state holds), req (accept request), req_vec[15:0] (one bit per pending destination register), q_open, r_close.
Outputs: wb_valid, wb_idx[3:0].

State registers:
- pend[15:0]: outstanding destination lines.
- busy (1 bit): a drain is in progress.
- cnt[7:0]: countdown.
- win (1 bit): property window.

Combinational encoder: wb_idx is the index of the lowest set bit of pend (a for-loop priority encoder, 0 if pend==0), and low = pend & (~pend + 1).

Behaviour when en is high:
- Reset: pend=0, busy=0, cnt=0, win=0.
- Window: if q_open then win<=1, else if r_close then win<=0. The window can therefore open and close repeatedly.
- Accept: if !busy && req && req_vec!=0, then pend<=req_vec, busy<=1, cnt<=8'd16. The completion bound is k=16, matching the 16 entries.
- Drain: else if busy, then:
  - wb_valid=1;
  - pend<=pend & ~low (retire the encoded index);
  - cnt<=cnt-1;
  - if (pend & ~low)==0 then busy<=0.

Relation R (holds by construction): busy ? (pend!=0 && popcount(pend) <= cnt) : (pend==0).
- Accept loads at most 16 bits into pend and sets cnt=16.
- Each drain step removes exactly one bit and decrements cnt by exactly one.
- busy drops exactly when pend empties.

Property P (safety bounded response between Q=q_open and R=r_close):
always @(*) assert (!(win && busy) || cnt != 8'd0);
In words: inside the window, the countdown never expires while the request is still outstanding. P holds because R gives cnt >= popcount(pend) >= 1 whenever busy.

Counterexample to induction (satisfies P, violates R):
- win=1, busy=1, cnt=8'd1, pend=16'h0003.
- P holds because cnt!=0.
- R is violated because popcount(pend)=2 > cnt=1.
- With en=0 the state is held indefinitely, so it is reachable inside any induction window of idle steps.
- On one step with en=1 (q_open=1, r_close=0), the encoder retires index 0, giving pend=16'h0002. Since that is nonzero, busy stays 1, and cnt becomes 0 with win=1. P is violated.
- k-induction alone therefore fails; supplying R (the popcount bound together with busy implying pend nonzero) makes P inductive.

What it is: Belt register file: Replaces named destinations with a fixed-length queue of recent results addressed by position from the front, storing the belt slots and a head index advanced as each result drops onto it.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module relo_belt: a belt register file that collects relocation offsets of pre-implemented modules (RapidWright-style placement results) as they are produced. Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds its value, including the window), drop (a result is ready), din[63:0], rd_pos[4:0], ckpt_open (Q), ckpt_close (R). Output: dout[63:0] = slot[head - 1 - rd_pos], which reads the belt by position counted from the front.

State registers:
- slot[0:31], each 64-bit: the belt storage.
- head, 5-bit: the index where the next result will be written.
- drops, 64-bit: the total number of results dropped since reset.
- win_cnt, 64-bit: the number of drops since the window last opened.
- win, 1-bit: the checkpoint window register.

Behaviour when en=1:
- On drop: slot[head] <= din, head <= head+1 and drops <= drops+1. If win is 1, win_cnt also increments.
- On ckpt_open (when not closing): win <= 1 and win_cnt <= 0.
- On ckpt_close: win <= 0.
- Reset clears all registers.
- The window can open and close any number of times.

Relation R, which holds by construction: head == drops[4:0] in every state. Both registers reset to 0, and both increment on exactly the same condition, so the 5-bit head always equals drops mod 32.

Property P (universality, scoped to the checkpoint window, guarded style):
always @(posedge clk) if (win && !rst) assert (head == drops[4:0]);
The antecedent lists the window register win. P is true because R holds everywhere, and therefore holds inside every window.

Why k-induction fails without R: P constrains nothing while win=0, so the induction hypothesis says nothing about head versus drops outside a window. Counterexample state:
- win=0, head=5'd3, drops=64'd0, win_cnt=0, slots arbitrary.
- P holds vacuously because win=0. R is violated because 3 != 0.
- With en=0 the state is held unchanged for any number of cycles. Those idle steps all satisfy P, so the state can sit at the end of an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix and defeat any induction depth k.
- Then a step with en=1, ckpt_open=1, drop=0 sets win=1 while head and drops stay unchanged. P now checks 3 == 0 and fails.

Given R as a lemma, the state is excluded and P becomes 1-inductive: drop advances head and drops together, open and close leave them untouched, and en=0 freezes everything.

What it is: Lockstep duplicate-and-compare checker: Runs two copies of a logic block on the same inputs and raises a fault on any output mismatch, keeping a registered mismatch flag and a sticky error-status register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module rdf_lockstep_wl: a lockstep checker for a duplicated 'wirelength cost accumulator' stage of a physical-design flow. Copy A and copy B each sum the same 64-bit net-length input. A registered mismatch flag and a sticky error register report any divergence. A 'closure reached' flag marks flow sign-off readiness.

Ports: clk, rst (synchronous), en (enable; when low every register holds), wl_in[63:0], close_in, eco_in.

State registers:
- acc_a[63:0], acc_b[63:0]: the two copies.
- step_cnt[63:0]: count of accumulated nets.
- mism_q (1): registered mismatch.
- err_q (1): sticky error.
- ok_q (1): closure flag.
- pre_eco (1): the scope register.

Reset values: all zero, except pre_eco=1.

Behavior when en=1:
- acc_a<=acc_a+wl_in and acc_b<=acc_b+wl_in.
- step_cnt<=step_cnt+1.
- mism_q<=(acc_a+wl_in)!=(acc_b+wl_in).
- err_q<=err_q|mism_q.
- ok_q<=ok_q|close_in. ok_q is never cleared, and it is independent of the checker.
- pre_eco<=pre_eco&~eco_in. The first ECO override is event R of the scope.

When en=0, all registers hold.

Relation R (holds by construction, since both copies start equal and receive identical updates): acc_a==acc_b && !mism_q && !err_q.

Property P (absence, before-R scope, clock-edge style): the mismatch flag and the closure flag are never high together while no ECO has occurred.
always @(posedge clk) assert (!pre_eco || !(mism_q && ok_q));
Antecedents: pre_eco.

Why k-induction fails without R: P constrains only mism_q and ok_q. The mismatch can arise only from diverged accumulators, which P never mentions.

Counterexample to induction:
- State: acc_a=64'd1, acc_b=64'd0, mism_q=0, err_q=0, ok_q=1, pre_eco=1, step_cnt arbitrary.
- It satisfies P, since mism_q=0, and it violates R, since acc_a!=acc_b.
- With en=0 it can be held for any number k of cycles, and P holds on every one of them.
- On a single en=1 step with eco_in=0 (any wl_in, any close_in), mism_q becomes (1+wl_in)!=(0+wl_in)=1. ok_q stays 1 and pre_eco stays 1, so P is violated.

Given R as a lemma, the step is trivially inductive: equal accumulators keep mism_q at 0 forever.

What it is: Automatic gain control loop: Adjusts an applied gain from measured signal amplitude, keeping an amplitude estimate register and a gain register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
HDMI luminance AGC (hdmi_agc): a per-frame automatic gain loop that scales incoming pixel luma before TMDS encoding. It holds an amplitude estimate and a gain register, and it runs a three-step arm/start/finish sequence inside each frame window.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), vsync_rise (Q), frame_end (R), pix_valid, luma[31:0].

State registers:
- amp_est[31:0]: leaky peak estimate of |luma|.
- gain[31:0]: Q16.16 gain.
- hist[0:63][31:0]: 64-entry ring of recent scaled samples.
- wr_ptr[5:0].
- adapt_cnt[31:0].
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, ADAPT=2, DONE=3.
- arm_seen, start_seen, done_flag: 1-bit each.
- win: 1-bit window register.

Behavior (only when en=1):
- vsync_rise sets win=1 and clears phase, all three flags and adapt_cnt.
- frame_end clears win. Q and R can recur every frame, so the window opens and closes many times.
- Inside the window, on pix_valid, hist[wr_ptr] is written with luma*gain>>16, wr_ptr increments, and amp_est is updated.
- Arm: when phase==IDLE and amp_est > ARM_TH, set phase=ARMED and arm_seen=1.
- Start: when phase==ARMED and hist is full (wr_ptr wraps), set phase=ADAPT and start_seen=1.
- While in ADAPT, each pix_valid nudges gain toward TARGET/amp_est and increments adapt_cnt.
- Finish: when phase==ADAPT and adapt_cnt==63, set phase=DONE and done_flag=1.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- arm_seen == (phase>=ARMED)
- start_seen == (phase>=ADAPT)
- done_flag == (phase==DONE)
- adapt_cnt != 0 implies phase>=ADAPT

Property P (scope: between Q and R; both assertions list win in the antecedent):
- A1: assert (win && done_flag |-> start_seen). Finish is never observed without start.
- A2: assert (win && start_seen |-> arm_seen). Start is never observed without arm.
- Neither assertion is inductive alone, because each relies on the flag-to-phase correspondence in R. Adding R makes both inductive.

Counterexample to induction for A1:
- State: en=1, win=1, phase=ADAPT, adapt_cnt=63, start_seen=0, arm_seen=0, done_flag=0, frame_end=0.
- A1 and A2 both hold, but R is violated (phase is ADAPT while start_seen=0).
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0.
- With en=1 and pix_valid, finish fires: done_flag becomes 1 while start_seen stays 0, violating A1.

Counterexample to induction for A2:
- State: win=1, phase=ARMED, arm_seen=0, start_seen=0, wr_ptr=63.
- Both assertions hold, R is violated, and the state can be held with en=0.
- With en=1 and pix_valid, wr_ptr wraps and start fires: start_seen becomes 1 with arm_seen=0, violating A2.

invariants: inflight == 64'd0 + valid_pipe[0] + valid_pipe[1] + valid_pipe[2] + valid_pipe[3] + valid_pipe[4]
description:
What it is: Benes permutation network: Realizes arbitrary permutations through two butterfly halves of 2x2 switches whose settings are held in configuration registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
RiftCore-style issue-lane shuffler: a pipelined 8x8 Benes network (5 stages of 4 2x2 switches = 20 switch bits) that permutes eight 64-bit operand words from rename lanes to execution ports. Switch settings come from a 256-entry permutation table, so each beat can pick a different routing.

Inputs:
- clk, rst.
- en: the idle input. When en is low, every register holds.
- in_valid; in_data[8][64]; in_sel[7:0], which picks the table entry.
- cfg_we, cfg_addr[7:0], cfg_bits[19:0]: table write port.

State registers:
- cfg_tab[256][20]: permutation table.
- stage_cfg[5][4]: settings latched per stage for the beat in flight.
- data_pipe[5][8][64]: words held between stages.
- valid_pipe[4:0]: one valid bit per stage.
- inflight[63:0]: number of beats currently in the network.
- beats_done[63:0]: retired-beat counter, not used in P.
- armed (1 bit): sticky; set the first time cfg_we is high while en is high, never cleared.

Behaviour when en is high:
- cfg_we writes cfg_tab[cfg_addr].
- valid_pipe shifts left: valid_pipe <= {valid_pipe[3:0], in_valid}.
- data_pipe and stage_cfg advance one stage. Each stage swaps or passes its lane pairs according to its 4 bits, wired as a Benes network (butterfly, then inverse butterfly).
- inflight <= inflight + in_valid - valid_pipe[4].
- beats_done increments when valid_pipe[4] is set.
- Reset clears everything.

Relation R (holds by construction): inflight == popcount(valid_pipe). The counter rises exactly when a valid bit enters and falls exactly when one leaves stage 4.

Property P (after-Q bounded existence, at most 5):
always @(posedge clk) assert (!armed || inflight <= 64'd5);
The bound 5 is the network depth, far below the 2^64 the width allows, so it is a real fact about reachable states.

Counterexample to induction (state satisfying P, violating R):
- armed = 1, inflight = 5, valid_pipe = 5'b00000; the other registers are arbitrary.
- P holds because 5 <= 5.
- R fails because popcount(valid_pipe) = 0 but inflight = 5.
- With en low the state is held indefinitely, so it is consistent for any induction depth.
- Then raise en with in_valid = 1. Since valid_pipe[4] = 0, inflight becomes 6 and P is violated.
- k-induction alone cannot exclude this state. Given R, inflight <= popcount of 5 bits <= 5, and P follows immediately.

What it is: Quadrature decoder: Derives position and direction from two phase-shifted encoder inputs, keeping previous-sample flops and a position counter.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module wrapped_quad_dec: a Caravel-style wrapped sub-project that decodes a quadrature encoder. The project is activated by a logic-analyser bit proj_en, which is the enable: when proj_en is low every register holds its value. Inputs: clk, rst (synchronous, clears all state), proj_en, enc_a, enc_b, and a minimal Wishbone read port (wbs_stb_i, wbs_cyc_i, wbs_we_i, wbs_adr_i[3:0]). Outputs: wbs_dat_o[31:0] (pos or err_cnt by address) and wbs_ack_o.

State registers:
- a_q, b_q (1 bit each): previous samples of enc_a and enc_b.
- pos[15:0]: signed position counter.
- err_cnt[15:0]: count of illegal double-phase transitions.
- seen_step (1 bit): sticky shadow register, set on the first valid step.
- armed (1 bit): sticky arm register, set on the first Wishbone read of the position address (Q = proj_en && wbs_stb_i && wbs_cyc_i && !wbs_we_i && wbs_adr_i==0). It is never cleared except by rst.

Behaviour when proj_en is high: a_q<=enc_a and b_q<=enc_b. A valid step occurs when exactly one phase changed, i.e. step = (enc_a^a_q)^(enc_b^b_q). Its direction is up = a_q ^ enc_b. On a step, pos increments if up and decrements otherwise, and seen_step<=1. If both phases changed, err_cnt increments and pos is unchanged. The ack is a one-cycle registered pulse.

Relation R (by construction): !seen_step -> (pos == 16'd0). The position can only leave zero through a valid step, and that same step sets seen_step.

Property P (precedence, scoped after Q), written unclocked at module level:
assert property (!(armed && (pos != 16'd0)) || seen_step);
In words: once the position has been read over the bus, any nonzero position must have been preceded by an encoder step.

Why induction fails without R: consider the state armed=0, seen_step=0, pos=16'd5, with a_q, b_q and err_cnt arbitrary. P holds because armed=0, but R is violated. Holding proj_en low keeps this state indefinitely. If proj_en is then raised for one cycle with a Wishbone read of address 0 and enc_a, enc_b equal to a_q, b_q (no step), the next state is armed=1, pos=5, seen_step=0. That state violates P. Adding R excludes the starting state, after which P becomes inductive: from any state satisfying R and P, pos changes only together with seen_step being set.

What it is: Microcode sequencer: Selects the next control-store address from branch, jump, and increment sources, keeping a microprogram counter and a microsubroutine return register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Tensil-style TCU microcode sequencer (module tcu_useq). It picks the next control-store address for the accelerator's instruction decoder (MatMul / DataMove / SIMD microroutines).

Inputs:
- clk, rst.
- en: idle/enable. When low, every state register holds.
- op[2:0]: INC=0, JMP=1, BR=2, CALL=3, RET=4.
- cond: branch condition.
- sel[1:0]: picks a jump-table entry.
- tw_en, tw_idx[1:0], tw_data[15:0]: write port for the jump table.

State registers (reset values in brackets):
- upc[15:0]: microprogram counter [0].
- jt[0:3][15:0]: 4-entry jump/branch target table, written through the tw_* port when en is high [0].
- ret_reg[15:0]: microsubroutine return register [0].
- ret_valid (1 bit): set means a return is pending [0].
- shadow_ret[15:0]: verification shadow holding the link address captured at the most recent CALL [0].
- pv (1 bit): past-valid flag, set to 1 after the first cycle.

Next-state rules (all apply only when en=1):
- INC: upc <= upc+1.
- JMP: upc <= jt[sel].
- BR: upc <= cond ? jt[sel] : upc+1.
- CALL: ret_reg <= upc+1, shadow_ret <= upc+1, ret_valid <= 1, upc <= jt[sel].
- RET with ret_valid=1: upc <= ret_reg, ret_valid <= 0.
- RET with ret_valid=0: upc <= upc+1.
The outputs are upc and ret_valid.

Relation R (holds by construction): ret_reg == shadow_ret. Both are written only on CALL, from the same upc+1 value, and both reset to 0.

Property P (precedence, global, $past style): a return-target address seen in upc must have been recorded earlier by a CALL.
  always @(posedge clk) if (pv && $past(en) && $past(op)==4 && $past(ret_valid)) assert (upc == $past(shadow_ret));

Why k-induction fails without R. Take this induction state:
- pv=1, ret_valid=1, ret_reg=16'h0040, shadow_ret=16'h0013.
- upc and jt arbitrary.
- The past-cycle registers record en=0.

It satisfies P, because the previous cycle was idle, so the antecedent is false. It violates R, since 0x0040 != 0x0013.

Holding en=0 for any number of cycles keeps all state frozen, and P stays vacuously true at each step. That yields an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix, so no depth k rules it out.

The next step is en=1, op=RET. Then upc becomes 0x0040 while $past(shadow_ret)=0x0013, so P fails.

With R supplied as a lemma, the RET step gives upc = old ret_reg = old shadow_ret. P then becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Reset escalation controller: Promotes repeated local fault resets to a broader subsystem or chip-wide reset, keeping a fault occurrence counter, an escalation level register and a decay timer.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
NFC reader RF-fault reset escalator (nfc_rst_escalator). Context: the ISO14443A PCD receive chain flags rx_fault (CRC, parity or collision error from the PICC demodulator). Repeated faults escalate from no reset, to a subsystem reset of the RF front-end/ADC (sub_rst_q), to a chip-wide reset (chip_rst_q). A decay timer slowly forgives faults.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle/enable: when en=0 every register holds its value), rx_fault.
Parameters (64-bit): T1=4, T2=8, DECAY=1000.

State registers:
- fault_cnt[63:0]: fault occurrence counter, saturating at 2^64-1.
- decay_tmr[63:0]: decay timer.
- sub_rst_q (1 bit): subsystem level.
- chip_rst_q (1 bit): chip level. Together sub_rst_q and chip_rst_q form the escalation level.
- armed (1 bit): sticky.

Behaviour, only when en=1:
- Fault: if rx_fault, fault_cnt <= fault_cnt+1 (saturating). If fault_cnt+1==T1, set sub_rst_q<=1. If fault_cnt+1==T2, set chip_rst_q<=1 and sub_rst_q<=0. On a fault cycle decay_tmr holds.
- Decay: when there is no fault, decay_tmr counts up. When decay_tmr reaches DECAY, it returns to 0 and, if fault_cnt>0, fault_cnt is decremented. If fault_cnt-1==T2-1, set chip_rst_q<=0 and sub_rst_q<=1. If fault_cnt-1==T1-1, set sub_rst_q<=0.
- Arm: armed <= armed | sub_rst_q. Q is the first time a subsystem reset is issued; armed is never cleared except by rst_n.
- Reset: everything is 0.

Relation R, which holds by construction:
- sub_rst_q == (fault_cnt>=T1 && fault_cnt<T2)
- chip_rst_q == (fault_cnt>=T2)

Property P, absence after Q, in plain combinational style:
  always @(*) assert (!(armed && sub_rst_q && chip_rst_q));
The subsystem and chip reset levels are never asserted together once armed.

Why induction fails without R: each level flag is updated only at the threshold crossings, never recomputed from the count, so P alone is not inductive.

Counterexample to induction (CTI) state:
- armed=1, chip_rst_q=1, sub_rst_q=0, fault_cnt=T1-1=3, decay_tmr=0.
- It satisfies P, since sub_rst_q=0.
- It violates R, since chip_rst_q=1 while fault_cnt<T2.
- It is held indefinitely while en=0.

Step to violation: with en=1 and rx_fault=1, fault_cnt becomes 4==T1, so sub_rst_q<=1. chip_rst_q is untouched because there is no decay crossing. The next state has armed && sub_rst_q && chip_rst_q, which violates P.

Supplying R as a strengthening invariant makes P 1-inductive. R pins the two level flags to disjoint ranges of fault_cnt, and every update preserves R.

What it is: Bidirectional associative map: Holds paired fields that can each be searched in parallel, so a lookup by either key or value returns the address and the partner field, keeping two content arrays and valid bits.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module pix_palette_bimap: a bidirectional palette map for an FPGA OLED pixel-art renderer. Each of 48 entries pairs an 8-bit RGB332 colour code (key) with an 8-bit glyph/palette tag (value). A lookup can search either array in parallel: by colour it returns the address and tag, by tag it returns the address and colour. Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (when low, all state holds), op[1:0] (00 lookup-by-colour, 01 lookup-by-tag, 10 insert, 11 flush), din_a[7:0], din_b[7:0]. State: key_mem[0:47][7:0], val_mem[0:47][7:0], valid[47:0], wr_ptr[5:0] (wraps at 47), hit_q (1 bit, registered hit), addr_q[5:0], partner_q[7:0], ever_ins (1 bit, shadow set on first insert, cleared by flush), pre_flush (1 bit, resets to 1, cleared on the first flush and never set again). Reset: valid=0, hit_q=0, ever_ins=0, pre_flush=1, wr_ptr=0. With en=1, insert writes key_mem[wr_ptr]=din_a, val_mem[wr_ptr]=din_b, sets valid[wr_ptr], sets ever_ins, and advances wr_ptr. A lookup sets hit_q to the OR over i of (valid[i] and the selected array[i]==din_a), with the lowest matching index giving addr_q and the partner field giving partner_q. Flush clears valid, hit_q, ever_ins and pre_flush. Relation R (holds by construction): ((|valid) -> ever_ins) && (hit_q -> ever_ins). No valid bit can be set and no hit can be registered without a prior insert, and flush clears all three together. Property P (precedence, before-flush scope): a registered hit observed now requires that an insert happened earlier. Written as: always @(posedge clk) assert (!(pre_flush && hit_q) || ever_ins); pre_flush is listed as an antecedent. Why induction fails without R, with a counterexample to induction (CTI): valid[5]=1, key_mem[5]=8'hE0, ever_ins=0, hit_q=0, pre_flush=1, other entries invalid. This state satisfies P because hit_q=0. It violates R because a valid bit is set while ever_ins=0. It can be held for any number of cycles with en=0, which also defeats induction depth. Then one step with en=1, op=00, din_a=8'hE0 registers hit_q=1 while ever_ins stays 0 and pre_flush stays 1, so P is violated. Given R, hit_q implies ever_ins directly, so P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Keypad row-drive decoder: Cycles a row counter and decodes it so one keypad row is driven low at a time while the columns are sampled, keeping the row counter and a per-row scan timer.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
CHC5 camera back-panel keypad scanner (focus/zoom/ISP-menu buttons on a 32-row x 8-column matrix). Module cam_key_scan(clk, rst, en, col_in[7:0], output row_n[31:0], output key_map). en is the scan enable; when en is low, every state register holds its value.

State registers:
- row_idx [7:0]: current row, legal range 0..31.
- scan_tmr [7:0]: per-row dwell timer, counts 0..DWELL-1 with DWELL=200.
- row_n [31:0]: registered active-low row drive. Exactly one bit is low.
- key_map [0:31][7:0]: 32-entry storage of the sampled columns for each row.

Behavior when en=1:
- scan_tmr increments.
- When scan_tmr==DWELL-1:
  - scan_tmr resets to 0.
  - key_map[row_idx] <= ~col_in.
  - nxt = (row_idx==31) ? 0 : row_idx+1.
  - row_idx <= nxt.
  - row_n <= ~(32'b1 << nxt), a 32-bit shift where shifting by 32 or more gives 0.

Reset values: row_idx=0, scan_tmr=0, row_n=32'hFFFF_FFFE.

Relation R (holds by construction): row_idx < 32 && scan_tmr < DWELL && row_n == ~(32'b1 << row_idx).

Property P (universality, global, $past style):
reg pv = 0; always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
always @(posedge clk) if (pv) assert (row_n == $past(row_n) || row_n == {$past(row_n)[30:0], $past(row_n)[31]});
In words, the row drive either holds or rotates left by exactly one row. It never jumps, never drives two rows, and never releases all rows.

Why P is true: under R, row_n is the decode of row_idx. Advancing row_idx by one, including the 31->0 wrap, rotates the single low bit left by one position.

Counterexample to induction (CTI) state, which satisfies P, violates R, and is idle-holdable:
- row_idx=40 (out of range).
- scan_tmr=199.
- row_n=32'hFFFF_FFFE (the decode of row 0, so it is inconsistent with row_idx).
- pv=1, and the past values equal the current ones.

With en=0 this state repeats unchanged for any number of cycles, and P holds trivially because row_n equals its past value. That defeats k-induction for every k. Then raise en=1:
- scan_tmr hits DWELL-1.
- nxt=41.
- row_n <= ~(32'b1<<41) = 32'hFFFF_FFFF.

The result is neither the past value (FFFF_FFFE) nor its left rotation (FFFF_FFFD), so P fails.

Giving the prover R removes this state, because row_idx must be < 32 and row_n must be its decode. With R in hand, P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Microwire interface: Implements the National Microwire half-duplex serial protocol with start bit, opcode, address and data phases, keeping a phase state register, an opcode/address shift register and a data shift register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
QPSK-modem configuration port over Microwire: a slave holding 64 entries x 64-bit of modem parameters, such as carrier DDS frequency words and Costas loop-filter gains. The host reads and writes them through the Microwire protocol.

Inputs: clk, rst (synchronous), en (one SK-edge strobe; when en=0 every state register holds its value), cs, di. Outputs: dout, do_oe.

State registers:
- phase[2:0]: IDLE=0, START=1, OPCODE=2, ADDR=3, DATA=4.
- cnt[63:0]: bits remaining in the current phase.
- oa_sr[7:0]: opcode/address shift register; opcode = oa_sr[7:6], address = oa_sr[5:0].
- dat_sr[63:0]: data shift register.
- mem[0:63][63:0]: configuration store.
- do_oe (1 bit): output-driver enable.
- wr_cnt[63:0]: count of committed writes.
- pre_commit (1 bit): resets to 1 and is cleared on the first write commit.

Behaviour, applied on each en=1 cycle:
- If cs=0, set phase<=IDLE and do_oe<=0.
- IDLE: when di=1 (start bit), go to START, then to OPCODE with cnt<=2.
- OPCODE and ADDR: shift di into oa_sr and decrement cnt. When cnt reaches 1, OPCODE goes to ADDR with cnt<=6.
- ADDR leaving to DATA (cnt=1): set cnt<=64. Set do_oe<=(opcode==READ=2'b10). For a read, also load dat_sr<=mem[addr].
- DATA, read: shift dat_sr out on dout.
- DATA, write: shift di into dat_sr. When cnt reaches 1, write mem[addr]<=dat_sr, increment wr_cnt, clear pre_commit, and return to IDLE with do_oe<=0.
- do_oe is changed only at the ADDR-to-DATA transition, on cs=0, or on leaving DATA. Otherwise it holds.

Relation R (holds by construction): do_oe == (phase==DATA && oa_sr[7:6]==2'b10). It is also true that phase<=4.

Property P: the slave never drives the line while the address is still being shifted in, which would cause bus contention on DI/DO. In a combinational block:
always @(*) if (pre_commit) assert (!(phase==3'd3 && do_oe));
Antecedent: pre_commit.

Counterexample to induction:
- State: pre_commit=1, phase=OPCODE, cnt=1, do_oe=1, oa_sr=0, all other registers 0.
- P holds, because phase is not ADDR.
- R is violated, because do_oe=1 outside DATA.
- With en=0 the state is held indefinitely. This idle self-loop defeats any bound k.
- The next en=1, cs=1 cycle moves phase to ADDR, while do_oe stays 1. P then fails while pre_commit is still 1.

Given R, P follows immediately: phase==ADDR implies do_oe==0.

What it is: Layer-2 MAC learning table: Learns source addresses with their ingress ports and looks up destination addresses in parallel to return a port, keeping MAC keys, port fields, valid bits and per-entry aging bits refreshed on hits.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module vcd_mac_learn: a 12-entry L2 learning table. Its reinterpreted VCD theme is a capture window restricted to a timestamp range, like the VCD time-range cut.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), learn_v, src_mac[31:0], src_port[3:0], look_v, dst_mac[31:0], age_tick, win_open (Q), win_close (R).

State registers:
- key[0:11][31:0]
- port[0:11][3:0]
- valid[0:11] (1 bit each)
- age[0:11] (1 bit each)
- rr_ptr[3:0], wraps 0..11
- learn_cnt[31:0]: the shadow register, a saturating count of learn events
- hit_q (1 bit): registered lookup hit
- out_port[3:0]
- win (1 bit): window register

Behaviour when en=1:
- Learn: if src_mac matches a valid entry, update its port and set its age bit. Otherwise write to the lowest invalid entry, or to entry rr_ptr if all are full, then advance rr_ptr. Set valid and age. learn_cnt increments, saturating at 32'hFFFFFFFF.
- Lookup: dst_mac is compared against all 12 valid keys in parallel. hit_q<=any match, and out_port<=the matching entry's port. A hit sets that entry's age bit.
- age_tick: entries with age=0 have valid cleared; all other age bits are cleared.
- Window: win<=1 on win_open and win<=0 on win_close (close wins on a tie). It can open and close any number of times.
- rst clears everything.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- for all i: valid[i] -> learn_cnt!=0
- hit_q -> learn_cnt!=0
It holds because valid bits are only ever set by a learn, the learn increments learn_cnt in the same cycle, and the saturating count never returns to 0.

Property P (precedence between Q and R, written as an edge check):
 assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) (win && $rose(hit_q)) |-> (learn_cnt != 0));
In words: whenever a lookup hit rises inside the open window, some learn must have happened earlier.

State that satisfies P but violates R:
- valid[5]=1, key[5]=32'hA5A5_0001, port[5]=3
- learn_cnt=0, hit_q=0, win=1
- all other valid bits 0
P holds here because hit_q is not rising. With en=0 this state is frozen indefinitely, so arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefixes exist and k-induction cannot rule it out.

Step to violation: raise en with look_v=1 and dst_mac=32'hA5A5_0001 (no learn, no age_tick, no close). Next cycle hit_q rises while win=1 and learn_cnt==0, so P fails.

Why R is needed: P alone says nothing about valid bits, so the inductive step admits this unreachable state. Adding R as a strengthening invariant excludes it, because any valid entry forces learn_cnt!=0, and P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Hilbert transformer: Produces a 90-degree phase-shifted quadrature copy of a real input with an antisymmetric FIR, holding a delay line of input samples and a matched delay that aligns the in-phase output.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
WAL-style 'quadrature probe': a 4-tap Hilbert transformer that a waveform analyzer arms with a capture request. It reports when the delay line has refilled with fresh samples, so the analytic (I,Q) pair is trustworthy.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (global enable; when low every register holds), x_in[63:0], cap_req (Q), stop (R, may never arrive).

State registers:
- d0..d3 [63:0]: 4-entry sample delay line, shifted on en.
- i_dly [63:0]: matched delay, which takes d1 so that I aligns with the FIR centre.
- q_out [63:0]: antisymmetric FIR output, (d0 - d3) + 3*(d1 - d2).
- cnt [63:0]: completion countdown.
- fill [2:0]: fresh samples seen since arming, range 0..4.
- pending (1): request outstanding.
- win (1): property window.

Behaviour (all updates only when en=1):
- Accept: when cap_req && !pending, set pending=1, fill=0, cnt=5, win=1.
- While pending, each cycle sets fill<=fill+1 and cnt<=cnt-1.
- Completion: if fill+1==4, then pending<=0 and cnt<=0 in the same cycle, and done is pulsed.
- Window: stop clears win unless an accept happens that cycle, in which case accept has priority. Otherwise win holds.
- Reset: everything is 0.

Relation R (by construction): pending -> (cnt + fill == 5 && fill <= 3). Also !pending -> cnt == 0.

Property P (after Q until R, bounded-response safety, edge form):
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) (win && $rose(cnt == 0)) |-> !pending);
The countdown may only reach zero together with completion, never while the request is still outstanding. This must hold from the accept onward, whether or not stop ever arrives.

Why P holds: under R a pending request has fill <= 3, so cnt >= 2 before the step. The cycle where cnt becomes 0 is exactly the cycle where pending falls.

Counterexample to induction (CTI):
- State: win=1, pending=1, fill=0, cnt=1, with arbitrary data registers.
- R is violated, since cnt + fill = 1, not 5.
- P holds in this state, because cnt != 0 and so there is no rose.
- With en=0 the state is frozen indefinitely, which satisfies P for any induction depth.
- Next step with en=1: cnt becomes 0 and fill becomes 1. Since fill+1 != 4, pending stays 1 and win stays 1.
- So $rose(cnt==0) fires while pending=1, violating P.

Therefore k-induction fails without R and succeeds once R is supplied as a strengthening invariant. The datapath registers (d0..d3, i_dly, q_out) are irrelevant noise for the prover.

What it is: Serializer: Converts a parallel word into a high-rate serial bitstream using a load register, shift register, and bit counter.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
FemtoRV32 SoC debug trace serializer: a 32-bit instruction word captured from the Quark core's fetch bus is shifted out MSB-first on a trace pin. A three-step order applies: arm (latch the word), start (copy it to the shifter), finish (all 32 bits sent).

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), arm, start, ack, flush, data_in[31:0]. Output: sout = shift_reg[31].

State registers:
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, SHIFT=2, DONE=3
- load_reg[31:0]
- shift_reg[31:0]
- bit_cnt[31:0]
- armed_f, started_f, finished_f (1 bit each)
- win (1 bit, the property window)

Behaviour (only when en=1):
- IDLE & arm: load_reg<=data_in, armed_f<=1, phase<=ARMED, win<=1. The arm event is Q.
- ARMED & start: shift_reg<=load_reg, bit_cnt<=0, started_f<=1, phase<=SHIFT.
- SHIFT: shift_reg<=shift_reg<<1 and bit_cnt<=bit_cnt+1. When bit_cnt==31: finished_f<=1, phase<=DONE.
- DONE & ack: clear all three flags, phase<=IDLE. win is unchanged.
- flush: clears win, all flags and phase to IDLE, and has priority. flush is R and may never arrive.
- rst: zeroes everything.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- phase==IDLE -> !armed_f & !started_f & !finished_f
- phase==ARMED -> armed_f & !started_f & !finished_f
- phase==SHIFT -> armed_f & started_f & !finished_f & bit_cnt<=31
- phase==DONE -> armed_f & started_f & finished_f

Property P (scope: after arm until flush; two assertions):
- A1: assert (win && finished_f -> started_f)
- A2: assert (win && started_f -> armed_f)

Neither assertion is inductive alone, because each depends on how phase relates to the flags. With R as a strengthening invariant, both become 1-inductive.

Counterexample to induction for A1:
- State: phase=SHIFT, bit_cnt=31, armed_f=0, started_f=0, finished_f=0, win=1, other registers arbitrary.
- It satisfies A1 and A2 (both antecedents are false) but violates R (SHIFT without started_f).
- It is held indefinitely with en=0.
- With en=1 and flush=0 it steps to phase=DONE with finished_f=1 and started_f=0, violating A1.

Counterexample to induction for A2:
- State: phase=ARMED, armed_f=0, started_f=0, finished_f=0, win=1.
- It satisfies both assertions, violates R, and is held with en=0.
- With en=1 and start=1 it reaches started_f=1 with armed_f=0, violating A2.

The window register win appears in both antecedents. Because flush may never come, both assertions must hold forever once arm has occurred.

What it is: GF(2^m) multiplier: Multiplies two binary-field elements with polynomial reduction, keeping an accumulator register and the irreducible-polynomial configuration.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
LiteX-style CSR peripheral 'GF8MulCore': a bit-serial GF(2^8) shift-and-add multiplier with a software-programmable reduction polynomial and a watchdog countdown that bounds response latency.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (global enable; when low ALL state registers hold their values), req, a_in[7:0], b_in[7:0], poly_in[7:0] (low 8 bits of the irreducible polynomial, x^8 implicit), poly_we.

State registers:
- acc[7:0]: product accumulator
- a_reg[7:0]: multiplicand, multiplied by x each step (shift left; XOR poly if bit 7 was set)
- b_reg[7:0]: multiplier, shifted right each step
- poly[7:0]: irreducible-polynomial configuration (written when en && poly_we && !busy)
- bitcnt[3:0]: remaining multiply steps
- deadline[3:0]: response countdown
- busy (1 bit): request outstanding
- armed (1 bit): sticky, set on the first accepted request, never cleared except by rst
Output: done pulse and result = acc.

Behaviour (all updates gated by en): on reset everything is 0. Accept when en && req && !busy: busy<=1, armed<=1, acc<=0, a_reg<=a_in, b_reg<=b_in, bitcnt<=8, deadline<=9. While en && busy && bitcnt!=0: if b_reg[0] then acc<=acc^a_reg; a_reg<=xtime(a_reg,poly); b_reg<=b_reg>>1; bitcnt<=bitcnt-1; deadline<=deadline-1. While en && busy && bitcnt==0: busy<=0, deadline<=0, done<=1.

Relation R (holds by construction): busy -> (deadline == bitcnt + 1) && (bitcnt <= 8); and !busy -> deadline == 0 && bitcnt == 0.

Property P (after-Q scope, Q = first accepted request, tracked by armed; unclocked module-level form):
assert property (!(armed && busy) || (deadline != 4'd0));
i.e. once armed, the countdown never expires while the multiply request is still outstanding.

Why k-induction fails without R: consider state armed=1, busy=1, bitcnt=5, deadline=1 (other data arbitrary). It satisfies P (deadline!=0) but violates R (deadline != bitcnt+1). With en=0 the state is held indefinitely, so an induction trace of any length k can sit in this state satisfying P on every step. Asserting en for one cycle with bitcnt!=0 performs a step: bitcnt->4, deadline->0, busy stays 1, so armed && busy && deadline==0 violates P. Supplying R as a lemma excludes this state (busy forces deadline=bitcnt+1>=1, and both decrement together, reaching deadline=1 exactly when bitcnt=0, where busy clears), making P 1-inductive.

What it is: Command/address parity retry unit: Computes parity on each issued command and address, logs commands in a replay history and re-issues them after the DRAM signals a parity alert, holding the history buffer, a replay pointer and an error status register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module atalanta_ca_retry: a DDR command/address parity retry unit with a built-in self-check that compares two redundant issue counters, much as an ATPG tool watches for stuck-at faults.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (global enable; when low every register holds), cmd_valid, cmd_addr[63:0], alert_n (DRAM parity alert, active low).

Outputs: ca_out[63:0], ca_par.

State registers:
- hist[0:31] (64-bit each): replay history of issued command/address words.
- hist_par[0:31] (1-bit each): even parity of each stored word.
- wr_ptr[4:0]: next history slot to write.
- replay_ptr[4:0]: next slot to re-issue.
- replaying (1).
- issue_cnt[63:0]: commands issued.
- log_cnt[63:0]: commands logged; a redundant shadow of issue_cnt.
- err_status[63:0]: error status register. Bit0 is a sticky counter-mismatch flag, bit1 is a sticky parity-alert flag, bits[63:32] hold the replay count.
- no_alert_yet (1): reset to 1, cleared the first time alert_n is sampled low while en is high.

Behaviour (all updates only when en is high):
- Issue: when cmd_valid is high and replaying is low, ca_out <= cmd_addr, ca_par <= ^cmd_addr, hist[wr_ptr] <= cmd_addr, hist_par[wr_ptr] <= ^cmd_addr, and wr_ptr, issue_cnt and log_cnt all increment.
- Alert: on an alert, replaying <= 1, replay_ptr <= wr_ptr - 1, err_status[1] <= 1 and no_alert_yet <= 0.
- Replay: while replaying, the unit re-drives hist[replay_ptr] together with hist_par, steps replay_ptr and increments err_status[63:32]. Replaying stops when replay_ptr wraps back to wr_ptr.
- Self-check: every enabled cycle, err_status[0] <= err_status[0] | (issue_cnt != log_cnt).

Relation R (holds by construction, since both counters reset to 0 and increment under the same condition): issue_cnt == log_cnt.

Property P (before-R scope; event = first parity alert; antecedent no_alert_yet):
always @(*) assert (!no_alert_yet || err_status == 64'd0);
Before any alert, no bit of the error status register is set.

Why k-induction fails without R:
- Consider this state: no_alert_yet=1, err_status=0, issue_cnt=5, log_cnt=3, replaying=0, with the other registers arbitrary.
- It satisfies P and violates R.
- With en held low it repeats indefinitely, which gives an induction trace of any length on which P holds.
- One enabled cycle with alert_n high then sets err_status[0]=1 while no_alert_yet is still 1, violating P.
- Given R as a lemma, the mismatch term is always 0, err_status[0] stays 0, and only an alert can set bit1 or the replay count. Because an alert simultaneously clears no_alert_yet, P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Stochastic computing ALU: Operates on random bitstreams whose density encodes values, using AND gates for multiplication and multiplexers for scaled addition, then counts output ones to recover a result; it keeps the output ones counter and a stream-length counter.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Stochastic parking-load estimator (sc_park_alu). It estimates combined car-park load from random bitstreams. Each cycle the multiplier output m = uni_bit & util_bit, where util_bit is the bitstream for the university-car fraction. The scaled adder picks s = win_bit ? vis_bit : m, where win_bit is the time-of-day window stream. Inputs: clk, rst, en, arm_req, start_req, uni_bit, util_bit, vis_bit, win_bit. When en is low, every register holds its value.

State registers:
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, RUN=2, DONE=3.
- arm_seen (1 bit) and start_seen (1 bit): sticky flags.
- done_seen (1 bit).
- len_cnt[15:0]: stream-length counter.
- ones_cnt[15:0]: output-ones counter.
- log_q[0:7][15:0]: an 8-entry result log.
- log_ptr[2:0].

Behaviour when en=1:
- IDLE with arm_req: go to ARMED and set arm_seen.
- ARMED with start_req: go to RUN, set start_seen, and clear len_cnt and ones_cnt.
- In RUN: len_cnt increments and ones_cnt += s.
- When phase==RUN and len_cnt==699 (a 700-sample stream, one per parking space): go to DONE, set done_seen, write ones_cnt into log_q[log_ptr], and increment log_ptr.
- DONE with arm_req: set phase=ARMED. The sticky flags stay set.
- rst clears everything.

Relation R (holds by construction), a conjunction of:
- (phase!=IDLE) -> arm_seen
- (phase==RUN || phase==DONE) -> start_seen
- (len_cnt!=0) -> start_seen
- start_seen -> arm_seen
- done_seen -> start_seen
- ones_cnt <= len_cnt
- len_cnt <= 700

Property P (chain precedence, global, no arming register):
always @(posedge clk) assert ((!done_seen || start_seen) && (!start_seen || arm_seen));
In words, a finish is never observed without a start, and a start never without an arm.

Counterexample to induction: phase=RUN, len_cnt=699, ones_cnt=0, arm_seen=0, start_seen=0, done_seen=0.
- P holds, because every flag is 0.
- R is violated, because phase==RUN while start_seen=0.
- With en=0 the state is held unchanged for any number of cycles. This gives an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix, which defeats k-induction for any k.
- With en=1 the design sees phase==RUN and len_cnt==699. It moves to DONE and sets done_seen=1 while start_seen stays 0, so P fails.

Once R is supplied as a strengthening invariant, that state is excluded and P becomes 1-inductive. Every transition preserves R: start_seen is set exactly when entering RUN, arm_seen is set exactly when leaving IDLE, and done_seen is set only from RUN.

What it is: Clocked SR flip-flop: Keeps one state bit that is set by the S input or cleared by the R input, with changes taking effect only on the active clock edge.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module metron_trace_latch: a bank of six clocked SR flip-flops, styled as Metron's 'traced signal' latches. Each latch marks that a C++ field has been written in the current tick, and a 32-bit occupancy counter tracks how many are marked.

Inputs:
- clk, rst (synchronous, active high)
- en: the enable; when low, all state holds.
- s[5:0] and r[5:0]: per-latch set and reset. Set has priority.
- trace_on: the window-open event Q.
- trace_off: the window-close event R. It may never arrive.

State registers:
- q[5:0]: the six SR flip-flop bits.
- live_cnt[31:0]: occupancy counter.
- win (1 bit): the after-Q-until-R window register.

Behavior on posedge clk:
- If rst: q=0, live_cnt=0, win=0.
- Else if en:
  - For each i: q_n[i] = s[i] ? 1 : (r[i] ? 0 : q[i]).
  - live_cnt <= live_cnt + popcount(q_n & ~q) - popcount(q & ~q_n).
  - q <= q_n.
  - win <= trace_on ? 1 : (trace_off ? 0 : win).
- Else: everything holds.

Relation R (by construction): live_cnt == popcount(q). The counter is updated by exactly the number of bits that rise minus the number that fall, so it always equals the number of set latches.

Property P (Bounded Existence, at most 6, scoped after trace_on until trace_off, unclocked module-level form):
  assert property (!win || live_cnt <= 32'd6);
The bound 6 is far below the 2^32-1 that the width allows. It is a real fact only because live_cnt mirrors a 6-bit popcount. P holds from trace_on onward whether or not trace_off ever arrives, and win is the antecedent.

Counterexample-to-induction state:
- win=1, q=6'b000000, live_cnt=6.
- P holds, since 6 <= 6.
- R is violated, since popcount(q)=0 but live_cnt=6.
- With en=0, the state is held unchanged for any number of cycles, so an induction trace of any depth k can sit in it.

Then take one step with en=1, s=6'b000001, r=0, trace_on=0, trace_off=0:
- q becomes 000001 and live_cnt becomes 7.
- win stays 1, so P fails (7 > 6).

k-induction alone therefore cannot prove P. Supplying R as a strengthening invariant gives live_cnt = popcount(q) <= 6, which makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: I2C spike suppression filter: Removes glitches shorter than a programmed width from SCL and SDA inputs, keeping a per-line sample shift register, a stable-output register and a filter-length configuration register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module mips_i2c_deglitch: a spike-filter front end for the I2C controller peripheral of a NaiveMIPS-style SoC. It has inputs clk, rst, en, scl_in, sda_in, cfg_we and cfg_din[7:0], and outputs scl_o and sda_o. When en is low, every register holds its value, including configuration writes and the arm register.

State registers:
- sh_scl[3:0], sh_sda[3:0]: 4-entry sample shift registers. Each cycle the line's input shifts in, and the line's sample is sh_x[3].
- st_scl, st_sda (1 bit each): stable-output registers, driven out as scl_o and sda_o.
- cnt_scl[7:0], cnt_sda[7:0]: per-line glitch-width counters.
- flen[7:0]: filter-length configuration register. Reset value is 3.
- armed (1 bit): sticky register.
- pv (1 bit): past-valid register.

Behaviour when en is high:
- Configuration write: if cfg_we, then flen <= (cfg_din > 12 ? 12 : cfg_din), and both counters are cleared.
- Line update otherwise, per line x:
  - If sh_x[3] differs from st_x and cnt_x >= flen, then st_x <= sh_x[3] and cnt_x <= 0.
  - If sh_x[3] differs from st_x and cnt_x < flen, then cnt_x <= cnt_x + 1.
  - If sh_x[3] equals st_x, then cnt_x <= 0.
- Event Q is the first falling edge of st_scl, i.e. the first accepted bus activity. Q sets armed, and armed is never cleared except by rst.
- pv: reg pv=0; always @(posedge clk) pv<=1.

Relation R (holds by construction): flen <= 12 && cnt_scl <= flen && cnt_sda <= flen.
- flen is only ever loaded with a clamped value.
- A counter increments only when it is strictly below flen.
- Whenever flen changes, the counters are cleared.

Property P (Bounded Existence, at most 12 < 255; after-Q scope; $past style):
always @(posedge clk) if (pv && $past(armed)) assert ($past(cnt_scl) <= 8'd12 && $past(cnt_sda) <= 8'd12);
P is true because R gives cnt <= flen <= 12.

Why P is not k-inductive alone: consider the state flen=200, cnt_scl=12, armed=1, pv=1, st_scl=0, sh_scl=4'b1111.
- It satisfies P, since cnt_scl=12 <= 12.
- It violates R, since flen > 12.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0, which supplies an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix for any induction depth k.
- When en rises, sh_scl[3] differs from st_scl and cnt_scl (12) < flen (200), so cnt_scl becomes 13.
- On the following cycle, $past(cnt_scl)=13 with $past(armed)=1, so P fails.

Supplying R as a strengthening invariant rules out flen > 12 and cnt > flen, and P becomes inductive.

invariants: (({req_tgl ^ req_s1, req_s1 ^ req_s2, req_s2 ^ tgt_seen, ack_tgl ^ ack_s1, ack_s1 ^ ack_s2}) & ({req_tgl ^ req_s1, req_s1 ^ req_s2, req_s2 ^ tgt_seen, ack_tgl ^ ack_s1, ack_s1 ^ ack_s2} - 5'd1)) == 5'd0
description:
What it is: Cross-domain register access bridge: Carries bus read/write transactions between domains by holding address, write data and read data in registers and exchanging request and response toggles through synchronizers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
LispDebugBridge: a host-side debug port that reads and writes the 16-entry, 64-bit register file of a Lisp core in a slower domain. Domains are modeled on one clock, with two-flop toggle synchronizers in each direction. All state holds when the input en is low.

State registers:
- Host side: busy(1), req_tgl(1), ack_s1(1), ack_s2(1), addr_q(4), wr_q(1), wdata_q(64), rdata_q(64), txn_cnt(64).
- Core side: req_s1(1), req_s2(1), tgt_seen(1), ack_tgl(1), regs[16](64 each).
- Verification: shadow_addr(4), shadow_wdata(64), win(1).

Operation:
- Launch (Q): when en, start, and !busy, load addr_q, wr_q and wdata_q from the inputs, flip req_tgl and set busy. In the same cycle, shadow_addr and shadow_wdata capture the same inputs and win is set.
- Core side: tgt_fire = (req_s2 != tgt_seen). On tgt_fire it writes regs[addr_q] <= wdata_q if wr_q, else captures regs[addr_q] into rdata_q. It then sets tgt_seen <= req_s2 and flips ack_tgl.
- Completion (R): when ack_s2 == req_tgl while busy, clear busy, clear win and increment txn_cnt. Windows open and close once per transaction, repeatedly.

Relation R (by construction):
- win == busy.
- busy == (req_tgl != ack_s2).
- The token chain req_tgl, req_s1, req_s2, tgt_seen (== ack_tgl), ack_s1, ack_s2 has at most one value change along it, i.e. it reads as 1…10…0 or 0…01…1.
- win -> (addr_q == shadow_addr && wdata_q == shadow_wdata).

Property P (precedence, window-scoped, two assertions): the core may act only on what the host launched earlier.
- A1: assert (win && tgt_fire) -> addr_q == shadow_addr.
- A2: assert (win && tgt_fire && wr_q) -> wdata_q == shadow_wdata.
- The window register win appears in both antecedents.
- Neither is inductive alone: between fires, nothing in either assertion constrains addr_q or wdata_q. Both are closed by the same clause of R, win -> (addr_q == shadow_addr && wdata_q == shadow_wdata), together with the handshake clauses.

Counterexample to induction (violates R, satisfies P):
- State: win=1, busy=1, req_tgl=1, req_s1=1, req_s2=0, tgt_seen=0, ack_tgl=0, ack_s1=0, ack_s2=0, wr_q=1, addr_q=3, shadow_addr=5, wdata_q=0, shadow_wdata=1.
- P holds because tgt_fire=0.
- R is violated because the addresses and data differ inside the window.
- With en=0 the state is frozen indefinitely.
- With en=1, req_s2 becomes 1 on the next step, so tgt_fire=1. With win still 1, both A1 and A2 fail (3≠5 and 0≠1).

What it is: Fletcher checksum unit: Computes a Fletcher checksum over a byte stream using two modular running-sum registers that are updated on every input word.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module fletcher_seg_offload: a TCP/UDP-style checksum offload engine that computes a Fletcher-32 over a packet segment of at most 24 words of 128 bits each.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds its value), arm (a header descriptor is accepted), in_valid, in_last, in_data[127:0].

State registers:
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, RUN=2, DONE=3.
- armed_seen (1 bit).
- started_seen (1 bit).
- fin_q (1 bit): the checksum-valid output.
- cnt[4:0]: words consumed, 0..24.
- sumA[15:0] and sumB[15:0]: Fletcher running sums.

Behaviour, applied only when en=1; rst clears everything:
- IDLE with arm: go to ARMED and set armed_seen<=1.
- ARMED with in_valid: go to RUN, set started_seen<=1 and cnt<=1, and fold the word.
- RUN with in_valid: fold the word and increment cnt. If in_last or cnt==23, go to DONE and set fin_q<=1.
- DONE: go to IDLE and clear armed_seen, started_seen, fin_q and cnt. sumA and sumB are kept as the output.

Folding a word: its eight 16-bit lanes are added one at a time, combinationally. For each lane, sumA=(sumA+lane) mod 65535, then sumB=(sumB+sumA) mod 65535.

Relation R holds by construction:
- (phase!=IDLE) -> armed_seen
- (phase==RUN || phase==DONE) -> started_seen
- started_seen -> armed_seen
- fin_q -> (phase==DONE)
- (phase==RUN) -> (cnt>=1 && cnt<=23)

Property P (chain precedence: arm, then start, then finish). It holds globally, with no arming register:
always @(posedge clk) assert (!fin_q || (armed_seen && started_seen));

A finish can never be observed unless both an arm and a start have already happened.

Why P is not k-inductive alone. Take this state:
- phase=RUN, cnt=23
- armed_seen=0, started_seen=1
- fin_q=0
- sumA and sumB arbitrary

The state:
- Satisfies P, because fin_q=0.
- Violates R, because phase is RUN but armed_seen=0.
- Can be held indefinitely by keeping en=0, since all state freezes. This produces arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefixes, so no depth k excludes it.
- Steps to a violation of P. With en=1 and in_valid=1, the RUN branch sees cnt==23, moves to DONE and sets fin_q<=1, while armed_seen stays 0.

Given R as a strengthening invariant, the induction closes. fin_q=1 is only set on a RUN-to-DONE transition. R guarantees that RUN implies both armed_seen and started_seen. Neither flag is cleared until DONE also clears fin_q.

What it is: Performance counter block: Counts selected microarchitectural events in programmable counters with per-counter event-select registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module ol_flow_perfmon: a performance-counter block for an OpenLane-style flow sequencer. Eight event lines ev[7:0] come from the flow: synth_done, floorplan_ok, place_iter, cts_buf, route_iter, drc_viol, lvs_mismatch, gds_write. Four programmable counters ctr0..ctr3 (16-bit each) each have a 3-bit event-select register sel0..sel3 (written via cfg_we/cfg_idx[1:0]/cfg_sel[2:0]). When a counter wraps from 16'hFFFF to 0, a 16-bit snapshot word {cnt_id[1:0], cycle_stamp[13:0]} is pushed into a 64-entry overflow log (mem[0:63], 16-bit). Software drains it with rd_en. clr_all zeroes the counters and the log.

State registers: ctr0..ctr3 [15:0], sel0..sel3 [2:0], stamp [13:0], mem [63:0][15:0], wr_ptr [6:0], rd_ptr [6:0], occ [6:0] (occupancy count), pre_clr (1 bit, reset 1), pv (1 bit, reset 0). Input en is the idle/enable: when en=0 every register except pv holds its value (pv still sets).

Flags: empty = (occ == 0). full = ((wr_ptr - rd_ptr) == 7'd64), computed 7-bit modulo. A push happens only when !full. A pop happens only when rd_en && !empty. Every push increments wr_ptr and occ. Every pop increments rd_ptr and decrements occ. A simultaneous push and pop leaves occ unchanged. clr_all, when en is high, zeroes wr_ptr, rd_ptr and occ.

Relation R (holds by construction): occ == (wr_ptr - rd_ptr) mod 128, and occ <= 64.

Scope register: pre_clr starts 1 and is cleared the first time en && clr_all occurs. It stays 0 after that.

Property P: always @(posedge clk) if (pv && $past(pre_clr)) assert(!($past(full) && $past(empty))). In words: before the first clear, the log was never reported full and empty in the same cycle. The antecedents are pv and $past(pre_clr).

CTI state (satisfies P, violates R): occ = 1, wr_ptr = 65, rd_ptr = 0, so the pointer difference is 65. Then full = 0 and empty = 0, so P holds. R is violated because 1 != 65. Also set pre_clr = 1 and pv = 1. With en = 0 this state holds indefinitely, and P stays true while it is held.

Step to violation: assert en = 1 and rd_en = 1, with no overflow push and no clr_all. The pop is allowed because empty = 0. Next state: occ = 0 and rd_ptr = 1, so the difference is 64. Now empty = 1 and full = 1, with pre_clr still 1. On the following edge, $past(full) && $past(empty) is true and P fails.

k-induction cannot exclude this state without R: it can be held with en = 0 for arbitrarily many steps that all satisfy P. Supplying R, occ == wr_ptr - rd_ptr, makes P inductive.

What it is: GPIO port: Provides software-controlled pin output, input sampling, and direction, keeping output-data, direction, and input-capture registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module lfsr_gpio: a 32-bit GPIO port with a registered pin driver and a 3-entry boxcar input-capture history. Themed on ZipCPU's moving-average filter.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (global enable/idle: when en=0 every register holds its value), wr_out, wr_dir, wr_lock, wr_unlock, wdata[31:0], pins_in[31:0], sample.

State registers:
- out_data[31:0]: software output value.
- dir[31:0]: direction mask, 1 = output.
- pin_drive[31:0]: registered pad driver.
- cap0, cap1, cap2[31:0]: 3-entry input-capture shift line.
- box_sum[33:0]: running boxcar sum of the three captures.
- lock_win[0]: the window register.

Behavior on each cycle with en=1:
- wr_out loads out_data; wr_dir loads dir.
- pin_drive <= out_data & dir, so it is recomputed from the current registers every enabled cycle.
- When sample is high, the capture line shifts in pins_in & ~dir, and box_sum <= box_sum + new - cap2.
- wr_lock sets lock_win (Q). wr_unlock clears it (R, with priority to unlock). Software can lock and unlock any number of times.
- Reset clears everything.

Relation R (holds by construction): pin_drive == (out_data & dir). Proof sketch: after reset all three are 0. On every enabled cycle pin_drive is reloaded from the pre-update out_data & dir. A write changes out_data or dir, so $stable fails that cycle and P is vacuous. On the next cycle pin_drive catches up. Any cycle in which both out_data and dir were unchanged therefore already sees R. Strictly, R holds in every state whose previous cycle had no out/dir write; it is stated as the strengthening lemma: (!$past(wr_out|wr_dir) || !$past(en)) -> pin_drive == (out_data & dir).

Property P (universality, window-scoped, $stable style):
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) (lock_win && $past(lock_win) && $stable(out_data) && $stable(dir)) |-> $stable(pin_drive));
Meaning: while the lock window is open, if the software-visible output and direction registers did not change, the physical pin driver must not change either. lock_win is listed in the antecedent.

Counterexample to induction (CTI) without R:
- State: lock_win=1, out_data=32'h0, dir=32'hFFFF_FFFF, pin_drive=32'h0000_0001. Captures and sum are arbitrary but consistent.
- It satisfies P: if it is held for several cycles with en=0, every register is stable, so the consequent holds.
- It violates R: pin_drive != out_data & dir = 0.
- It steps to a violation of P. Take a cycle with en=1 and no writes (wr_* = 0). out_data, dir and lock_win stay stable, but pin_drive reloads to 0. $stable(pin_drive) fails inside the window.
- k-induction cannot exclude this: arbitrarily long idle (en=0) prefixes keep the bad state stable, so no induction depth k suffices.

With the R lemma supplied, the step is closed: stable out_data/dir implies pin_drive already equals out_data & dir and reloads the same value.

What it is: Pulse-swallow counter: Combines a dual-modulus prescaler with a program counter and a swallow counter to realize an overall division ratio of N times P plus S; it keeps the program count register and the swallow count register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module hls_pixclk_swallow: a pulse-swallow clock divider that generates the line-buffer pixel strobe for a Halide-HLS stencil pipeline. It combines a dual-modulus 8/9 prescaler, a program counter and a swallow counter, giving an overall ratio of N*8+S per output strobe.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), load, N[7:0], S[7:0].

State registers:
- pre_cnt[3:0]: prescaler count.
- p_cnt[7:0]: program count.
- s_cnt[7:0]: swallow count.
- n_reg[7:0], s_reg[7:0]: latched N and S.
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, STARTED=2, DONE=3.
- armed_seen, started_seen: 1-bit step records.
- q_seen: 1-bit sticky scope register.

Behavior (all updates only when en=1):
- Prescaler: pre_cnt counts up and reaches terminal tc at 8 when s_cnt!=0 (divide by 9). Otherwise tc is at 7 (divide by 8). pre_cnt returns to 0 on tc.
- Counters: on tc, s_cnt decrements if it is nonzero, and p_cnt decrements. When p_cnt reaches 0, the module emits strobe and reloads p_cnt=n_reg, s_cnt=s_reg.
- load:
  - latches n_reg, s_reg, p_cnt, s_cnt and clears pre_cnt;
  - sets phase=ARMED and armed_seen=1, clears started_seen;
  - sets q_seen=1, which is never cleared afterwards (event Q = first load).
- Phase steps:
  - ARMED to STARTED on the first tc; only this transition sets started_seen=1.
  - STARTED to DONE when the decrement makes p_cnt hit 0 (the strobe).
  - DONE returns to ARMED only on load.
  - IDLE ignores tc.
- rst clears everything.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- (phase==STARTED || phase==DONE) -> started_seen.
- phase!=IDLE -> armed_seen.

Property P (chain precedence arm, then start, then finish, scoped after Q):
always @(*) assert (!(q_seen && phase==2'd3) || (started_seen && armed_seen));

Why k-induction fails without R:
- Take the state q_seen=1, phase=STARTED, armed_seen=1, started_seen=0, p_cnt=1, s_cnt=0, pre_cnt=7, with load=0.
- P holds there, because phase is not DONE.
- R is violated, because the phase is STARTED while started_seen=0.
- With en=0 the state is held indefinitely, so arbitrarily long induction prefixes all satisfy P.
- One step with en=1 and load=0 fires tc (pre_cnt==7 and s_cnt==0), decrements p_cnt to 0, and moves phase to DONE.
- started_seen stays 0, since only the ARMED-to-STARTED transition sets it. P is then violated.
- Adding R as a strengthening invariant makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: eFuse/OTP controller: Sequences programming and sensing of one-time-programmable bits, keeping a shadow register of read fuse values and a program state machine.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module dnn_wfuse_ctrl: an OTP/eFuse controller that burns the 8 quantization-scale/model-key words of a DNN accelerator's weight-buffer config and keeps a sensed shadow copy. Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (when low every register holds its value), prog_req, prog_addr[2:0], prog_data[31:0], lock_req, sense_req. State registers: fuse_shadow[0:7] (8 x 32-bit shadow of the fuse words), prog_done[7:0] (one burned-flag per word), prog_cnt[31:0] (number of burned words before lock, reused as a sense-access counter after lock), fsm[1:0] (IDLE/BURN/SENSE), and pre_lock (1 bit, reset to 1). Reset values: shadows 0, prog_done 0, prog_cnt 0, fsm IDLE, pre_lock 1. Behaviour when en=1. In IDLE, if pre_lock and prog_req and !prog_done[prog_addr], go to BURN. In BURN, write fuse_shadow[prog_addr] <= prog_data, set prog_done[prog_addr], increment prog_cnt, and return to IDLE. A program request for an already burned word is ignored, since the fuse is one-time. lock_req clears pre_lock for good; this is the scope event. After lock, sense_req goes to SENSE, which re-reads the shadow and increments prog_cnt as an access counter. prog_cnt is therefore unbounded after lock. Relation R, holding by construction while pre_lock=1: prog_cnt == popcount(prog_done), which implies prog_cnt <= 8. The counter and the flag mask are updated in the same BURN cycle, and a bit can only be set if it was previously clear. Property P, in the bounded-existence 'at most 8' pattern, where 8 is far below the 2^32 range of prog_cnt; antecedent pre_lock: always @(posedge clk) assert (!pre_lock || prog_cnt <= 32'd8); Counterexample to induction (CTI): pre_lock=1, fsm=IDLE, prog_cnt=8, prog_done=8'b0111_1111. This satisfies P (8 <= 8) but violates R, because popcount is 7. With en=0 the state is frozen indefinitely. When en=1 with prog_req=1 and prog_addr=7, the FSM enters BURN because word 7 is unburned. On the next edge prog_cnt becomes 9 while pre_lock is still 1, violating P. k-induction on P alone cannot exclude this state: an idle prefix of any length can lead into it. Supplying R (prog_cnt == popcount(prog_done) while pre_lock) makes P inductive.

What it is: Data bus inversion encoder: Inverts a byte lane on write when more than half its bits would be driven low and restores data on read, keeping the per-lane DBI flag registers for the current beat.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module issie_dbi_lane: a 64-bit (8 byte-lane) data bus inversion encoder modelling a schematic-simulator bus probe. Each write encodes the word for the wire and keeps a restored-data shadow, so the read path can show the restored data and the user can check it against the bus.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (holds ALL state when low), wr, wdata[63:0], q_start, r_stop.

State registers:
- bus_q[63:0]: encoded word driven on the bus.
- dbi_q[7:0]: per-lane DBI flags for the current beat.
- plain_q[63:0]: restored data.
- beat_cnt[63:0]: count of write beats.
- win (1 bit): observation window.

Behaviour, only when en=1:
- Lane encoding: for lane i, zeros_i = 8 - popcount(wdata[8i+:8]). The flag f_i = (zeros_i > 4). The encoded lane is wdata lane ^ {8{f_i}}.
- On wr: bus_q <= encoded word; dbi_q <= f; plain_q <= wdata; beat_cnt <= beat_cnt + 1.
- Window: win <= q_start ? 1 : (r_stop ? 0 : win). Set wins if both are high.
- Read output: rdata = bus_q ^ X(dbi_q), which is combinational. X(d) replicates each d[i] across byte i.
- Reset clears all registers to 0, which is consistent with R.

Relation R (holds by construction): plain_q == bus_q ^ X(dbi_q). This holds because every write loads all three registers together from the same wdata, and the encoding is an involution per lane.

Property P (universality, scope after Q=q_start until R=r_stop, which may never arrive; $stable style):
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) (win && $past(win) && $stable(bus_q) && $stable(dbi_q)) |-> $stable(plain_q));
Meaning: inside the window, if the encoded bus word and the flags did not change, the restored data did not change either. P is true because, by R, plain_q is a function of bus_q and dbi_q.

Counterexample to induction (satisfies P, violates R):
- State: win=1, bus_q=64'hFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF, dbi_q=8'h00, plain_q=64'h0, beat_cnt arbitrary. R fails, since bus^X(dbi) is all-ones but plain_q is 0.
- Held while idle: with en=0 every register is unchanged, so plain_q is stable and P holds for any number of k-induction steps. The window stays open because r_stop is ignored.
- Step to violation: en=1, wr=1, wdata=all-ones, q_start=0, r_stop=0. Every lane has 0 zeros, so no lane is inverted.
- Result: bus_q stays all-ones and dbi_q stays 0, both stable, while plain_q changes 0 -> all-ones. P fails.

Giving the prover R (plain_q == bus_q ^ X(dbi_q)) excludes this state and makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: Von Neumann debiaser: Removes bias from a raw random bitstream by examining non-overlapping bit pairs and emitting one bit for each unequal pair, storing the pending first bit of a pair and an output-valid flag.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Zkr-style entropy seed unit for a RISC-V CPU lab: a Von Neumann debiaser that feeds an entropy pool read through a seed CSR. Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), raw (raw bit), q_open (seed CSR read begins), r_close (seed CSR read completes).

State registers:
- half (1): the first bit of the current pair is pending.
- first_bit (1): that pending first bit.
- out_valid (1): a debiased bit is ready.
- out_bit (1): the debiased bit.
- pair_cnt (8): pairs started.
- emit_cnt (8): debiased bits consumed into the pool.
- pool (64): 64-entry 1-bit entropy shift buffer.
- wr_ptr (6): pool write pointer.
- win (1): the property window.

Behaviour on each cycle with en=1:
- If half==0: first_bit<=raw, half<=1, pair_cnt<=pair_cnt+1. If out_valid is also set, the pending debiased bit is consumed: pool[wr_ptr]<=out_bit, wr_ptr++, emit_cnt++, out_valid<=0.
- If half==1: half<=0. If raw!=first_bit, set out_bit<=first_bit and out_valid<=1.
- Separately, emit_cnt increments on every enabled cycle where out_valid==1. As written, this only happens in the half==0 branch.
- win<=1 on q_open and win<=0 on r_close, so the window can open and close any number of times. win also holds when en=0.

Relation R (holds by construction): out_valid -> !half. out_valid is set only on a step that clears half. The next enabled step sets half and clears out_valid in the same cycle.
