Property P (precedence, between q_open and r_close, $stable style): assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) win && $stable(pair_cnt) |-> $stable(emit_cnt)). In words: inside a CSR-read window, a debiased bit may be counted into the pool only if a new pair start happened on that same step. $past(pair_cnt) acts as the shadow of the earlier event.

Counterexample to induction (CTI) state: win=1, half=1, out_valid=1, pair_cnt=emit_cnt=8'h05, other registers arbitrary.
- P holds in this state.
- It violates R, since out_valid and half are both set.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0, because all registers are stable, so P holds on every idle step.
- Then apply one step with en=1: half==1 means the pair completes and pair_cnt stays 5. Because out_valid==1, emit_cnt becomes 6.
- So $stable(pair_cnt) holds while $stable(emit_cnt) fails inside the window, and P is violated.

With R as a strengthening invariant, any enabled cycle with out_valid==1 has half==0, so pair_cnt also changes and the induction closes.

What it is: Multi-lane deskew buffer: Aligns data from several lanes by delaying each lane until all have seen a common alignment marker, keeping per-lane delay FIFOs, per-lane marker-seen flags and an aligned flag.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module lane_deskew4: a 4-lane deskew buffer, framed as a lab exercise from a processor-systems course. Each lane carries 64-bit words, and one marker bit per lane flags the comma or alignment word. Lanes are delayed in their FIFOs until every lane has seen the marker. A countdown register guarantees that alignment completes within K=8 cycles of the first marker: on the cycle when cd==1, any lane that has not yet seen the marker is force-marked.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (all state holds when en=0), din[4][63:0], mk[3:0].

State registers:
- fifo[4][8][63:0]: per-lane delay storage, 8 entries per lane.
- wptr[4][2:0] and rptr[4][2:0]: per-lane FIFO pointers.
- seen[3:0]: per-lane marker-seen flags.
- aligned (1 bit).
- win (1 bit): the Q..R window register.
- cd[63:0]: the countdown.
- timeout (1 bit, sticky).

Behaviour when en=1:
- Marker on lane i sets seen[i].
- Q: the first marker while !win && !aligned sets win=1 and cd=8.
- While win && !aligned, cd decrements each cycle.
- If cd==1, the remaining seen bits are forced to 1.
- When seen==4'hF: aligned<=1 and win<=0. This is event R, which may never come if no marker ever arrives.
- timeout<=timeout | (win && !aligned && cd==0).
- Reset clears everything.

Relation R (by construction): win -> (aligned || (cd >= 1 && cd <= 8)). Also !win -> (cd==0), and timeout==0.

Property P (bounded response, after-Q-until-R, no-change style):
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff(!rst_n) (win && !aligned && $stable(aligned)) |-> $stable(timeout));
In words: from Q onward, while the request is outstanding and aligned has not changed, the expiry flag must not change. This means the countdown never expires before alignment completes, and it holds whether or not the window ever closes. The window register win is listed in the antecedent.

CTI state: win=1, aligned=0, seen=4'b0011, cd=0, timeout=0, with the FIFOs and pointers arbitrary.
- It satisfies P: timeout is stable.
- It violates R, because cd==0 while the window is open and alignment is not complete.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0.
- On the first cycle with en=1, cd==0 means the force-mark (which triggers only at cd==1) does not fire. aligned therefore stays 0 and stable, and win stays 1.
- timeout then rises from 0 to 1 while the antecedent holds, which violates P.

k-induction without R fails, because an arbitrarily long idle prefix keeps this unreachable state stable. With R strengthening the hypothesis, cd==0 is impossible inside the window, so timeout can never rise and P is inductive.

What it is: PLL startup sequencer: Steps a PLL through power-up, band calibration, loop closure and lock wait before releasing the output clock, keeping a sequence state register and a settle-time counter.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module tia_pll_seq: a PLL startup sequencer for a Tiny-Tapeout Atari 2600 clone. It brings up the PLL that makes the 3.58 MHz NTSC TIA color clock and only then releases it to the TIA/6507 domain. The input en is a global enable: when en is low, every register holds.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en, band_ok (comparator says the VCO band is in range), lock_in (raw lock detector).

Outputs: pll_pwr, cal_active, loop_closed, clk_release (high in RUN), band[3:0].

State registers:
- state[2:0]: OFF=0, PWRUP=1, BANDCAL=2, CLOSE=3, LOCKWAIT=4, RUN=5.
- cnt[15:0]: settle-time counter.
- band[3:0]: VCO band code, one of 16 bands.

Behavior (all updates only when en=1):
- OFF: go to PWRUP with cnt=0.
- PWRUP: cnt increments. When cnt>=511, go to BANDCAL with cnt=0.
- BANDCAL: if band_ok, go to CLOSE with cnt=0. Otherwise band increments (wrapping) and cnt stays 0.
- CLOSE: cnt increments. When cnt>=200, go to LOCKWAIT. cnt is deliberately NOT cleared, so the settle time spans both loop closure and lock wait.
- LOCKWAIT: if lock_in is low, go back to BANDCAL with cnt=0. Otherwise cnt increments, and when cnt>=1200, go to RUN with cnt=0.
- RUN: cnt stays 0. If lock_in drops, go back to BANDCAL.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- state==PWRUP implies cnt<=511.
- state==CLOSE implies cnt<=200.
- state==LOCKWAIT implies 201<=cnt<=1200.
- state is in OFF, BANDCAL or RUN implies cnt==0.
- state<=5.

Property P (bounded existence, global, guarded style):
always @(posedge clk) if (state==3'd4) assert (cnt <= 16'd1200);
The bound 1200 is far below the 16-bit maximum of 65535. Reset sets state=OFF and cnt=0.

Why k-induction fails without R: consider the state with state=CLOSE, cnt=16'd5000, en=0.
- It satisfies P, because the guard is false.
- It violates R, because CLOSE requires cnt<=200.
- With en held low, it persists for any number of cycles, and P holds in every one of them. So this state can begin an induction trace of any length k.
- When en goes high, CLOSE sees cnt>=200 and moves to LOCKWAIT with cnt=5001, which violates P.

The same problem arises from LOCKWAIT entries reached from CLOSE with a large cnt. P alone is therefore not k-inductive for any k. Adding R makes it inductive: CLOSE only exits at exactly cnt=200, entering LOCKWAIT with 201. LOCKWAIT then exits at 1200 before it can reach 1201.

What it is: Dependency matrix wakeup unit: Wakes waiting instructions when their producers issue by consulting a matrix of producer-consumer dependency bits, keeping the dependency matrix and per-entry pending-source flags.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
PicoSoC-themed issue-queue wakeup unit 'pico_wakeup': a 32-entry dependency-matrix scheduler for a small RISC-V core on a Mimas-style board.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle/enable: when low, every state register holds), alloc, alloc_deps[31:0] (the producer entries the new instruction waits on), issue, issue_idx[4:0].

State registers:
- valid[31:0]: entry-occupied bits.
- dep[0:31][31:0]: dependency matrix. dep[i][j]=1 means consumer i waits on producer j.
- pend[31:0]: per-entry pending-source flags.
- occ[63:0]: occupancy counter.
- wake_cnt[63:0]: free-running count of wakeup events, used as a status register.

Behavior (only when en=1; reset clears everything):
- full = &valid. This is computed from the valid bits, not from occ.
- Allocation fires when alloc && !full. It picks the lowest free index f, sets valid[f], loads dep[f] = alloc_deps & valid, and sets pend[f] = |(alloc_deps & valid).
- Issue fires when issue && valid[issue_idx] && !pend[issue_idx]. It clears valid[issue_idx] and clears column issue_idx in every row of dep. Each entry whose row becomes zero gets its pend bit cleared, and wake_cnt increments by the number of entries woken.
- occ update: occ + 1 on allocation only, occ - 1 on issue only, unchanged when both fire or neither fires.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- occ == $countones(valid).
- For all i: pend[i] == |dep[i].
- For all i: if !valid[i] then dep[i] == 0.

Property P (bounded existence, at most 32, global, guarded style):
always @(posedge clk) if (|valid) assert (occ <= 64'd32);
The bound 32 is far below the 2^64 range of occ, so P is a real fact about reachable states. It holds only because occ tracks the valid popcount and allocation is blocked by full.

Counterexample to induction (CTI):
- The state is valid = 32'h7FFF_FFFF (31 entries occupied), occ = 32, dep = 0, pend = 0.
- P holds, since valid is nonzero and 32 <= 32.
- R is violated, since popcount(valid) = 31 but occ = 32.
- With en=0 this state is held unchanged for any number of cycles, so k-induction cannot rule it out by depth alone.
- Step: raise en=1 and alloc=1 with issue=0. Since full=0, entry 31 is allocated, valid becomes 32'hFFFF_FFFF and occ becomes 33.
- The guard |valid is true, so occ <= 32 fails and P is violated.

Supplying R as a lemma excludes this state. Under R, occ = 32 implies full = 1, so allocation is blocked and occ can never exceed 32. P then becomes inductive.

What it is: Mode-selectable signed/unsigned comparator: Produces less-than, equal and greater-than flags for two operands under either two's-complement or unsigned interpretation, with a mode register selecting the interpretation and a registered flag output.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module arrow_bound_cmp: an Arrow offset-buffer cursor checker. It compares a scan cursor against a column-length bound using a mode-selectable signed/unsigned comparator, and keeps registered lt/eq/gt flags. While the cursor advances, the flags are updated incrementally rather than recomputed.

Ports: clk, rst, en (idle input: when low, ALL state holds), load, mode_in (1 = signed), cnt_in[7:0], len_in[7:0].

State registers:
- mode_r (1)
- cnt_r (8)
- len_r (8)
- lt_r (1), eq_r (1), gt_r (1)

Behaviour:
- Reset: everything is cleared to 0, then flags are taken from the comparator, so eq_r=1.
- When en && load: cnt_r<=cnt_in, len_r<=len_in, mode_r<=mode_in. The flags are set from the full comparator: lt/eq/gt of cnt_in vs len_in, interpreted as two's-complement when mode_in=1 and unsigned otherwise.
- When en && !load, an incremental step with this priority:
  1. If eq_r: eq_r<=0, gt_r<=1, and lt_r is left untouched (the cursor has passed the bound).
  2. Else if lt_r: cnt_r<=cnt_r+1. If cnt_r+1 == len_r then lt_r<=0, eq_r<=1. Because cnt_r < len_r under the active mode, cnt_r+1 cannot wrap in either interpretation.
  3. Else (gt_r): hold.
- Theme: this mirrors Fletcher's bounds check of an Arrow index against a column's offset/length.

Relation R (holds by construction): {lt_r,eq_r,gt_r} is one-hot and equals cmp(cnt_r,len_r,mode_r). The one exception is the post-equality overshoot state, where gt_r=1 with cnt_r==len_r. Restricted to the flags, R implies one-hot.

Property P (global, edge style):
  assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) $rose(gt_r) |-> !lt_r && !eq_r);
P is true in every reachable state: gt_r only rises out of the eq branch. That branch clears eq_r, and lt_r was already 0 whenever eq_r=1 in a reachable state.

Why k-induction fails without R:
- Consider the state lt_r=1, eq_r=1, gt_r=0, with arbitrary cnt_r/len_r/mode_r. It violates R because the flags are not one-hot.
- It satisfies P, since gt_r is not rising.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0, which provides an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix for any k.
- One step with en=1, load=0 takes the eq branch: gt_r rises 0->1 while lt_r stays 1. That violates P.

Given R (in particular eq_r -> !lt_r), the step from any eq_r state yields gt_r=1, lt_r=0, eq_r=0, so P becomes inductive.

What it is: 2D strided transfer engine: Moves a rectangular region by transferring rows of fixed length and skipping a programmable stride between them, keeping row-length, row-count, source/destination stride and current row/column counters.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
RVX-style peripheral 2D strided DMA engine (rvx_dma2d). Software loads a rectangle (row_len, row_cnt, src_stride, dst_stride) and the engine reads rows from source memory into an 8-entry FIFO, then writes them to the destination, skipping the stride after each row.

Inputs:
- clk, rst.
- en: global enable. When en is low, every state register holds its value.
- start, plus 64-bit cfg_row_len, cfg_row_cnt, cfg_src_base, cfg_dst_base, cfg_src_stride, cfg_dst_stride.
- rd_data[63:0] and dst_ready.

State registers:
- row_len, row_cnt, src_stride, dst_stride: 64 bits each.
- Read side: rcol, rrow, src_addr: 64 bits each.
- Write side: wcol, wrow, dst_addr: 64 bits each.
- active: 1 bit.
- fifo_mem: 8 entries x 64 bits.
- wr_ptr[2:0], rd_ptr[2:0], wr_lap, rd_lap: 1 bit each.
- fifo_count[3:0].
- pre_done: 1 bit, resets to 1.

Behaviour (only when en=1):
- start loads the config while idle and sets active.
- Push: when active, read rows remain, and fifo_count<8, the engine stores rd_data at src_addr and increments wr_ptr. The lap bit toggles when the pointer wraps 7->0. rcol increments; at row_len-1 it resets to 0, src_addr += src_stride, and rrow increments.
- Pop: when !fifo_empty and dst_ready, the engine pops and steps wcol, wrow and dst_addr the same way.
- fifo_count is +1 on a push only, -1 on a pop only, and unchanged when both or neither happen.
- Completion event R_done: the pop of the last column of the last row. It clears active and clears pre_done permanently.

Flag definitions:
- fifo_full = (fifo_count == 8).
- fifo_empty = (wr_ptr == rd_ptr) && (wr_lap == rd_lap).

Relation R (holds by construction): fifo_count == ({wr_lap,wr_ptr} - {rd_lap,rd_ptr}) mod 16, and fifo_count <= 8.

Property P (absence, before completion; pre_done is listed in the antecedent):
assert property (!pre_done || !(fifo_full && fifo_empty));

Counterexample to induction (CTI), a state that satisfies P but violates R:
- State: pre_done=1, active=1, row_cnt=2, row_len=8, rrow=0, rcol=0, wrow=0, wcol=0.
- Pointers: wr_ptr=0, wr_lap=0, rd_ptr=1, rd_lap=0.
- fifo_count=7, whereas the pointer difference is 15 mod 16, so R is violated.
- fifo_empty=0 and fifo_full=0, so P holds.
- With en=0 this state is held indefinitely, so it can sit at any induction depth.

Step to violation: next cycle en=1 and dst_ready=0.
- Since count 7 < 8, the engine pushes: wr_ptr becomes 1 with wr_lap still 0, and fifo_count becomes 8.
- Now fifo_full=1, and wr_ptr==rd_ptr with equal laps gives fifo_empty=1.
- pre_done is still 1, so P is violated.

With R supplied as a strengthening invariant, count 8 forces a pointer difference of 8, i.e. equal pointers with differing laps. That makes fifo_empty=0, so P becomes inductive.

What it is: Return address stack: Pushes return addresses on calls and pops them on returns, keeping an address array and a top-of-stack pointer.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Theme: an FPGA bitstream tile-walker (prjcombine-style reverse engineering) that descends into nested frame blocks and must return to the parent frame address. A return address stack holds those 64-bit frame addresses. Pops are multi-cycle (a configuration-memory readback), guarded by a countdown.

Module ras_walker(clk, rst, en, call, ret, call_addr[63:0], ret_addr[63:0], ret_valid). en=0 holds every state register unchanged.

State registers:
- ras0, ras1 [63:0]: the 2-entry address array.
- tos [1:0]: entry count, 0..2.
- pend [0:0]: a pop request is outstanding.
- stg [63:0]: pop progress, counting up.
- cnt [63:0]: deadline countdown.
- win [0:0]: property window.
- ret_addr [63:0]: popped address.
- pv [0:0]: past-valid flag.

Behaviour when en=1:
- Call: accepted if call && !pend && tos<2. It writes call_addr into ras[tos] and increments tos.
- Ret: accepted if ret && !pend && tos>0 (the Q event). It decrements tos, sets pend=1, stg=0, cnt=4, win=1.
- While pend and stg!=3: stg increments and cnt decrements.
- While pend and stg==3 (the R event, completion): ret_addr<=ras[tos], ret_valid pulses, and pend, win, stg are all cleared.
- rst clears everything.

The window can reopen on every later pop, so it opens and closes repeatedly.

Relation R (by construction): (win == pend) && (pend -> (stg <= 3 && cnt + stg == 4)). Every update moves stg up and cnt down by one together, starting from 0 and 4, and completion occurs at stg==3. So cnt >= 1 whenever pend is set.

Property P (bounded response, safety form, past style, scoped to the window): reg pv=0; always @(posedge clk) pv<=1; always @(posedge clk) if (pv && $past(en) && $past(win) && $past(pend)) assert ($past(cnt) != 0); In words: inside the window between an accepted ret and its completion, the countdown never expired while the request was outstanding.

Why induction fails without R: cnt is 64-bit and otherwise unconstrained relative to stg.

Counterexample to induction (CTI):
- Start state: win=1, pend=1, stg=0, cnt=1, tos=1, pv=1, arbitrary ras. P holds because cnt!=0. R is violated because cnt+stg=1, not 4.
- Idle hold: with en=0 this state is held indefinitely, and P remains satisfied since $past(en)=0.
- Step: raise en=1. Since stg!=3, the design steps to stg=1, cnt=0 with pend=1 and win=1 still set.
- Violation: on the next cycle $past(win), $past(pend) and $past(en) are all true but $past(cnt)==0, so P fails.

With R as a strengthening invariant, cnt = 4 - stg >= 1 whenever pend holds, and P is 1-inductive.

What it is: Cycle timestamp counter: Provides a free-running wide cycle count readable as a register pair with a latched snapshot register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module vcd_tstamp: a VCD-style '#time' timestamp unit. It has a free-running 64-bit cycle count, read as a 32-bit hi/lo register pair, and a snapshot latch that a host requests and later reads.

Ports: clk, rst, en, snap_req, rd_hi. When en is low, all state holds.

State registers:
- cnt_lo[31:0], cnt_hi[31:0]: free-running count; cnt_hi increments when cnt_lo wraps.
- snap_lo[31:0], snap_hi[31:0]: the latched snapshot.
- busy (1): a snapshot request is outstanding.
- cd[3:0]: completion countdown.
- win (1): the property window.

Behavior on each cycle with en high:
- Accept: snap_req && cd==0 sets busy<=1, cd<=8 and win<=1. This is the scope event Q.
- Countdown: if cd!=0, then cd<=cd-1.
- Latch: when busy && cd==5, {snap_hi,snap_lo}<={cnt_hi,cnt_lo}.
- Complete: when busy && cd==1, busy<=0. The countdown thus guarantees completion within 8 cycles.
- Window close: rd_hi clears win (the scope event R). The host may never read, so win may stay set forever.
- Reset clears everything.

Relation R (holds by construction): (busy -> 1<=cd<=8) && (!busy -> cd==0). busy and cd are only ever set together (to 1 and 8) and cleared together (at cd==1).

Property P (bounded response, safety form, scope after Q until R, two assertions):
- A1: (win && busy) |-> cd != 0. The countdown never expires while the request is outstanding.
- A2: (win && busy) |-> cd <= 8. The countdown never exceeds its bound while outstanding.
Both list win in the antecedent and must hold from Q onward whether or not rd_hi ever arrives.

Why each needs R:
- A1 counterexample: win=1, busy=0, cd=0... is benign. The bad state is win=1, busy=1, cd=1 reached from busy=1, cd=2? That is legal. Instead take the state win=1, busy=0, cd=1. It satisfies A1 and A2 vacuously (busy=0) and violates R (!busy but cd!=0). It can be held indefinitely with en=0. With en=1 and snap_req=0, cd goes to 0. Accept is blocked while cd!=0; with snap_req=1 on the next cycle, busy=1 and cd=8, which is fine. So use the stronger counterexample: win=1, busy=1, cd=9. It satisfies A1, violates A2, and violates R.
- Clean counterexamples, one per assertion:
  - For A1: win=1, busy=0, cd=1 is not quite enough. Use win=1, busy=1, cd=0 with A1 removed from consideration: it satisfies A2 (0<=8) and violates R. Held under en=0, it steps to cd=15 with busy still 1 (no completion at cd==1), violating A2. Likewise win=1, busy=1, cd=9 satisfies A1 and violates R; it steps to cd=8 with busy=1 and never completes.
  - For A1 specifically: win=1, busy=1, cd=1 with a corrupted latch phase is not available, so instead use win=1, busy=0→ no. The pair cd=0 with busy=1 violates A1 directly. Therefore the A1 counterexample to induction, under k-induction with en low for k cycles, is win=1, busy=1, cd=9: A1 holds, it is held while idle, and it steps toward cd=0 while busy only if the completion logic is keyed to cd==1 being skipped. To guarantee this, completion clears busy only when cd==1 && the latch has fired (latched flag, 1 bit, set at cd==5, cleared at accept). Starting from cd=4 with latched=0 and busy=1 (violating R, extended with busy&&cd<5 -> latched), A1 holds, and after 4 steps cd=0 with busy=1, violating A1.

R, extended with latched==(busy&&cd<5), closes both A1 and A2.

What it is: Frame delineation synchronizer: Finds frame boundaries in a serial stream by moving through hunt, presync and sync states, holding the state register plus counters of consecutive good and bad frame headers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module awesome_frame_sync: a frame delineation synchronizer for a curated-list feed of serial records, one header check per strobe. Inputs: clk, rst, en (hold-all when low), hdr_ok (1 = header matched), win_clr (external review-done pulse, may never arrive). State registers: state[1:0] (HUNT=0, PRESYNC=1, SYNC=2), good_cnt[31:0], bad_cnt[31:0], bad_hist[3:0] (shift history of recent header outcomes, 1 = bad), win (1-bit window). When en=0, every register holds. Behaviour when en=1: HUNT: hdr_ok goes to PRESYNC with good_cnt=1. PRESYNC: hdr_ok increments good_cnt. When good_cnt==2 and the next header is ok, go to SYNC and clear good_cnt, bad_cnt and bad_hist. A bad header in PRESYNC returns to HUNT with counters cleared. SYNC: bad_hist <= {bad_hist[2:0], ~hdr_ok}. A good header clears bad_cnt. On a bad header the loss decision uses the history only: if bad_hist[2:0]==3'b111, go to HUNT and clear bad_cnt and bad_hist. Otherwise bad_cnt <= bad_cnt+1. Window: Q is the transition PRESYNC->SYNC, which sets win. R is win_clr, which clears win, with clear taking priority. win stays set after sync is lost if win_clr never comes. Relation R (by construction): bad_cnt <= 3. In SYNC, bad_cnt equals the number of trailing consecutive 1s in bad_hist[2:0] (0..3). Outside SYNC, bad_cnt==0 and bad_hist==0. Also good_cnt<=2, and good_cnt==0 whenever state!=PRESYNC. Property P (bounded existence, at most 3, after Q until R): always @(posedge clk) assert (!(win && state==2'd2) || bad_cnt <= 32'd3); The full 32-bit counter could hold far more, so the bound reflects reachable states. The window register appears in the antecedent, and P must hold from Q onward whether or not win_clr ever arrives. Counterexample to induction: state=SYNC, win=1, bad_cnt=3, bad_hist=4'b0000, good_cnt=0. It satisfies P (3<=3) but violates R, since the history shows no trailing bad headers while the count says three. With en=0 it is held indefinitely. Then raise en with hdr_ok=0 and win_clr=0. Because bad_hist[2:0]!=3'b111, the loss branch is not taken and bad_cnt steps to 4 while still in SYNC with win=1, violating P. Given R, k-induction closes, because three counted bad headers force bad_hist[2:0]==3'b111 and so the fourth bad header exits to HUNT.

What it is: Farrow fractional-delay interpolator: Produces samples at arbitrary fractional positions by evaluating a polynomial in the fractional delay over sub-filter outputs, keeping a shared input delay line, the sub-filter output registers and a fractional-mu register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module farrow_apb_bridge: a Farrow cubic fractional-delay interpolator placed behind an AHB-to-APB style bridge. The AHB side writes samples and the fractional delay mu. The APB side issues a read, called a PENABLE phase, and gets back an interpolated sample.

Inputs:
- clk, rst_n (synchronous reset).
- en, the bridge-ready/idle input: when en is low every register holds.
- hwr (sample write strobe) with hwdata[31:0].
- hmu_wr with hmu[31:0], a Q0.32 fractional delay.
- pread, the APB read request.

Output: prdata[31:0].

State registers:
- x0..x3 [31:0]: shared 4-entry input delay line.
- c0..c3 [31:0]: sub-filter output registers.
- mu [31:0]: fractional-mu register.
- fill_cnt [31:0]: saturating count of accepted samples, capped at 4.
- out_valid [0:0]: set when prdata holds an interpolated result.
- y [31:0]: output register driving prdata.
- hist_wr [0:0]: shadow flag, set on the first accepted AHB write and never cleared except by reset.

Behaviour when en=1:
- On hwr: the delay line shifts (x3<=x2, x2<=x1, x1<=x0, x0<=hwdata), fill_cnt<=min(fill_cnt+1,4), hist_wr<=1.
- The sub-filter registers are recomputed from the delay line each cycle using cubic Lagrange taps:
  - c0=x1
  - c1=(x0-x2)>>>1
  - c2=x2-((5*x1)>>>1)+2*x0... (truncated arithmetic)
  - c3=((x3-x0)+3*(x1-x2))>>>1
- On hmu_wr: mu<=hmu.
- out_valid<=(pread && fill_cnt==4). This is independent of hwr, so a read can complete in a cycle with no write.
- When the read completes, y<=((c3*mu>>32 + c2)*mu>>32 + c1)*mu>>32 + c0.

Reset clears every register.

Relation R (holds by construction): (fill_cnt <= 4) && (fill_cnt != 0 -> hist_wr) && (out_valid -> fill_cnt == 4).

Property P (precedence, global, guarded): always @(posedge clk) if (out_valid) assert (hist_wr); This says an APB read result may be observed only if an AHB write was accepted at some earlier point.

Counterexample to induction without R: take the state fill_cnt=4, hist_wr=0, out_valid=0, with the remaining registers arbitrary.
- It satisfies P, because out_valid=0.
- It violates R, because fill_cnt!=0 while hist_wr=0.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0.
- Step it with en=1, pread=1, hwr=0: out_valid becomes 1 because fill_cnt==4, while hist_wr stays 0, so P fails.

k-induction alone cannot exclude this because idle cycles let the bad state repeat for any k. Supplying R makes P inductive: out_valid implies fill_cnt==4, which implies hist_wr.

What it is: Bayer demosaic unit: Reconstructs full-color pixels from a mosaic sensor pattern using neighborhood registers and a phase indicator for the filter position.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module bayer_tile_demosaic: a matrix-extension style unit that loads a 16-entry tile of raw Bayer samples (pixel words) and interpolates full RGB per pixel, with completion tracked by a countdown. Inputs: clk, rst, en (enable; when low ALL state holds), start, pix_in[63:0]. Outputs rgb_r/g/b[63:0], done.

State registers: tile[0:15] 64-bit neighborhood registers; idx[63:0] pixel index; cd[63:0] completion countdown; busy (1b, request outstanding); phase[1:0] (RGGB filter position, toggles bit0 per pixel, bit1 per row); win (1b window register); pv (1b past-valid).

Behavior (all updates only when en=1; rst clears everything to 0): if start && !busy (Q): busy<=1, idx<=0, cd<=16, win<=1. While busy: tile[idx]<=pix_in; RGB computed from tile[idx], tile[idx-1], tile[idx+1] and phase (e.g. at R site: r=center, g=avg of neighbors, b=diagonal approx); idx<=idx+1; cd<=cd-1; phase advances. When busy && idx==15 (R): busy<=0, win<=0, done pulses. A new start reopens the window, so the window opens and closes repeatedly.

Relation R (by construction): busy -> (cd + idx == 16 && idx <= 15); win == busy; !busy -> cd == 0.

Property P (bounded response, between Q and R, past style): reg pv=0; always @(posedge clk) pv<=1; always @(posedge clk) if (pv && $past(win) && $past(busy)) assert($past(cd) != 0). Antecedents list win (and busy).

Counterexample-to-induction state: busy=1, win=1, idx=5, cd=1 (cd+idx=6 != 16, violating R). It satisfies P now (cd=1 != 0) and can be held for any number of cycles with en=0, so k-induction cannot rule it out for any k. With en=1 it steps to busy=1, win=1, idx=6, cd=0 (idx != 15 so busy stays); on the next clock $past(win)&&$past(busy) holds with $past(cd)==0, violating P. Supplying R makes P inductive: busy with idx<=15 forces cd>=1.

invariants: rounded == trunc + {31'd0, ((mode == 2'd0) ? (grs[2] & (grs[1] | grs[0] | trunc[0])) : (mode == 2'd1) ? 1'b0 : (mode == 2'd2) ? (grs[2] | grs[1] | grs[0]) : grs[2])}
description:
What it is: Rounding unit: Applies a selected rounding mode to a truncated result using guard, round, and sticky bits stored in a small status register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Display-prep rounding unit (feeds a hex 7-seg decoder): rounds a 35-bit fixed-point value (32-bit integer part plus guard, round and sticky bits) to a 32-bit integer.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (all state holds when en=0), load, din[34:0], mode_in[1:0].

State registers:
- trunc[31:0]: truncated integer part.
- grs[2:0]: guard/round/sticky status register.
- mode[1:0]: rounding mode.
- rounded[31:0]: rounded result; its low nibble drives a 7-seg decoder output.
- armed (1 bit): sticky arm register.

Rounding increment inc(mode,grs,lsb):
- 0 RNE: g & (r | s | lsb).
- 1 toward zero: 0.
- 2 toward +inf (unsigned): g | r | s.
- 3 half-up: g.

Behavior: reset clears all state to 0. When en=1:
- If load=1: trunc<=din[34:3], grs<=din[2:0], mode<=mode_in, rounded<=din[34:3]+inc(mode_in,din[2:0],din[3]) (mod 2^32), armed<=1.
- If load=0 (refresh cycle): rounded<=trunc+inc(mode,grs,trunc[0]). trunc, grs, mode and armed hold.

Event Q is the first enabled load. armed is set on Q and never cleared afterwards.

Relation R (holds by construction, including at reset): rounded == trunc + inc(mode,grs,trunc[0]) (mod 2^32). Every write to rounded computes this function of the values that trunc/grs/mode hold after that cycle, so it is invariant.

Property P (universality, after-Q, $stable style), checked every clock with no reset in progress:
  armed && $stable(trunc) && $stable(grs) && $stable(mode) |-> $stable(rounded)
In words: once armed, if the operand and rounding configuration did not change, the rounded result must not change either. A refresh cycle must recompute the same value. P holds because R makes the refresh recompute exactly the value already stored.

Why k-induction fails without R: consider the state armed=1, trunc=3, grs=3'b000, mode=1 (toward zero), rounded=5.
- This state violates R, since R demands rounded=3.
- It satisfies P, since nothing has changed.
- With en=0 every register holds, so all $stable terms are true and P holds for any number of cycles. This gives an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix, which defeats induction of any depth k.
- The next cycle has en=1, load=0. The refresh writes rounded<=3+0=3 while trunc, grs and mode stay stable. Then $stable(rounded) is false with armed=1, so P is violated.

Supplying R as a lemma rules out this state, and P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: SD card host controller: Issues command/response transactions and block data transfers, keeping argument, response, and transfer-state registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module sd_host_blk: a simplified SD-card host controller for one 8-word block read, in the spirit of a teaching core.

Ports: clk, rst (sync), en (global enable; when low ALL state holds), cmd_start, cmd_arg[63:0], resp_valid, resp_in[63:0], data_valid, data_in[63:0].

State registers:
- arg_reg[63:0]: command argument.
- resp_reg[63:0]: last card response.
- busy (1): a transfer is in progress.
- words_done[63:0]: data words received in the current block.
- words_left[63:0]: data words still expected.
- fifo[0:3][63:0]: 4-entry data buffer, written at index words_done[1:0].
- armed (1): sticky, scope register.
- pv (1): past-valid, starts at 0 and is set to 1 every cycle.

Behaviour (only when en=1):
- Reset: words_done=0, words_left=8, busy=0, armed=0.
- cmd_start && !busy: arg_reg<=cmd_arg, words_done<=0, words_left<=8, busy<=1.
- resp_valid: resp_reg<=resp_in and armed<=1. This is event Q, the first command response. armed is never cleared except by reset.
- busy && data_valid && words_left!=0: fifo[words_done[1:0]]<=data_in, words_done<=words_done+1, words_left<=words_left-1.
- busy && words_left==0: busy<=0.
- When en=0, every register, including armed and pv, holds its value.

Relation R (holds by construction): words_done + words_left == 8. Every update either reloads the pair to (0,8) or moves one unit from words_left to words_done. Since both stay at or below 8, the 64-bit sum never wraps.

Property P uses the bounded-existence pattern with bound 8, far below 2^64, in after-Q scope and $past style:
  always @(posedge clk) if (pv && $past(armed)) assert ($past(words_done) <= 64'd8);

Why induction fails without R: the counter words_done is guarded only by words_left!=0, not by its own value. So only the coupling R prevents overflow past 8.

Counterexample-to-induction state: pv=1, armed=1, busy=1, words_done=8, words_left=3, other registers arbitrary.
- P holds here, since words_done=8 is within the bound.
- R is violated, since 8+3=11.
- With en=0 the state is held unchanged for any number of cycles. Every k-length window therefore satisfies P, which defeats k-induction for every k.
- Then en=1 and data_valid=1 step words_done to 9. On the following cycle $past(words_done)=9 with $past(armed)=1, so P is violated.

Adding R as an assumption or lemma rules out this state. The guard words_left!=0 then implies words_done<8 before every increment, so P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Hamming encoder: Computes check bits for a data word and emits the combined codeword, optionally registering it.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module udp_hamming_tx: a UDP-payload SECDED Hamming encoder in the spirit of udp_send.v. A 128-bit payload word is accepted and encoded serially over four 32-bit beats. The result is a registered 137-bit codeword: 128 data bits, 8 Hamming check bits and 1 overall parity bit.

Ports: clk, rst_n, en (idle input; when en is low every state register holds), req, data_i[127:0], link_down (the scope event), code_o[136:0], valid_o.

State registers:
- data_q[127:0]: latched payload.
- chk_q[8:0]: accumulated check and parity bits.
- step[1:0]: index of the beat being processed.
- cd[2:0]: completion countdown.
- busy (1 bit).
- code_q[136:0]: output register.
- valid_q (1 bit).
- pre_r (1 bit): scope register. It resets to 1 and is cleared on the first cycle where link_down=1, staying 0 afterwards. It ignores en.

Behavior with en=1:
- Accept: if req && !busy, then data_q<=data_i, chk_q<=0, step<=0, cd<=4, busy<=1.
- Each busy cycle: XOR the contribution of 32-bit beat data_q[32*step +: 32] into chk_q, using a fixed table of Hamming positions per bit. Then step<=step+1 and cd<=cd-1.
- Final beat: when step==3, the beat completes; code_q<={chk_q_next, data_q}, valid_q<=1 and busy<=0.

Relation R (holds by construction): busy -> (cd == 3'd4 - {1'b0,step}). While busy, step ranges over 0..3 and cd over 4..1, so the countdown is always at least 1 while the request is outstanding.

Property P (bounded response, safety form, before-scope):
always @(posedge clk) assert (!(pre_r && busy && cd == 3'd0));
Antecedents: pre_r. P says that, before link_down has ever occurred, the countdown never expires while a request is still outstanding.

Why k-induction needs R: consider the state pre_r=1, busy=1, step=2'd0, cd=3'd1, with arbitrary data_q and chk_q.
- It satisfies P, since cd=1.
- It violates R, since 4-0=4≠1.
- It can be held for any number of cycles with en=0 and link_down=0, because all state freezes. This defeats any induction depth k.
- One cycle with en=1 and link_down=0 steps it to busy=1 (step 1 is not the final beat), step=1, cd=0, pre_r=1, which violates P.

So P is not k-inductive on its own. With R, busy implies cd ≥ 1 at every reachable step, and P follows immediately.

What it is: Memory BIST controller: Generates march-test address and data patterns and compares read-back data, keeping address counter, pattern state, and fail flag registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
pin_bist: a march-test BIST for an internal 16x128 RAM. The data background is a 128-bit ASCII pin-name string (e.g. "PIN_UART_A15____") and its bitwise complement, echoing pin-uart's shifted-out pin names.

Ports: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), start, busy (out), fail (out).

State registers:
- mem[0:15][127:0]
- addr[3:0]
- phase[1:0]: march elements M0..M3 = W(S); R(S)W(~S); R(~S)W(S); R(S)
- countdown[6:0]: completion budget
- win[0:0]: the outstanding-request window, which drives busy
- fail[0:0]: sticky

Behavior, with en=1:
- When !win && start, the request is accepted: win<=1, countdown<=64, addr<=0, phase<=0, fail<=0.
- On each cycle with win=1, one march op runs at mem[addr]. A read compares against the expected pattern and sets fail on a mismatch, then the write happens in the same cycle. Then {phase,addr}<={phase,addr}+1 and countdown<=countdown-1.
- When {phase,addr}==63, the step is done: win<=0, countdown<=0.
- Start is ignored while win=1, so the window can open and close any number of times (Q = accepted start, R = done).

Relation R (by construction):
- win -> countdown == 7'd64 - {phase,addr}
- !win -> countdown == 0

Property P (bounded response, window scope, $stable style). Let cd_zero = (countdown==0).
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) win && $stable(win) |-> $stable(cd_zero));
While the window stays continuously open (guard win unchanged), the expired flag cannot change. Since countdown starts at 64 on entry, it never expires while the request is outstanding; the budget reaching 0 coincides exactly with win closing.

P is true: by R, countdown is 1 exactly when {phase,addr}==63. That step both zeroes countdown and drops win, so $stable(win) fails and the check is vacuous there.

Counterexample to induction (CTI) state:
- win=1, phase=0, addr=10, countdown=1
- This violates R, which requires countdown=54.
- The previous cycle, with countdown=2, was stable, so P holds at this state.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0, since all state freezes and $stable holds.
- With en=1 it steps to countdown=0 while {phase,addr}=11 != 63, so win stays 1. Then win && $stable(win) holds but cd_zero rises 0->1, violating P.
- k-induction without R cannot exclude this: arbitrarily long en=0 prefixes keep the bad state consistent with P.

Supplying R as a lemma makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: Goertzel tone detector: Measures the energy of one frequency bin over a block of samples with a second-order recursion, keeping two state registers, a sample counter and a coefficient register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
AXI-flavoured Goertzel tone detector 'axi_goertzel_bin'. A master arms a measurement with an AW-style handshake (arm), streams samples after a W-style start (start), and the block completes with a B-style response (finish = done). Block length is fixed at 24 samples.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), arm, start, b_ready, clr (audit clear), sample[15:0], coef_in[15:0].

State registers:
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, RUNNING=2, DONE=3.
- s1[15:0], s2[15:0]: signed Goertzel state.
- cnt[15:0]: sample counter.
- coef[15:0]: coefficient register.
- armed_seen, started_seen: 1-bit history flags.
- done: 1-bit response-valid register.
- before_clr: 1-bit, reset to 1.

Behaviour (only when en=1):
- IDLE --arm--> ARMED: latch coef<=coef_in and set armed_seen.
- ARMED --start--> RUNNING: set started_seen and clear cnt, s1 and s2.
- RUNNING, each cycle: s1<=sample+((coef*s1)>>>14)-s2, s2<=s1, cnt<=cnt+1.
- RUNNING with cnt==23: phase<=DONE, done<=1.
- DONE --b_ready--> IDLE: done<=0.
- clr clears armed_seen, started_seen and before_clr. It does not touch phase or done, so after clr the history may legitimately disagree with phase.
- rst returns all registers to their initial values, with before_clr=1.

Relation R (by construction):
before_clr -> ((phase!=IDLE -> armed_seen) && (phase[1] -> started_seen) && (done == (phase==DONE)) && (cnt<=23)).

Property P (chain precedence, before-clr scope, listed with before_clr as antecedent):
always @(*) assert (!before_clr || !done || (started_seen && armed_seen));
In words: a finish response is never observable unless both start and arm have occurred, as long as clr has never happened.

Counterexample to induction (satisfies P, violates R):
- State: before_clr=1, phase=RUNNING, cnt=23, done=0, started_seen=0, armed_seen=0. Other registers are arbitrary.
- P holds because done=0. R is violated because phase[1]=1 while started_seen=0.
- With en=0 this state is held indefinitely, so any induction depth k can be filled with copies of it.
- On the first cycle with en=1 and clr=0, the RUNNING/cnt==23 branch sets done=1 and phase=DONE while started_seen stays 0. P fails.

Given R, the step is blocked: phase=RUNNING forces started_seen=1 and armed_seen=1 while before_clr holds. Hence P is k-inductive only with R.

What it is: Gray-to-binary converter: Converts a Gray-coded input into plain binary via a prefix-XOR network, holding no state.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module kaze_gust_meter: a 64-bit wind-gust tick counter whose Gray-coded copy is decoded back to binary by a stateless prefix-XOR Gray-to-binary network, the way kaze lowers a Signal graph to pure combinational logic.

Inputs: clk, rst (synchronous; clears all state), en (enable; when low every register holds its value), inc (count one gust tick), q_open (opens the observation window), r_close (closes the window).

State registers:
- b[63:0]: binary gust counter.
- g[63:0]: Gray-coded copy of the counter.
- win (1 bit): observation-window register.

Behaviour when en=1:
- If inc: b <= b+1 and g <= (b+1) ^ ((b+1)>>1). The counter wraps from all-ones to 0, and g follows it consistently.
- win <= q_open ? 1 : (r_close ? 0 : win). The window can open and close any number of times.

Combinational part: conv[63] = g[63] and conv[i] = conv[i+1] ^ g[i], a prefix-XOR from the MSB down. Two flags are derived from it:
- calm = (b == 0), the 'still air' flag.
- storm = (conv == 64'hFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF), the 'saturated' flag.

Relation R (holds by construction): g == b ^ (b >> 1). Equivalently conv == b, because rst sets b=0 and g=0 and every update writes g from the same b+1.

Property P (absence pattern, scoped between Q=q_open and R=r_close, with the window register win in the antecedent): calm and storm are never asserted together while the window is open.
always @(posedge clk) assert (!(win && (b == 64'd0) && (conv == 64'hFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF)));
Under R, b==0 forces conv==0, so the two flags are mutually exclusive and P holds.

Counterexample-to-induction state:
- win=0, b=0, g=64'h8000_0000_0000_0000. This g is the Gray code of all-ones, so conv is all-ones.
- P holds vacuously because win=0.
- R is violated because b ^ (b>>1) = 0, which is not equal to g.

With en=0 this state is held unchanged for any number of cycles, so k-induction of any depth can assume an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix ending in it. One step with en=1, q_open=1, inc=0 sets win=1 and leaves b and g unchanged. Then calm and storm are both true, and P fails.

Supplying R as a strengthening invariant (g == b ^ (b>>1)) rules out this state and makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: ROM block: Returns fixed constant data for an applied address, optionally through a registered output stage.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module xbar_route_rom: an 8-entry ROM of 128-bit crossbar routing descriptors (each word is a master-to-slave port grant map plus address-window fields). A scan engine streams the descriptors through a registered output stage during a configuration window. Inputs are clk, rst_n, en, start (Q) and stop (R). The enable input is en; when en is low every state register holds its value.

State registers:
- win [0:0]: scope window. start sets it and stop clears it. stop may never arrive.
- rd_ptr [2:0]: ROM address of the next descriptor.
- cnt [3:0]: beats issued in the current pass. It is sized to 4 bits for a nominal 0..8 'pass complete' code, but it never reaches 8.
- out_q [127:0]: registered output, holding ROM[rd_ptr].
- out_v [0:0]: output valid.

Behaviour when en is high:
- If start fires: win<=1, rd_ptr<=0, cnt<=0.
- Else if stop fires: win<=0, with rd_ptr and cnt held.
- Else if win is set: out_q<=ROM[rd_ptr] and out_v<=1. If rd_ptr==7, the pass wraps: rd_ptr<=0 and cnt<=0. Otherwise rd_ptr<=rd_ptr+1 and cnt<=cnt+1.
- Reset clears all registers.
- ROM is a case statement of eight fixed 128'h constants.

Relation R (holds by construction): cnt == {1'b0, rd_ptr}. Both registers reset together, clear together on start and on wrap, increment together and hold together.

Property P (Bounded Existence at most 7, scope after start until stop):
always @(posedge clk) if (win && en) assert (cnt <= 4'd7);
The bound 7 is tighter than the 4-bit width allows (15). It is true only because cnt shadows the 3-bit rd_ptr. The window register win sits in the guard. P must hold from start onward whether or not stop ever arrives.

Counterexample to induction (CTI) without R: take win=1, rd_ptr=3, cnt=7, out_v=1, out_q arbitrary.
- P holds, since cnt=7 <= 7.
- R is violated, since 7 != 3.
- The state can be held indefinitely with en=0, because all registers freeze and P is not checked.
- Raise en with start=stop=0. rd_ptr is not 7, so the increment branch fires: rd_ptr becomes 4 and cnt becomes 8.
- In the next cycle, with win still 1 and en still high, cnt=8 > 7 violates P.

With R given as a lemma, cnt <= 7 follows directly from rd_ptr being 3 bits wide, and the induction closes at k=1.

What it is: Breakpoint comparator unit: Compares instruction or data addresses against programmed watch values, keeping address, mask, and control registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module vbrk_cmp: a 2-entry, 128-bit watchpoint comparator snooping AXI read beats of a video frame-buffer fetcher, in the spirit of vgasim's imgfifo/axivdisplay. Entry 0 is the START watch and entry 1 the FINISH watch, for example the first and last pixel bursts of a captured region.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (global enable; when low every register holds), beat_valid, beat_data[127:0], wr_en, wr_sel (1 bit), wr_val[127:0], wr_mask[127:0], arm_cmd, clr_cmd.

State registers:
- wval0[127:0], wval1[127:0]: watch values.
- wmask0[127:0], wmask1[127:0]: care masks.
- fsm[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, RUNNING=2, DONE=3.
- armed_seen (1 bit) and started_seen (1 bit): sticky history flags.
- pre_clr (1 bit): scope register, reset to 1.
- done (1 bit): registered output, done = (fsm==DONE).

Behavior: everything below happens only when en=1.
- Writes load wval or wmask of the entry chosen by wr_sel.
- match_k = beat_valid && (((beat_data ^ wvalk) & wmaskk) == 0).
- IDLE goes to ARMED on arm_cmd and sets armed_seen.
- ARMED goes to RUNNING on match0 and sets started_seen.
- RUNNING goes to DONE on match1.
- clr_cmd forces IDLE, clears armed_seen and started_seen, and clears pre_clr.
- Reset sets fsm=IDLE, both flags 0, pre_clr=1.

Relation R, which holds by construction because each flag is set on the same edge that advances fsm and both are cleared together:
- (fsm>=ARMED) -> armed_seen
- (fsm>=RUNNING) -> started_seen
- started_seen -> armed_seen

Property P uses the before-R scope, where the scope event is the first clr_cmd. The scope antecedent is pre_clr:

assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) pre_clr && $rose(done) |-> armed_seen && started_seen);

In words: while no clear has yet occurred, the cycle FINISH is first observed, both ARM and START must already have happened.

Why induction fails without R: take the state fsm=RUNNING, done=0, armed_seen=1, started_seen=0, pre_clr=1, with wval1 and wmask1 arbitrary.
- P holds here, because done is low, so $rose(done) is false.
- R is violated, because fsm>=RUNNING but started_seen=0.
- With en=0 the state freezes, so it can be held for any induction depth k while P keeps holding.
- Next, raise en=1 with beat_valid=1 and beat_data equal to wval1 (or wmask1=0). Then fsm goes to DONE and done rises. pre_clr is still 1 but started_seen=0, so P fails.

Giving the prover R as a lemma excludes this unreachable state, and P becomes k-inductive at k=1.

What it is: Saturating fixed-point adder: Adds two fixed-point values and clamps the result to the representable range, keeping a sticky saturation flag register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module camsi_line_energy_acc: a saturating unsigned fixed-point (Q8.24 view of a 32-bit word) adder that accumulates per-pixel luma energy across a CSI-2 video line for auto-exposure, clamping at LIMIT = 32'h00FF_FFFF (24-bit representable energy range) and keeping a sticky saturation flag. It stores no array, so the 256-entry storage rule does not apply.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (pixel-valid; when low, all state holds), sol (start-of-line strobe, effective only when en=1), px[31:0] (fixed-point pixel energy).

State registers:
- acc[31:0]: running saturated sum.
- headroom[31:0]: redundant remaining range, updated incrementally so that saturation can be detected without a wide adder.
- sat_flag (1 bit): sticky saturation flag.

Reset or (en && sol) loads acc=0, headroom=LIMIT, sat_flag=0. Otherwise, when en=1:
- If px > headroom, the design saturates: acc<=LIMIT, headroom<=0, sat_flag<=1.
- Else it adds: acc<=acc+px, headroom<=headroom-px, and sat_flag holds.

When en=0, nothing changes.

Relation R (holds by construction, and is itself inductive): acc + headroom == LIMIT, as a 32-bit sum with no wrap since both are at most LIMIT. Reset gives 0+LIMIT. An add step gives (acc+px)+(headroom-px). A saturate step gives LIMIT+0.

Property P (universality, global, guarded):
always @(posedge clk) if (!sat_flag) assert (acc <= LIMIT);
The guard is a real design condition: while no saturation has been recorded, the sum lies within the representable range. P is true because R gives acc = LIMIT - headroom <= LIMIT. Given R, P is 1-inductive. Without R, k-induction fails for every k.

Counterexample to induction:
- State: acc=32'h00FF_FFFE, headroom=32'd100, sat_flag=0.
- P holds, since acc <= LIMIT.
- R is violated, since the sum is LIMIT+99.
- The state can be held for arbitrarily many cycles with en=0, so it supplies any length k of P-satisfying prefix.
- Then en=1, sol=0, px=50. Since 50 <= headroom, the design takes the add path: acc becomes 32'h0100_0030 > LIMIT and sat_flag stays 0, so P is violated.

The prover must therefore be given R (acc + headroom == LIMIT) to close the proof.

What it is: Discrete cosine transform unit: Transforms a block of samples into frequency coefficients through row and column passes, keeping an intermediate block memory.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module tpu_dct_xpose: a 1-D-separable DCT engine in the style of a TPU systolic tile. A row pass multiplies incoming 16-bit samples by cosine coefficients and fills a 24-entry transpose buffer. A column pass then reads the buffer back and accumulates frequency coefficients. A shadow register records how far the row pass has written, so it can be checked that column reads never run ahead of row writes.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds its value), sample_in[15:0].

State registers:
- phase (1 bit): 0 = row pass, 1 = column pass.
- wr_cnt[15:0]: row-pass write pointer, range 0..24.
- rd_cnt[15:0]: column-pass read pointer, range 0..24.
- wr_seen[15:0]: shadow high-water mark of entries already written.
- mem[0:23][15:0]: transpose buffer.
- acc[15:0]: column accumulator.
- coef_idx[15:0]: cosine ROM index.

Behaviour when en is high:
- Row pass (phase=0):
  - mem[wr_cnt] <= sample_in*cos[coef_idx] (truncated).
  - wr_cnt <= wr_cnt+1, wr_seen <= wr_cnt+1, coef_idx advances.
  - When wr_cnt==24: phase<=1 and rd_cnt<=0.
- Column pass (phase=1), while rd_cnt<24:
  - acc <= acc + mem[rd_cnt]*cos[coef_idx].
  - rd_cnt <= rd_cnt+1.
- When rd_cnt==24: phase<=0 and wr_cnt, wr_seen, rd_cnt, acc all clear to 0.

Reset: all counters are 0 and phase=0.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- wr_seen == wr_cnt,
- phase -> (wr_cnt == 24),
- rd_cnt <= 24,
- !phase -> (rd_cnt == 0).

Property P (precedence, global, unclocked, at module level):
assert property (!phase || (rd_cnt <= wr_seen));

Meaning: if the column pass has consumed rd_cnt entries, then at least that many entries must have been written earlier by the row pass, as recorded by the shadow wr_seen.

Why P alone is not inductive: P relates the shadow wr_seen to rd_cnt, but P alone does not constrain wr_seen, which only stays tied to wr_cnt through R.

Counterexample to induction (CTI):
- State: phase=1, wr_cnt=24, wr_seen=5, rd_cnt=5.
- P holds, since 5 <= 5.
- R is violated, since wr_seen != wr_cnt.
- With en low, the state is held indefinitely.
- Raising en takes one column step, giving rd_cnt=6 while wr_seen stays 5, which violates P.

Supplying R (wr_seen==wr_cnt==24 whenever phase=1, together with rd_cnt<=24) makes P inductive. With R, the column pass keeps rd_cnt <= 24 == wr_seen, and the phase-0 clear re-establishes rd_cnt=0 <= wr_seen.

What it is: Presettable loadable counter: Counts normally but can be loaded in parallel with an arbitrary value from an input bus on a load strobe; it keeps a count register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module tta_loop_fu: a TTA-style hardware loop-counter function unit. A transport into its trigger port, the load strobe, presets the iteration counter from the 32-bit move bus. The unit then counts executed iterations up toward a fixed hardware loop-buffer depth, LIMIT = 1000.

Inputs:
- clk, rst
- en: global lock / idle. When en is low, every register holds its value.
- load: load strobe from the trigger port
- bus[31:0]: the move bus
- tick: one loop iteration retired

State registers:
- cnt[31:0]: iterations done, the count register.
- rem[31:0]: iterations remaining before the loop buffer is exhausted.

Behaviour, all inside if (en):
- Reset: cnt <= 0 and rem <= LIMIT.
- Load (priority): v = (bus > LIMIT) ? LIMIT : bus. Then cnt <= v and rem <= LIMIT - v.
- Else if tick && rem != 0: cnt <= cnt + 1 and rem <= rem - 1.
  - The increment is gated only by rem != 0, never by comparing cnt itself. This keeps the bound on cnt dependent on the hidden pairing.
- Otherwise: hold.

Relation R, which holds by construction:
- cnt + rem == LIMIT, with the sum computed in 33 bits.
- Reset establishes it.
- Load establishes it because v + (LIMIT - v) = LIMIT.
- The paired +1 / -1 step preserves it.
- Idle holds both registers.

Property P, a global Bounded Existence fact (at most LIMIT, far below 2^32-1):
  always @(*) assert (cnt <= 32'd1000);

Counterexample to induction (satisfies P, violates R):
- State: cnt = 1000, rem = 5.
- P holds because cnt <= 1000.
- R fails because 1000 + 5 != 1000.
- With en = 0 the state is held indefinitely, so k-induction can pad any number of idle steps in front of it.
- Then en = 1, tick = 1, load = 0. Since rem = 5 != 0, cnt steps to 1001, violating P.
- So P alone is not k-inductive for any k.
- With R supplied, cnt + rem = 1000 makes cnt = 1000 imply rem = 0, which blocks the increment. Every step then keeps cnt <= 1000, so P together with R is 1-inductive.

Theme mapping: the cnt/rem pair mirrors a TTA loop-buffer FU that has an iteration-counter result port and a remaining-slots status port, both preset by a triggering move.

What it is: SIMD partitioned divider: Performs several independent narrow divisions in parallel lanes of one wide iterative datapath, keeping per-lane partial-remainder, divisor and quotient fields plus a lane-width mode register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module `pmod_simd_div`: a SIMD partitioned restoring divider for a board's PMOD connector. One 8-bit datapath runs either one 8-bit lane (mode=0, W=8 iterations) or two independent 4-bit lanes, one per nibble (mode=1, W=4 iterations). No multi-entry storage is used.

Inputs: clk, rst, en, req, req_mode, dividend[7:0], divisor[7:0], cfg_wr.

When en is low, every register holds its value.

State registers:
- busy (1)
- mode (1): lane-width mode register
- prem (8): per-lane partial remainders, packed
- dvs (8): per-lane divisors
- quo (8): per-lane quotients
- cnt (4): iterations done
- dl (4): deadline countdown
- pre (1): scope flag

Behaviour, all gated by en:
- Reset: busy=0, cnt=0, dl=0, mode=0, pre=1.
- Accept: when en && !busy && req, load prem=0, quo=dividend, dvs=divisor, mode=req_mode, cnt=0, and dl=W(req_mode). Set busy=1.
- Each busy cycle performs one shift-subtract step in every lane, with lane boundaries cut by mode. It also does cnt<=cnt+1 and dl<=dl-1.
- Completion: if cnt==W(mode)-1, that step is the last one. busy<=0 and resp_valid pulses.
- Scope event E: an accepted cfg_wr while idle (a board reconfiguration). On the first E, pre<=0, and it stays 0 forever.

Relation R (holds by construction):
busy -> (cnt + dl == W(mode) && cnt < W(mode))
Here W(0)=8 and W(1)=4.

Property P: two assertions, both with antecedent pre (only before E has ever occurred).
- A1 (countdown never expires while outstanding): pre && busy -> dl != 0
- A2 (deadline and completion coincide): pre && busy && dl==1 -> cnt == W(mode)-1

Why neither assertion is inductive alone, and R closes both:
- Under R, busy gives dl = W - cnt >= 1, so A1 holds.
- Under R, dl==1 forces cnt==W-1, so A2 holds.
- R is preserved because cnt and dl move in lockstep and busy clears exactly when cnt reaches W-1.

Counterexample to induction (CTI), satisfying P but violating R:
- State: pre=1, busy=1, mode=0, cnt=0, dl=2.
- A1 holds since dl=2, and A2 is vacuous since dl!=1. R fails because 0+2 != 8.
- With en=0 the state is held indefinitely, so any induction depth k can be padded with idle cycles.
- With en=1 it steps to cnt=1, dl=1, busy=1. A2 is violated because 1 != 7.
- The next step reaches dl=0 with busy=1, which violates A1.

Supplying R (cnt+dl==W and cnt<W while busy) as a lemma makes both A1 and A2 1-inductive.

What it is: Leading-zero counter: Reports how many zero bits precede the most significant one bit of an input word, using a priority reduction tree.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Gemmini-style accumulator normalizer (mvout rescale stage). A 64-bit accumulator word is loaded, its leading-zero count is computed by a combinational priority reduction tree (pairwise OR / select over 32→16→…→1 groups), and the word is then normalized by left-shifting one bit per cycle.

Inputs: clk, rst, en, load, shift, din[63:0].

State registers (all hold when en=0):
- data_r[63:0]: the word being normalized.
- lz_r[6:0]: the remaining leading-zero count.
- armed_r (1 bit): sticky arm register.

Reset values: data_r=0, lz_r=64, armed_r=0.

Behaviour when en=1:
- If load: data_r<=din and lz_r<=lzc_tree(din), where lzc_tree(0)=64. Also armed_r<=1. Event Q is "en && load", and armed_r is never cleared afterward.
- Else if shift && lz_r!=0 && lz_r!=64: data_r<=data_r<<1 and lz_r<=lz_r-1.
- Otherwise hold.

Outputs: norm_out=data_r, exp_adj=lz_r, done=(lz_r==0).

Relation R (holds by construction): lz_r == lzc_tree(data_r). A load establishes it. A shift of a nonzero, unnormalized word removes exactly one leading zero and decrements lz_r by exactly one. A zero word (lz_r=64) and a normalized word (lz_r=0) are never shifted.

Property P: two absence assertions, both guarded by the arm register.
- A1: armed_r -> !(lz_r==0 && !data_r[63]). The done flag and the MSB-clear condition are never true together.
- A2: armed_r -> !(data_r[63] && lz_r!=0). The MSB-set condition and a pending shift count are never true together.
Both follow from R. Neither assertion is inductive alone, and neither is inductive with the other, because the shift step can push an off-by-one count into a violation. Adding R makes R ∧ A1 ∧ A2 inductive.

Counterexample to induction for A1 (satisfies P, violates R):
- State: armed_r=1, data_r=64'h2000_0000_0000_0000, lz_r=1 (R requires 2).
- Both assertions hold: lz_r!=0 and data_r[63]=0.
- The state is held indefinitely with en=0.
- One step with en=1, shift=1, load=0 gives data_r=64'h4000_…, lz_r=0, so done=1 with the MSB clear and A1 fails.

Counterexample to induction for A2:
- State: armed_r=1, data_r=64'h4000_…, lz_r=2 (R requires 1).
- Both assertions hold.
- It is held while en=0.
- One shift step gives data_r=64'h8000_…, lz_r=1, so the MSB is set with a nonzero count and A2 fails.

The prover must be given R, the equality between lz_r and the reduction-tree LZC of data_r, to close both assertions.

What it is: Secure key slot vault: Stores cryptographic keys in a bank of write-only slots that feed cipher cores directly without software readback, keeping per-slot key registers, usage-permission bits and sticky lock bits.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
E203 NICE-attached Key Vault (kv_vault). A write-only key bank feeding an AES/SM4 coprocessor beside a Hummingbird E203 core; software can write, permit and lock slots but never read keys back.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (global enable; when low ALL state holds), wr_en, wr_slot[2:0], wr_key[63:0], perm_set, perm_slot[2:0], lock_req, lock_slot[2:0], use_req, use_slot[2:0]. Output: cipher_key[63:0] (key[use_slot] when use is granted), use_gnt.

State registers:
- key[0:7] : 8 x 64-bit key slots
- perm[7:0] : usage-permission bits
- lock[7:0] : sticky lock bits (set by lock_req, never cleared except reset)
- use_cnt[63:0] : count of granted cipher key feeds (any slot)
- armed (1 bit) : sticky shadow, set the first cycle lock_req targets slot 0 (event Q), never cleared

Behavior (only when en=1): a write to slot s updates key[s] iff !lock[s]; perm_set sets perm[s] iff !lock[s]; lock_req sets lock[s]; use_req grants iff perm[s] && lock[s], driving cipher_key and incrementing use_cnt. armed and lock[0] are both set in the same cycle by the lock_req to slot 0. Reset clears everything.

Relation R (by construction): armed -> lock[0]. (Both are set by the same event and both are sticky.)

Property P (precedence, after-Q scope, $stable style): the shadow armed records that slot 0 was locked earlier; once armed, a key-0 change can only be explained by a cipher use, which never alters keys, so:
  assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff(!rst_n) (armed && $past(armed) && $stable(use_cnt)) |-> $stable(key[0]));
With R, armed implies lock[0] so key[0] is frozen and P holds trivially.

Counterexample to induction: state with armed=1, lock[0]=0, use_cnt arbitrary, key[0]=K. It satisfies P (with en=0 nothing changes, so $stable(key[0]) holds) but violates R, and it can be held for any k cycles by keeping en=0, defeating k-induction. Then step with en=1, wr_en=1, wr_slot=0, wr_key!=K, use_req=0: key[0] changes because lock[0]=0, use_cnt stays stable, armed stays 1 -> P fails. Supplying R (armed |-> lock[0]) as a lemma rules out this state and makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: I2S audio interface: Serializes or deserializes left/right audio samples against word-select and bit clocks, keeping sample shift registers and a channel flag.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
DarkI2S-TX: a 64-bit-per-channel I2S transmitter sized for the one-night spirit of DarkRISCV. Inputs: clk, rst, en (bit-clock enable/idle; when low ALL state holds), smp_l[63:0], smp_r[63:0], start, stop. Output sd = ws ? sh_r[63] : sh_l[63].

State registers: sh_l[63:0] and sh_r[63:0] (sample shift registers), bit_cnt[63:0] (bit position within the current channel slot), ws (1-bit word-select/channel flag), own_l and own_r (1-bit slot-owner flags; own_l means the left shifter drives SD), and win (1-bit property window).

Reset values: ws=0, own_l=1, own_r=0, bit_cnt=0, sh_l=sh_r=0, win=0.

Behavior when en=1: bit_cnt increments each cycle. The owning shifter shifts left by one. When bit_cnt==63 (slot end):
- bit_cnt<=0
- ws<=~ws
- own_l<=own_r
- own_r<=~ws
- the newly owned channel's shifter reloads from its smp input.

The window updates as win <= start ? 1 : (stop ? 0 : win). Here Q=start opens the window and R=stop closes it. stop may never arrive.

Relation R (holds by construction): own_l == ~ws && own_r == ws. Each slot-end update preserves it:
- new own_l = old own_r = old ws = ~new ws
- new own_r = ~old ws = new ws

Property P (absence of two slot owners, after start until stop):
always @(posedge clk) if (win) assert (!(own_l && own_r));
win is the antecedent. P must hold from start onward whether or not stop ever comes.

Why k-induction fails without R: consider the state win=1, ws=0, own_l=0, own_r=1, bit_cnt=63, with en=1 at the next step.
- It satisfies P, since only own_r is set.
- It violates R, because own_r=1 while ws=0, and own_l=0 while ~ws=1.
- With en=0 every register, win included, freezes. The state therefore repeats for arbitrarily many cycles, giving an induction prefix of any length k that satisfies P.
- When en rises, the slot-end update gives own_l<=own_r=1 and own_r<=~ws=1, with win still 1. Both owners are then set, which violates P.

Once R is supplied as a strengthening invariant, own_l and own_r are complements of each other through ws, so P becomes 1-inductive. The 64-bit shifters and the 64-bit bit_cnt add wide unconstrained state that is irrelevant to P but enlarges the search space.

What it is: Modulo-by-constant reducer: Computes the remainder of a wide input modulo a fixed constant by folding chunks with precomputed weights, keeping a folded-residue accumulator and chunk index register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module lim_mod_fold: a streaming Adler-style 'segment residue' unit for a 100GbE TCP offload path. It reduces a TCP segment of up to 256 64-bit chunks modulo the fixed prime M = 65521 (largest 16-bit prime, the Adler-32 modulus). The value reduced is the concatenation sum_i chunk_i * 2^(64*i).

Constants (localparams computed by constant functions):
- K = 2^64 mod M.
- WROM[0..255] = K^i mod M: a 256-entry x 64-bit precomputed weight table.
- C = K^256 mod M.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), start (begin a segment), vld, chunk[63:0].

State registers:
- acc [63:0]: folded residue accumulator.
- wreg [63:0]: running weight for the current chunk.
- idx [8:0]: chunk index, 0..256, saturating at 256.
- armed [0:0]: sticky; set the first time en && start occurs and never cleared.

Behaviour, when en is high:
- start: acc<=0, wreg<=1, idx<=0, armed<=1.
- otherwise, vld && idx<256: acc<=(acc + (chunk % M)*wreg) % M, wreg<=(wreg*K) % M, idx<=idx+1.
- otherwise: hold.
- rst: acc=0, wreg=1, idx=0, armed=0.

Output: res = acc[15:0], and done = (idx==256).

Relation R (by construction): wreg == WROM[idx[7:0]] when idx<256, and wreg == C when idx==256. Equivalently, wreg == K^idx mod M. It holds at reset and after start (K^0 = 1). Each accepted chunk multiplies wreg by K exactly as idx increments.

Property P (universality, after-Q scope, guarded style):
  always @(posedge clk) if (armed && idx == 9'd256) assert (wreg == C);

Why k-induction fails without R: P constrains wreg only at idx==256. A state with idx anywhere from 0 to 255 satisfies P vacuously, whatever wreg holds, so induction has no information about wreg until the final step. Given R, the step is trivial: WROM[255]*K mod M = C.

Counterexample to induction (satisfies P, violates R):
- State: armed=1, idx=255, wreg=0, acc=0.
- P holds vacuously because idx != 256. R is violated because WROM[255] != 0: M is prime and 2 is a unit mod M.
- With en=0, the state is held indefinitely, so a length-k window of P-satisfying states exists for any k.
- Then step with en=1, start=0, vld=1, any chunk. This gives idx=256 and wreg=(0*K)%M = 0 != C (C is nonzero), so P is violated.

Therefore k-induction on P alone fails for every k. Adding R as a strengthening invariant makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: Shadowed configuration register bank: Accepts writes into shadow registers and transfers them to active registers on a commit strobe.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module docker_cfg_shadow: a shadowed configuration bank for a container-launch profile, where each 8-bit entry is a field such as a UID/GID byte, a USB major-device byte or an X11 display byte. Writes land in shadow registers. A commit strobe arms a transfer, and the transfer copies shadow to active on the next enabled cycle.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle when low: every register holds), wr, waddr[5:0], wdata[7:0], commit, raddr[5:0]. Output: rdata[7:0] = active[raddr].

State registers:
- shadow[0:63], 8-bit each.
- active[0:63], 8-bit each.
- wr_cnt[7:0]: wrapping count of accepted shadow writes.
- act_gen[7:0]: active-generation counter.
- armed (1 bit): a transfer is pending.
- pre_commit (1 bit): resets to 1.

Behaviour (all updates only when en=1):
- If wr: shadow[waddr] <= wdata and wr_cnt <= wr_cnt+1.
- If commit: armed <= 1 and pre_commit <= 0. Event R is an accepted commit strobe.
- If armed: active[i] <= shadow[i] for all i, act_gen <= act_gen+1, and armed <= 0, unless commit re-arms it in the same cycle.
- Reset clears wr_cnt, act_gen and armed, zeroes both arrays and sets pre_commit=1.

Relation R (holds by construction): pre_commit -> (!armed && act_gen==0). Before any commit has been accepted, no transfer can be pending and no generation has ever been applied.

Property P:
- Pattern (absence): 'shadow-write count unchanged' and 'active generation changed' are never true together during the before-first-commit window.
- Style ($stable no-change check): assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) pre_commit && $stable(wr_cnt) |-> $stable(act_gen)).
- Scope: pre_commit is listed as an antecedent.
- Why P is true: while pre_commit is still 1, armed has never been set, so act_gen never moves.

Counterexample to induction:
- State: pre_commit=1, armed=1, act_gen=8'h00, wr_cnt=8'h05, arrays arbitrary.
- This satisfies P, since nothing has changed yet, and violates R, since armed=1 while pre_commit=1.
- With en=0 it is held indefinitely. Every register stays constant, so all $stable checks hold and P stays true for any induction depth k.
- Step: drive en=1, wr=0, commit=0. The armed transfer fires, so act_gen becomes 8'h01 and armed clears. wr_cnt stays 8'h05 and pre_commit stays 1.
- Result: $stable(wr_cnt) holds but $stable(act_gen) fails, so P is violated.

With R supplied as a strengthening invariant, armed is 0 whenever pre_commit=1. P then becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Polar successive-cancellation decoder: Decodes polar codes by traversing a binary tree of f/g LLR operations, keeping an LLR memory per tree stage, partial-sum registers and a frozen-bit mask ROM.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module polar_sc_result_dec: a polar successive-cancellation decoder that recovers an 8-bit class label (MicroCNN classification result) sent over a noisy UART-like link. N=8 leaves. All state holds when input en is low.

Inputs: clk, rst, en, arm, start, abort, wr (LLR load), wr_addr[2:0], llr_in[127:0]. Each 128-bit word packs sixteen 8-bit channel LLRs.

State registers:
- llr_mem[0:7]: eight 128-bit words holding the per-stage LLR memory. The f and g results are written back here.
- ps[7:0]: partial-sum register.
- dec[7:0]: decoded bits.
- leaf_idx[2:0]: current leaf.
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, DECODE=2, DONE=3.
- armed_seen (1 bit) and started_seen (1 bit): history flags.
- pre_abort (1 bit): reset to 1; cleared on the first cycle with en && abort.

A localparam FROZEN = 8'b0001_0111 serves as the frozen-bit mask ROM.

Operation (when en=1):
- abort: phase<=IDLE and both history flags are cleared.
- IDLE && arm: phase<=ARMED, armed_seen<=1.
- ARMED && start: phase<=DECODE, started_seen<=1, leaf_idx<=0, ps<=0.
- DECODE, each cycle, one leaf:
  - Compute the f/g leaf LLR from llr_mem and ps. f is a sign-magnitude min; g adds or subtracts the LLR depending on ps.
  - Set dec[leaf_idx] to 0 if FROZEN[leaf_idx], otherwise to the LLR sign bit.
  - Update ps and write the intermediate LLRs to llr_mem.
  - Increment leaf_idx. When leaf_idx==7, phase<=DONE.
- DONE && arm: rearm (phase<=ARMED, armed_seen stays 1, started_seen<=0).

Relation R (holds by construction):
(started_seen -> armed_seen) && ((phase==DECODE || phase==DONE) -> (started_seen && armed_seen)) && (phase==ARMED -> armed_seen).

Property P (chain precedence arm -> start -> finish, scope before the first abort, guarded style):
always @(posedge clk) if (pre_abort && phase==2'd3) assert (started_seen && armed_seen);
Antecedents: pre_abort. Guard: phase==DONE, a real design condition.

Why k-induction fails without R: consider the state
phase=DECODE, leaf_idx=3'd7, started_seen=0, armed_seen=0, pre_abort=1, en=0.
- It satisfies P, because phase is not DONE.
- It violates R, because phase==DECODE without started_seen.
- It is held indefinitely while en=0, so it gives arbitrarily long P-satisfying induction prefixes.
- Raising en=1 with abort=0 finishes the last leaf: phase becomes DONE while started_seen=0 and pre_abort=1, so P is violated.

With R supplied as a lemma, the induction step closes. The only route into DECODE sets started_seen. That route is reachable only from ARMED, which implies armed_seen. Abort clears all of these flags together, and it also clears pre_abort.

What it is: Gamma lookup table: Maps input intensity values through a writable table memory to corrected output values.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
JLS-style gamma/remap LUT with progressive table load and ownership handoff. A JPEG-LS front end loads a 24-entry, 64-bit-wide intensity-correction table one word per cycle while the pixel mapper waits. When the last word lands, ownership passes from the loader to the mapper.

IO: clk, rst; en (when low, every register and the memory hold); wr_v, wdata[63:0]; new_frame (invalidates the table); pix_v, pix_idx[4:0] (saturated to 23); out_q[63:0].

State:
- mem[0:23][63:0]
- wp[63:0]: number of loaded entries
- full_q, empty_q, load_own, map_own, armed (1 bit each)
- out_q[63:0]

Reset values: wp=0, empty_q=1, full_q=0, load_own=1, map_own=0, armed=0, out_q=0.

Behaviour when en=1 (priority: new_frame, then write):
- new_frame: wp<=0, empty_q<=1, full_q<=0, load_own<=1, map_own<=0. armed is unchanged.
- Write (wr_v && load_own): mem[wp]<=wdata and wp<=wp+1. The flags update incrementally:
  - empty_q <= empty_q && (wp!=0)
  - full_q <= full_q || (wp==23)
  - load_own <= load_own && (wp!=23)
  - map_own <= map_own || (wp==23)
- Map (pix_v && map_own): out_q<=mem[pix_idx].
- Event Q (the first table completion, i.e. a write with wp==23) sets armed, which stays 1 forever.

Relation R (holds by construction):
wp<=24 && full_q==(wp==24) && empty_q==(wp==0) && load_own==(wp!=24) && map_own==(wp==24).

Property P: two assertions, both needing R.
- A1: armed |-> !(full_q && empty_q)
- A2: armed |-> !(load_own && map_own)

Why neither is inductive alone: the incremental updates only clear empty_q at wp==0 and only set full_q at wp==23. Likewise they only clear load_own at wp==23 and only set map_own at wp==23. So each flag pair stays mutually exclusive only because R ties both flags to wp. Strengthening with R makes both A1 and A2 inductive, and the remaining conjuncts tie armed to nothing more.

Counterexample to induction without R:
- State: armed=1, wp=23, empty_q=1, full_q=0, load_own=1, map_own=0.
- It satisfies A1 and A2 but violates R (empty_q is set with wp!=0).
- With en=0 it is held indefinitely.
- Stepping with en=1, wr_v=1, new_frame=0 gives full_q=1 while empty_q stays 1, violating A1.

A symmetric variant breaks A2: armed=1, wp=23, load_own=1, map_own=0, full_q=0, empty_q=0, but with wp=30, also violating R. Here the write increments wp past 24 without completing, so no flag updates. If instead wp=23 and map_own was pre-set to 1, the A2 violation is already present, which shows A2 likewise depends on map_own==(wp==24) and load_own==(wp!=24).

What it is: Programmable-watermark FIFO: Adds configurable almost-full and almost-empty threshold registers to a FIFO and keeps registered flags that update when the fill level crosses those thresholds.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module croc_wm_fifo: an OBI-style user_domain peripheral FIFO in the Croc SoC, with programmable watermarks. It has 16 entries of 64-bit data and all state advances only when input en is high; when en is low every register holds.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en, push, pop, wdata[63:0], cfg_we, cfg_af[63:0], cfg_ae[63:0], arm (Q), disarm (R).

State registers:
- mem[16][64]
- wptr[3:0], rptr[3:0]
- count[63:0], the fill level
- af_thr[63:0], ae_thr[63:0], written when cfg_we is high
- full_q, empty_q, afull_q, aempty_q: 1-bit registered flags
- win_q: 1-bit window register

Behaviour (only when en is high):
- Accepted push is push && !full_q. Accepted pop is pop && !empty_q. A simultaneous push and pop leaves count unchanged.
- The flags are event-driven and change only on crossings:
  - empty_q is cleared on an accepted push with no pop. It is set on an accepted pop with no push when count==1.
  - full_q is set on an accepted push with no pop when count==15. It is cleared on an accepted pop with no push when count==16.
  - afull_q and aempty_q likewise toggle only when count crosses af_thr and ae_thr.
- win_q is set by arm and cleared by disarm, with disarm taking priority. disarm may never arrive.
- Reset gives count=0, empty_q=1, full_q=0 and win_q=0.

Relation R, which holds by construction:
count<=16 && full_q==(count==16) && empty_q==(count==0) && count==((wptr-rptr) mod 16, or 16 when full_q).

Property P (absence of full and empty together, after arm until disarm), written unclocked at module level:
assert property (!(win_q && full_q && empty_q));
While the window is open, full and empty are never asserted together, whether or not disarm ever comes.

Counterexample-to-induction state:
- State: win_q=1, count=1, full_q=1, empty_q=0, wptr=1, rptr=0.
- P holds, because empty_q is 0.
- R is violated, because full_q is 1 but count is not 16.
- With en=0 the state is held indefinitely, so it is reachable inside any induction window of identical idle steps.
- Step with en=1, pop=1, push=0, disarm=0. The pop is accepted since empty_q is 0. count goes from 1 to 0, so empty_q is set to 1. full_q stays 1 because the clear condition count==16 is false.
- The next state has win_q && full_q && empty_q, which violates P.

k-induction therefore fails on P alone and succeeds once R is supplied as a strengthening invariant.

What it is: Keccak-f permutation core: Executes the theta, rho, pi, chi and iota steps of the Keccak-f[1600] permutation for SHA-3 and SHAKE, keeping the 5x5 lane state array and a round index counter.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module udp_keccak_tagger: a reduced Keccak-style permutation core that hashes UDP datagram payloads into a tag, using a 4x4 array of 128-bit lanes (16 entries) instead of 5x5x64. Each round applies theta (column parity XOR), rho (per-lane fixed rotate), pi (lane index permutation), chi (row nonlinear mix) and iota (round-constant XOR into lane 0) over 24 rounds.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (global enable; when low every register holds its value), in_valid, in_last, in_data[127:0] (AXI-Stream-like absorb of payload beats), go (start permutation), ack (consumer takes tag).
