State registers: lane[0:15] (16 x 128-bit state array); absorb_ptr[3:0] (next lane to XOR a beat into); rnd[4:0] (round index 0..23); phase[1:0] (0=IDLE, 1=ARMED, 2=RUN, 3=DONE); armed_flg (1b, set when phase enters ARMED, i.e. in_valid&in_last absorbed); started_flg (1b, set when go moves ARMED->RUN); done (1b output, registered, high in DONE); seen_q (1b sticky, set the first time a UDP datagram end-of-frame, in_valid&in_last, is absorbed; never cleared except by reset).

FSM: IDLE absorbs beats; in_last -> ARMED, armed_flg<=1. ARMED & go -> RUN, rnd<=0, started_flg<=1. RUN: one round per cycle; rnd==23 -> DONE, done<=1. DONE & ack -> IDLE, done<=0, armed_flg<=0, started_flg<=0. All transitions gated by en.

Relation R (by construction): (done -> phase==DONE) and ((phase==RUN || phase==DONE) -> (armed_flg && started_flg)) and (phase==ARMED -> armed_flg) and (phase==RUN -> rnd<=23).

Property P (chain precedence arm->start->finish, after-Q scope, edge style): assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff(!rst_n) (seen_q && $rose(done)) |-> (armed_flg && started_flg)); i.e. once a datagram has been seen, the tag-done edge is only ever observed if arm and start already happened.

Counterexample-to-induction state: phase=RUN, rnd=23, done=0, armed_flg=0, started_flg=0, seen_q=1, lanes arbitrary. P holds (done is not rising), R is violated (RUN without flags). With en=0 this state is held indefinitely, so any k-length induction window stays P-consistent. When en=1, rnd==23 moves phase to DONE and sets done, so $rose(done) occurs with seen_q=1 while armed_flg=started_flg=0, violating P. Supplying R as a lemma rules this state out and makes P inductive.

What it is: Translation lookaside buffer: Caches virtual-to-physical page translations in a tag/data array with valid, ASID, and permission bits.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module tlb32_ice40: a 32-entry fully associative TLB for a hobby soft-CPU, the kind of block found in an ECP5/iCE40 gateware repo. Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds its value), lookup_vpn[51:0], lookup_asid[7:0], fill, fill_vpn[51:0], fill_asid[7:0], fill_ppn[51:0], fill_perm[2:0] (R/W/X), flush_all, flush_asid (with asid_sel[7:0]). Outputs: hit, ppn_out[51:0], perm_out[2:0].

State registers: valid[31:0]; tag_vpn[32][51:0]; tag_asid[32][7:0]; data_ppn[32][51:0]; data_perm[32][2:0]; occ[63:0], the occupancy counter; hits[63:0], a lookup hit counter; victim[4:0], a round-robin replacement pointer.

Behaviour when en=1, in priority order:
- flush_all sets valid to 0 and occ to 0.
- flush_asid clears every valid entry whose tag_asid equals asid_sel. It then sets occ to occ minus the popcount of the cleared mask.
- fill with any invalid slot writes the lowest-indexed invalid slot, sets its valid bit and increments occ.
- fill with all slots valid overwrites entry victim, increments victim and leaves occ unchanged.
- A lookup hit increments hits.

On rst, valid, occ, hits and victim are all cleared.

Relation R (holds by construction): occ == $countones(valid). Every path that changes valid adjusts occ by exactly the number of bits that changed.

Property P (bounded existence, global, unclocked): assert property (occ <= 64'd32);
The bound of 32 is far below the 2^64 range of occ, so it is a real fact about reachable states and not a width truism.

Why k-induction needs R: consider the state occ = 32 with valid = 32'h7FFF_FFFF, which has 31 bits set.
- It satisfies P, because occ is 32.
- It violates R, because 32 is not equal to 31.
- It can be held indefinitely with en = 0, so a k-step induction trace can sit in it for any k without breaking P.
- With en = 1 and fill = 1 it steps to a violation. The free slot 31 is seen as invalid, so the fill takes the increment path, occ becomes 33 and P fails.

With R supplied, occ = popcount(valid), which is at most 32, and the fill-increment path is only taken when popcount(valid) is at most 31. So occ stays at or below 32 and P becomes 1-inductive.

The 64-bit hits counter and the wide tag and data arrays add realistic state without touching the argument.

What it is: Snoop filter: Tracks which caches may hold which lines using a presence-vector array indexed by address.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
SPI-fed snoop filter. A 16-entry presence-vector array tracks which of 16 caches may hold each line. Update commands arrive as 16-bit SPI words.

Inputs: clk, en (idle when low: every register holds), sclk_rise (sample strobe), mosi.

State registers:
- sr[15:0]: SPI shift register.
- bitcnt[3:0]: bit counter.
- pvec[0:15][15:0]: presence vectors, one bit per cache.
- occ_cnt[4:0]: number of nonzero entries. It is 5 bits because the count can reach 16.
- armed (1 bit): sticky.
- pv (1 bit): past-valid.

Behavior: when en and sclk_rise are both high, the design shifts mosi into sr and increments bitcnt. When bitcnt wraps from 15 to 0, it executes the completed word w={sr[14:0],mosi}:
- op=w[15:14], idx=w[13:10], cid=w[9:6].
- op=01 (snoop-fill): set pvec[idx][cid]. If pvec[idx] was zero, increment occ_cnt.
- op=10 (cache-evict): clear pvec[idx][cid]. If that leaves the vector zero and it was nonzero, decrement occ_cnt.
- op=11 (back-invalidate): clear pvec[idx]. If it was nonzero, decrement occ_cnt, and set armed (event Q). armed is never cleared.
- op=00: no operation.

Reset values: all zero.

Relation R (holds by construction): occ_cnt == the number of indices i with pvec[i] != 0. Every increment and decrement of occ_cnt happens exactly when an entry moves between zero and nonzero.

Property P (scope: after the first back-invalidate; past style):
reg pv=0; always @(posedge clk) pv<=1;
always @(posedge clk) if (pv && $past(armed)) assert($past(occ_cnt) <= 5'd16);
Only 16 entries exist, so R bounds occ_cnt at 16. The 5-bit register alone could reach 31.

Counterexample to induction:
- State: armed=1, occ_cnt=16, pvec[0]=0, and every other pvec arbitrary.
- P holds: 16 <= 16.
- R is violated: at most 15 entries are nonzero, but occ_cnt=16.
- The state can be held for any number of cycles with en=0, so it is k-inductive for every k.
- The bad step: a word op=01, idx=0, cid=any finishes shifting with bitcnt=15 and en=1. pvec[0] goes from zero to nonzero, so occ_cnt becomes 17. On the next cycle $past(occ_cnt)=17 > 16, so P fails.

With R supplied as a strengthening invariant, occ_cnt can never exceed 16, the step is blocked, and P becomes inductive.
What it is: Stepper motor sequencer: Drives coil phase patterns in order at a programmable step rate, keeping a phase index register and step-rate divider.

What it is: Range mask decoder: Takes start and end bit indices and produces a contiguous mask of asserted lines between them, as used for bit-field insert and extract, holding the start and end index registers.

What it is: NaN propagation and canonicalization unit: Selects which input NaN, if any, propagates to the result, quiets signaling NaNs or replaces them with a canonical NaN, and registers the chosen payload and an invalid indication.

What it is: Trivium stream cipher core: Generates keystream bits from three coupled nonlinear shift registers totaling 288 bits, holding that register state and a warm-up cycle counter used during initialization.

What it is: Mutual-exclusion request arbiter: Resolves two asynchronous requests with a cross-coupled latch followed by a metastability filter, holding which requester currently owns the shared resource.
What it is: Instruction fetch unit: Generates fetch addresses and captures returned instruction bytes, keeping a fetch pointer and an alignment buffer.
What it is: Doorbell register block: Lets a remote agent set notification bits that a local agent reads and clears, keeping per-channel pending bits.

What it is: Exponential backoff controller: Schedules retransmission after collisions in a shared-medium protocol, holding a collision-attempt counter, a randomly loaded backoff slot counter and a waiting/transmitting state.

What it is: Dirty-bit tracking RAM: A RAM that sets a per-block dirty flag whenever any word in that block is written so software can find modified regions; it keeps the data array and a dirty-bit array.
What it is: LZ77 match finder: Searches a history window for the longest match with current input, keeping a history memory, candidate position registers, and match-length register.

What it is: Asynchronous SRAM/NOR bus controller: Generates chip-select, output-enable and write-enable strobes with programmable setup, access and hold wait states for external parallel memories, keeping per-chip-select timing registers and a phase counter.

What it is: Stream buffer: Prefetches sequential lines after a miss into a small FIFO beside the cache and supplies them on later misses, keeping the stream head address, entry tags, valid bits and line data.

What it is: Welch spectral averager: Averages power spectra across successive FFT frames by accumulating squared bin magnitudes in per-bin memory, keeping the bin accumulation RAM, a bin index counter and a frame counter.
What it is: Hardware page-table walker: Issues memory reads to traverse page-table levels, keeping level counter, current descriptor, and walk-state registers.

What it is: Leading-zero anticipator: Predicts the normalization shift amount in parallel with mantissa addition from the two aligned operands, holding a registered indicator string and predicted shift count.
What it is: Bitfield insert unit: Left-shifts a field to a given offset and merges it into a destination word under a generated mask, keeping the destination, field, offset and length registers.
What it is: Parity tree: Reduces a data word to a single parity bit through an XOR tree, with an optional output register.

What it is: Valid/ready stream demultiplexer: Forwards a handshaked input to one selected output channel, propagating that channel's ready back upstream, and keeps a registered select plus a per-output valid register.
What it is: Gated JK latch: A level-enabled latch whose J and K inputs set, reset or invert the stored bit while the enable is asserted, and it holds that bit otherwise.

What it is: Chipkill symbol-correcting decoder: Corrects failure of an entire DRAM device by treating each chip's bits as one symbol of a symbol-based code, keeping a syndrome register and a failed-chip identifier register.

What it is: Convolutional interleaver: Spreads burst errors by delaying successive symbols through branches of increasing length, implemented with per-branch delay memories and a commutator branch counter.
What it is: MISR signature analyzer: Compresses an observed data stream into a signature register updated each cycle by feedback and XOR.

What it is: Synchronous binary up counter: Increments a binary count register by one on every enabled clock edge, using a common clock and parallel carry logic; it keeps a single N-bit count register.

What it is: Snooping bus cache controller: Watches the shared bus for other masters' transactions, looks up their addresses in a duplicate tag copy and supplies data, invalidates or downgrades lines, keeping the duplicate tags and a pending-snoop register.
What it is: Min/max selector: Routes the smaller and the larger of two inputs to separate outputs using a single magnitude decision, holding the selected results in output registers.

What it is: Metastability-detecting synchronizer: Samples an asynchronous input in parallel flops and flags disagreement between the main and a shadow sampling register, keeping both sample registers and an error-flag register.

What it is: Registered 1-to-N demultiplexer: Steers one input word onto the output chosen by a select code and holds every output in its own register, with the select itself captured in a select register.

What it is: Vending machine controller: Accepts coin inputs, tracks deposited value in a credit register and the transaction step in a state register, and issues vend and change-return outputs when a selection is made.
What it is: Polyphase resampler: Changes sample rate using sub-filter banks selected by a phase accumulator, keeping sample history and phase registers.

What it is: PRBS checker with error counter: Self-synchronizes to an incoming PRBS stream and counts bit mismatches, keeping a local reference shift register, a sync flag and a saturating error counter.
What it is: Tri-state buffer: Drives its input onto the output when enabled and leaves the output high-impedance otherwise, holding no stored state.

What it is: RMS power meter: Measures signal power by squaring samples, accumulating them over a programmable window and outputting the mean square or its root, keeping a sum-of-squares accumulator, a window counter and a result register.
What it is: Xorshift PRNG: Generates pseudorandom words by shifting and XORing an internal state register each cycle.

What it is: Sticky-bit right-shift register: Shifts a mantissa-style word right one position per clock while ORing every bit that falls off the low end into a sticky flip-flop, storing the data register and the sticky bit.
What it is: Table-based routing lookup: Maps a packet's destination ID to an output port through a programmable routing table memory, with configuration write registers for updating entries.

What it is: Memory-to-stream reader: Reads a memory buffer and emits it as a stream with start and last markers on packet boundaries, keeping read pointer, remaining-length counter and packet-size registers.

What it is: Memory-protection region checker: Compares an access address against several base/limit region pairs to decide whether it falls inside a permitted region, storing per-region base, limit and permission registers plus a registered fault flag.

What it is: Vector register file: Stores wide vector registers sliced into lanes, each lane with its own read and write ports feeding a vector ALU lane, plus per-register element-length configuration state.

What it is: Branch mask allocator: Assigns each in-flight speculative branch a tag bit and broadcasts kill or clear signals when branches resolve, keeping a free-tag vector and per-instruction branch dependency masks.

What it is: DFE tap adaptation engine: Adjusts decision-feedback equalizer tap weights using sign-sign LMS on slicer errors, keeping a coefficient register per tap, a history of past decided bits and a step-size register.
What it is: Framebuffer scanout controller: Reads pixel data from memory in raster order to feed a display, keeping a base-address register, current-address counter, and line counter.
What it is: Scan lockup latch: A latch placed between scan segments in different clock domains that holds the shifted bit for half a cycle to prevent hold races during scan shift.
What it is: SPI master: Drives chip-select, clock, and serial data for a transfer, keeping a shift register, bit counter, and mode configuration bits.

What it is: SIMD packed ALU: Performs one selected add, subtract or logic operation in parallel on byte, halfword or word lanes of a wide operand, breaking carries at lane boundaries per a lane-size control; it keeps a result register and a per-lane flag vector register.

What it is: LIN bus controller: Sends and receives LIN frames including the break field, sync byte, protected identifier and classic or enhanced checksum, keeping a frame-phase state register, an identifier register, a data buffer and a running checksum register.

What it is: IQ imbalance corrector: Compensates gain and phase mismatch between the I and Q branches by applying a correction matrix to each complex sample, holding programmable gain and phase coefficients and pipelined corrected outputs.
What it is: Ring-oscillator entropy harvester: Samples free-running oscillator phases to collect raw entropy bits into a collection shift register and sample counter.
What it is: 8b/10b encoder: Maps data bytes to balanced ten-bit symbols, keeping a running disparity bit.
What it is: DVFS controller: Requests voltage and frequency operating points based on load inputs, keeping current-point and request-pending registers.
What it is: Trace buffer: Records a rolling window of sampled signals into a circular memory with a write pointer and trigger-position register.

What it is: Gated event counter: Counts external input edges only while a gate input is asserted and latches the total when the gate closes, keeping an edge counter, a gate-state flop and a latched-result register.

What it is: Complex digital mixer: Multiplies incoming I/Q samples by a complex local-oscillator sample to shift the signal in frequency, holding pipeline registers for the four partial products and the summed outputs.
What it is: Zigzag scan reorder buffer: Reorders an 8x8 coefficient block between raster and zigzag order using a block memory and an index-sequence ROM.
What it is: USB endpoint buffer manager: Manages per-endpoint data buffers and toggle bits, keeping endpoint configuration, buffer pointers, and data-toggle flags.

What it is: Flow-hash steering demultiplexer: Hashes header fields of each incoming packet and uses the hash to index an indirection table that names the destination queue, storing the hash register and the programmable table.

What it is: Fractional-N modulus controller: Generates a per-cycle divide-ratio sequence whose average equals an integer plus a fraction using a multi-stage sigma-delta modulator, keeping the integer and fraction setting registers and the modulator accumulator registers.

What it is: UART auto-baud detector: Measures the width of the start bit or a known sync character on the receive line to derive a baud divisor, holding an edge-capture timer, a measurement-state register and the resulting divisor register.
What it is: AXI interconnect address decoder: Routes transactions to target ports based on address ranges stored in region base/limit registers.

What it is: Serial Wire Debug target port: Decodes SWD request packets, drives acknowledge and data phases with parity, and handles line turnaround, keeping a request register, a data shift register, a parity accumulator and a protocol-phase register.

What it is: Residue number system ALU: Performs addition, subtraction and multiplication independently in several small moduli channels with no carry between them; it keeps one residue register per modulus channel.

What it is: Programmable delay pulse generator: Outputs a pulse of programmed width starting a programmed delay after an input trigger, keeping a delay register, a width register, a phase counter and a delay/width/idle phase register.

What it is: Read-after-write hazard detector: Compares incoming read addresses against pending entries in the write queue and forwards or stalls on a match, keeping an address/byte-mask array of queued writes and a match vector.
What it is: Interrupt vector table unit: Translates an accepted interrupt id into a handler address through a programmable table memory.
What it is: Carry-save adder: Reduces three input vectors to a sum vector and a carry vector, optionally registering both outputs for the next reduction stage.

What it is: WS2812 single-wire LED encoder: Translates 24-bit colour words into the timed high/low pulse pattern for addressable LED strings followed by a reset latch interval, keeping a pixel shift register, a bit counter, a pulse-width timer and a reset-gap counter.

What it is: Integer-to-float converter: Normalizes an integer into mantissa and exponent fields and rounds to the target format, keeping an optional output register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module tapeout_i2f: an 8-bit unsigned integer to 8-bit minifloat converter (4-bit exponent, 3-bit mantissa, round-to-nearest-even), styled as a tape-out flow. It is gated by a three-step chain: arm (capture the operand), then start (normalize), then finish (round into the output register). All state holds when input en is low.

Inputs: clk, en, arm, start, din[7:0], q_sess (Q, session open), r_sess (R, session close).

State registers:
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, NORM=2, DONE=3.
- arm_f (1 bit) and start_f (1 bit): chain history flags.
- mant[7:0]: the working mantissa.
- exp[3:0]: the exponent.
- fout[7:0]: the optional output register.
- fin (1 bit): registered finish pulse.
- win (1 bit): the session window.

Behaviour when en=1:
- q_sess sets win=1, clears arm_f and start_f, sets phase=IDLE and fin=0. r_sess clears win and may never arrive.
- In IDLE, arm loads mant<=din and exp<=7, sets arm_f=1 and phase=ARMED.
- In ARMED, start sets start_f=1 and phase=NORM.
- In NORM, while mant!=0 and mant[7]==0, mant shifts left and exp decrements. Otherwise phase goes to DONE, fin<=1, and fout<={exp, rounded mant[6:4]}. Rounding uses guard bit mant[3] and sticky bits mant[2:0], and saturates on mantissa carry.
- In DONE, fin<=0 and the next arm restarts the chain. arm_f and start_f are never cleared except by q_sess.

Relation R (holds by construction):
(phase>=NORM -> start_f) && (start_f -> arm_f) && (phase!=IDLE -> arm_f).

Property P (chain precedence, scope after Q until R, $past style):

reg pv=0; always @(posedge clk) pv<=1;
always @(posedge clk) if (pv && win && $past(win) && fin) assert($past(arm_f) && $past(start_f));

In words: inside the window, an observed finish implies that arm and start both happened before it.

Why k-induction fails without R: consider the state phase=NORM, mant=8'h80, arm_f=0, start_f=0, win=1, fin=0, en=0, pv=1.
- P holds there, because fin=0.
- R is violated, because phase is NORM while start_f=0.
- The state is held indefinitely while en=0, since everything freezes. This gives an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix.
- Raising en=1 with no q_sess or r_sess moves the design to DONE with fin=1, because mant[7]=1. In that cycle win=1 and $past(win)=1, but $past(arm_f)=0, so P fails.

So P is true from reset only because R holds, and an inductive proof needs R as a strengthening invariant.

What it is: Wear-leveling mapping table: Translates logical to physical blocks and records per-block erase counts in a mapping memory.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module wl_map_scan: a wear-leveling logical-to-physical table, themed after svinst's module-to-instance map. Each of 32 logical module slots maps to a physical block, and each block keeps an erase count. A remap request runs a 32-entry scan to find the least-worn block, then commits it.

Ports: clk, rst, en (when low, all state holds), req, lblk[4:0]; outputs busy and done.

State registers:
- map_mem[0:31], 5-bit each (physical index)
- erase_cnt[0:31], 16-bit each
- busy, 1-bit
- scan_idx, 6-bit
- countdown, 6-bit
- best_idx, 5-bit
- best_cnt, 16-bit
- tgt, 5-bit (latched lblk)

Behavior (every update is gated by en):
- Reset: busy=0, scan_idx=0, countdown=0, map_mem[i]=i, erase_cnt[i]=0.
- Accept (en && req && !busy): busy=1, tgt=lblk, scan_idx=0, countdown=33, best_cnt=16'hFFFF.
- Scan step (en && busy && scan_idx<32): if erase_cnt[scan_idx] < best_cnt, set best_idx=scan_idx and best_cnt=erase_cnt[scan_idx]. Then scan_idx++ and countdown--.
- Commit (en && busy && scan_idx==32): map_mem[tgt]=best_idx, erase_cnt[best_idx]++ (saturating), busy=0, countdown=countdown-1 (to 0), done pulses.

Relation R, which holds by construction: busy -> (scan_idx <= 32 && countdown == 33 - scan_idx). Equivalently countdown + scan_idx == 33 while busy, plus !busy -> countdown == 0.

Property P (bounded response, safety form, global, guarded): always @(posedge clk) if (busy) assert (countdown != 0);
In words, the countdown never expires while a remap is outstanding. Completion is guaranteed within 33 enabled cycles.

Why k-induction fails without R:
- Take the state busy=1, scan_idx=5, countdown=1, with arbitrary memory contents.
- P holds, since countdown != 0.
- R is violated, since 1 != 33-5.
- With en=0 the state is held unchanged for any number of cycles, so arbitrarily long P-satisfying induction prefixes exist.
- Raising en to 1 performs a scan step: scan_idx=6, countdown=0, busy still 1. This violates P.

Such a state is unreachable: from reset, countdown and scan_idx move in lockstep from 33/0, so countdown reaches 1 exactly when scan_idx==32, and that commit cycle clears busy. Supplying R as a strengthening invariant makes P 1-inductive. The 32 x 16-bit erase-count memory and map memory are irrelevant to P but enlarge the state space.

What it is: Latency-matched bank read multiplexer: Selects the read data of the memory bank that was addressed several cycles earlier, keeping a pipeline of delayed bank-select codes.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module mempool_bank_rdata_mux: a tile-local L1 read-return mux for 16 SPM banks with 16-bit words and a fixed 3-cycle bank latency. A core request (req_valid, req_bank[3:0]) is captured when the enable input en is high. The bank index is decoded into a one-hot select and pushed through a 3-stage delay pipeline, so the data selected at the output always comes from the bank addressed 3 cycles earlier. Output rdata[15:0] is the OR over b of (sel_q2[b] ? bank_rdata[b] : 0), and rvalid = v_q2.

State registers (all hold their value when en=0):
- v_q0, v_q1, v_q2: 1-bit valid per stage.
- idx_q0, idx_q1, idx_q2: 4-bit encoded bank index per stage.
- sel_q0, sel_q1, sel_q2: 16-bit one-hot bank grant per stage.
- rsp_cnt: 16-bit count of returned responses (it increments when en && v_q2).

Update when en=1:
- v_q0 <= req_valid; idx_q0 <= req_bank; sel_q0 <= req_valid ? (16'h1 << req_bank) : 16'h0.
- Stages 1 and 2 copy the previous stage's v, idx and sel.

Reset clears every register.

Relation R (holds by construction): for each stage i in {0,1,2}, sel_qi == (v_qi ? (16'h1 << idx_qi) : 16'h0). R therefore implies that every stage's grant is one-hot or zero.

Property P (absence of two grants; global; checked on the clock edge): no two banks are ever granted the shared read-data bus in the same cycle.
always @(posedge clk) assert ($onehot0(sel_q2));

Why k-induction fails without R: consider this state.
- v_q0=1, idx_q0=0, sel_q0=16'h0003.
- Stages 1 and 2 are all zero (v=0, idx=0, sel=16'h0000).
- rsp_cnt=0.

In this state P holds, because sel_q2 is zero. R is violated, because sel_q0 has two bits set and does not match 1<<idx_q0. Driving en=0 holds the state unchanged for any number of cycles, so an induction trace of arbitrary length k satisfies P at every step. Raising en=1 for two cycles moves 16'h0003 into sel_q2, where bank 0 and bank 1 are granted simultaneously and P fails.

Given R as a strengthening invariant, every stage's grant is one-hot-or-zero. R is inductive: stage 0 is regenerated from a fresh decode, the later stages copy R-consistent triples, and en=0 preserves everything. P then follows in one step.

What it is: SIMD partitioned multiplier: Can be configured to perform one full-width multiply or several independent narrower lane multiplies by breaking carry and partial-product paths at lane boundaries; it keeps a mode register, operand registers and a lane-packed result register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
anl_dsp_simd_mul: an Anlogic-EG4-style DSP slice (theme: translated datasheet of an FPGA multiplier block) that multiplies as 1x32, 2x16 or 4x8 lanes. Carries and partial products are cut at lane boundaries. Each product is pushed into a 4-entry lane-packed result buffer.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, ALL state holds), cfg_mode[1:0], ld, a_in[31:0], b_in[31:0], push, pop, start, stop.

State registers:
- mode_q[1:0]: 0=1x32, 1=2x16, 2=4x8.
- a_q[31:0] and b_q[31:0]: operand registers, loaded when ld.
- res_q[63:0]: lane-packed product. In 2x16 mode each lane gives a 32-bit product at bits [32i+31:32i]. In 4x8 mode each lane gives a 16-bit product at bits [16i+15:16i]. In 1x32 mode it is the full 64-bit product.
- buf_q[0:3][63:0]: the result buffer.
- valid_q[3:0]: slot-occupied mask.
- occ_q[31:0]: occupancy counter.
- win_q (1 bit): observation window.

Behaviour (all updates only when en=1):
- Push is accepted when push && !(&valid_q). It writes res_q into the lowest free slot, sets that slot's valid bit and increments occ_q.
- Pop is accepted when pop && |valid_q. It clears the lowest set valid bit and decrements occ_q.
- A push and a pop in the same cycle update the valid bits and leave occ_q unchanged.
- win_q: if start, set to 1; else if stop, clear to 0; else hold. start and stop may recur, so the window can open and close many times.
- rst zeroes everything.

Relation R (holds by construction): occ_q == popcount(valid_q). Every change to occ_q is paired with exactly one valid-bit change.

Property P (Bounded Existence, at most 4, inside the window):
always @(*) assert (!win_q || occ_q <= 32'd4);
The bound 4 is far below what 32 bits allow. It holds only because R ties occ_q to a 4-bit mask.

Why k-induction fails without R: take the state win_q=1, occ_q=4, valid_q=4'b0111, with arbitrary operands and mode.
- It satisfies P, since occ_q=4 <= 4.
- It violates R, since popcount(valid_q)=3.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0, so the inductive prefix can be made arbitrarily long.
- Then step with en=1, push=1, pop=0, stop=0, start=0. The push is accepted because valid_q is not full. The next state is valid_q=1111, occ_q=5 and win_q=1, which violates P.

Giving the prover R (occ_q == popcount(valid_q)) excludes this state. With R, P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Dynamic range compressor: Reduces audio dynamic range by tracking the signal envelope and applying a gain reduction above a threshold with attack and release smoothing, keeping an envelope register, a current gain register and the threshold and ratio parameters.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module axis_luma_compressor: a dynamic range compressor applied to the luminance of an AXI-Stream video pixel stream (UG934 style: tvalid/tready/tuser=SOF/tlast=EOL), compressing bright highlights before writing frames to a bitmap sink. Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds its value), s_tvalid, s_tuser, s_tlast, s_luma[63:0], thr[63:0], ratio_sh[5:0], eof (end-of-frame pulse, may never come). State registers: env[63:0] (envelope: on accepted pixel, env <= env + ((luma-env)>>>2) for attack when luma>env, >>>5 for release); gain[63:0] (current gain, Q32.32); tgt[63:0] (target gain); pend (1 bit, gain-slew request outstanding); cd[63:0] (countdown deadline); step[63:0] (slew progress); hist[0:7][63:0] (8-entry ring of applied gains, indexed by step[2:0]); win (1 bit, scope window). Behaviour: when en and !pend and env>thr on an accepted pixel, a slew request is accepted: tgt <= gain reduction computed from (env-thr)>>ratio_sh, pend<=1, cd<=8, step<=0. Each en cycle with pend: gain moves one eighth of the way toward tgt, hist[step[2:0]]<=gain, cd<=cd-1, step<=step+1, and if step==7 then pend<=0 (completion). win <= 1 on an accepted pixel with s_tuser (Q = start of frame), win <= 0 on eof (R), set dominating. Output m_luma = (s_luma*gain)>>32. Relation R (by construction): pend -> (cd + step == 8 && step <= 7); !pend -> cd==0 is not required. Property P (bounded response, after-SOF-until-EOF scope, combinational): always @(*) assert (!(win && pend) || cd != 0); i.e. inside the window the deadline countdown never reaches zero while the slew request is still outstanding (completion happens at step 7, when cd is 1). Counterexample to induction: win=1, pend=1, cd=1, step=3 (cd+step=4, violating R) — P holds now (cd!=0); with en low this state is held indefinitely; on the next en cycle cd becomes 0, step becomes 4, pend stays 1 (step!=7) and win stays 1, so P fails. With R supplied, cd+step==8 and step<=7 force cd>=1 whenever pend, so P becomes 1-inductive. Widths: all data/counters 64-bit, storage 8 entries.

What it is: Run-length encoder: Emits value and repeat-count pairs from a stream, keeping a current-value register and a run-length counter.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module tf2_wrle: run-length encoder for a pruned/quantized weight stream, packing runs of identical 16-bit weights (e.g. pruned zeros) into (value, count) pairs. Ports: clk, rst, en (idle when low; all state holds), in_valid, in_data[15:0], drain (end-of-tensor), out_valid, out_val[15:0], out_cnt[15:0]. MAX = 24 is the longest run per pair, matching a 24-entry decompressor buffer.

State registers:
- cur[15:0]: current run value.
- cnt[15:0]: current run length.
- dl[15:0]: countdown of beats left before a forced flush.
- busy (1 bit): a run is outstanding.
- pre_drain (1 bit): resets to 1 and is cleared on the first enabled cycle with drain=1.
- pv (1 bit): past-valid flag.

Behaviour, only when en=1:
- Start a run (idle with in_valid): cur<=in_data, cnt<=1, dl<=MAX, busy<=1.
- Busy, in_valid, in_data==cur and cnt<MAX: cnt<=cnt+1, dl<=dl-1.
- Busy, in_valid and (in_data!=cur or cnt==MAX): emit (cur, cnt) with out_valid=1, then restart the run with cnt<=1, dl<=MAX, cur<=in_data.
- drain while busy: emit (cur, cnt), then busy<=0, cnt<=0, dl<=0.

The countdown is the bounded-response guarantee: an accepted run is emitted within MAX matching beats.

Relation R (holds by construction): busy -> (cnt + dl == MAX+1 && 1 <= cnt <= MAX), and !busy -> (cnt == 0 && dl == 0).

Property P (bounded response in safety form, scope 'before drain', $past style). pre_drain is listed as the antecedent:
  reg pv = 0; always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1;
  always @(posedge clk) if (pv && $past(pre_drain) && $past(busy)) assert ($past(dl) != 0);
In words: before any drain has occurred, the countdown is never zero while a run is still outstanding.

Why P is true: under R, dl = MAX+1-cnt >= 1 whenever busy. Why k-induction fails without R: dl is never compared against MAX inside the logic; it only decrements in lockstep with cnt, so any k-step trace starting from an inconsistent (cnt, dl) pair is unconstrained.

Counterexample-to-induction state: busy=1, pre_drain=1, pv=1, cur=16'h0000, cnt=10, dl=1.
- It satisfies P, since dl != 0.
- It violates R, since cnt+dl = 11 != 25.
- It can be held for any number of cycles with en=0, which defeats k-induction for every k.
- With en=1, in_valid=1, in_data=16'h0000 and drain=0: the input matches and cnt=10 < MAX, so the next state is cnt=11, dl=0 with busy=1.
- On the following edge, $past(busy)=1 and $past(dl)=0, so P fails.
Supplying R as a lemma excludes this state and makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: LED breathing engine: Smoothly ramps a PWM duty value up and down to fade an LED, keeping a PWM counter, a current-duty register, a ramp-step register, a ramp-rate prescale counter and a ramp-direction bit.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module hbpf_breathe: an LED breathing engine framed as a tiny eBPF-style 'ramp program', where each prescaled tick executes one ADD of the step to the duty word. Parameters: STEP = 64'h1_0000_0000 (2^32), NSTEPS = 2^31, MAX = NSTEPS*STEP = 2^63, PRESC_MAX = 64'd999. Input en gates everything: when en=0 every register holds its value.

State registers (reset values in brackets):
- pwm_cnt[63:0] [0]: free-running; led = (pwm_cnt < duty).
- presc[63:0] [0]: counts up to PRESC_MAX, then wraps to 0 and fires tick.
- pos[63:0] [0]: ramp position, i.e. the program counter of the ramp.
- duty[63:0] [0]: current duty register.
- headroom[63:0] [MAX]: ramp-step budget remaining.
- dir[0] [1]: 1 means ramping up.
- first_rise[0] [1]: cleared on the first peak.

On each tick:
- If dir=1 and pos<NSTEPS: pos+=1, duty+=STEP, headroom-=STEP.
- If dir=1 and pos==NSTEPS (the peak, event R): dir<=0 and first_rise<=0.
- If dir=0 and pos>0: pos-=1, duty-=STEP, headroom+=STEP.
- If dir=0 and pos==0: dir<=1.

The step guard only examines pos. Duty and headroom are never compared against MAX.

Relation R (holds by construction): duty == (pos<<32) && headroom == MAX - duty && pos <= NSTEPS && (first_rise -> dir).

Property P (universality, before-R scope, two assertions). first_rise is listed as the antecedent of both:
- A1: first_rise -> duty <= MAX
- A2: first_rise -> headroom <= MAX

Why neither assertion is inductive alone, and how R closes both:
- A1 alone fails: duty can sit at MAX while pos<NSTEPS, and the next up-step pushes duty above MAX.
- A2 alone fails: pos can be below NSTEPS while headroom<STEP, and the next subtraction wraps headroom above MAX.
- With R, duty = pos*STEP <= NSTEPS*STEP = MAX. Headroom = MAX - duty also lies in [0,MAX] and never wraps. first_rise forces dir=1, so no down-step can occur before the peak.

Counterexample to induction without R: the state first_rise=1, dir=1, pos=0, duty=MAX, headroom=MAX, presc=PRESC_MAX, pwm_cnt arbitrary.
- It satisfies A1 and A2 (both values equal MAX).
- It violates R, since duty != pos<<32.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0.
- One cycle with en=1 fires tick with pos<NSTEPS, so duty becomes MAX+STEP > MAX and A1 fails.

A symmetric state breaks A2: duty=0, headroom=0, pos=0. One tick wraps headroom to 2^64-2^32 > MAX.

What it is: TRNG health-test monitor: Runs continuous repetition-count and adaptive-proportion tests on raw entropy samples, keeping the last sample, a repeat counter, a window sample counter and an alarm flag.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module degate_trng_health: a TRNG health monitor framed as a Degate-style probe that watches 128-bit raw entropy words read from a die. Inputs are clk, rst (synchronous, active high), en and sample[127:0]. When en is low, all state holds.

State registers:
- last_smp[127:0]
- ref_smp[127:0], the APT reference word
- hist[0:7][127:0], an 8-entry sample log indexed by win_cnt
- rep_cnt[2:0], the repetition count, saturating at 7
- win_cnt[2:0], the number of samples taken in the current 8-sample window
- apt_cnt[3:0], the adaptive-proportion match count; it is deliberately 4 bits so that value 8 is representable
- alarm (1), sticky
- armed (1), sticky

Behavior when en=1:
- hist[win_cnt] <= sample.
- RCT: if sample==last_smp, rep_cnt increments (saturating); otherwise rep_cnt <= 0. last_smp <= sample.
- APT: if win_cnt==0, then ref_smp <= sample, apt_cnt <= 1, win_cnt <= 1. Otherwise apt_cnt increments when sample==ref_smp. If win_cnt==7, the window closes: win_cnt <= 0 and apt_cnt <= 0. Otherwise win_cnt increments.
- alarm <= 1 when the next rep_cnt reaches 5 or the next apt_cnt reaches 6; it is never cleared.
- Event Q is the first completed window (win_cnt==7 with en=1). It sets armed, which is never cleared.
- Reset clears all control registers.

Relation R (holds by construction): apt_cnt <= win_cnt. Both counters restart together, and apt_cnt rises by at most one only on a step where win_cnt also rises by one. Consequently apt_cnt <= 7 and apt_cnt[3]==0 always.

Property P (absence pattern, after-Q scope, $stable style):
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) armed && $stable(alarm) |-> !(apt_cnt[3] && win_cnt != 0));
In words: once armed, whenever alarm did not change, an overflowed proportion count and an open window are never present together.

Why k-induction fails without R:
- Take the state armed=1, alarm=1, win_cnt=1, apt_cnt=7, with arbitrary samples.
- It satisfies P, because apt_cnt[3]=0.
- It violates R, because 7 > 1.
- With en=0 it can be held for any number of cycles. alarm stays stable, so P keeps holding along an arbitrarily long induction prefix.
- Then apply en=1 with sample==ref_smp. apt_cnt becomes 8 and win_cnt becomes 2, while alarm stays 1 and is therefore $stable. Now apt_cnt[3] && win_cnt!=0 holds, so P is violated.
- Given R as a helper invariant, apt_cnt <= win_cnt <= 7 excludes apt_cnt[3], and P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Bus performance monitor: Observes handshakes on an interconnect port and accumulates statistics, holding counters for transactions, bytes moved, stall cycles and cumulative latency plus a sampling-window register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module lvds_port_perfmon: a bus performance monitor sitting on the 128-bit valid/ready pixel-word port that feeds a 7:1 LVDS serializer (each beat packs several 7-bit lane groups). Inputs: clk, rst, en (enable; when low ALL state holds), valid, ready, data[127:0] (observed only), win_start (sampling-window start pulse). A handshake is hs = en & valid & ready. A stall is en & valid & !ready. State registers: txn_cnt[31:0] (+1 on hs); hs_d[0:0] (registered hs, one-cycle pipeline into the byte accumulator); byte_cnt[35:0] (+16 when en & hs_d, i.e. one 128-bit beat = 16 bytes, updated a cycle after the handshake); stall_cnt[31:0] (+1 per stall); lat_cur[15:0] (cycles valid has waited, cleared on hs); lat_cum[47:0] (+= lat_cur on hs); win_cnt[15:0] (sampling-window cycle counter, cleared on win_start, else +1); armed[0:0] (sticky, set on first en & win_start, never cleared except reset); seen_txn[0:0] (precedence shadow: sticky, set on first hs). Reset clears everything. When en=0 nothing changes, including hs_d. Relation R (holds by construction): (hs_d -> seen_txn) and (byte_cnt != 0 -> seen_txn) and byte_cnt == {txn_cnt - hs_d, 4'b0} (modulo widths). Property P (precedence, after-Q scope, guarded style): always @(posedge clk) if (armed && byte_cnt != 0) assert (seen_txn); i.e. once a sampling window has ever been started, any nonzero byte count must have been preceded by an observed handshake. P is true because byte_cnt only grows from a pending hs_d, and every hs_d was produced by a handshake that also set seen_txn. Counterexample to induction: armed=1, seen_txn=0, byte_cnt=0, txn_cnt=0, hs_d=1, other counters arbitrary. P holds (byte_cnt==0) but R is violated (hs_d without seen_txn). With en=0 this state is frozen indefinitely, so any k-length induction trace can idle in it; then one cycle with en=1, valid=0 gives byte_cnt=16 while seen_txn stays 0, violating P. Supplying R (specifically hs_d -> seen_txn together with byte_cnt != 0 -> seen_txn) makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: Exception/trap controller: Captures faulting cause and address and redirects control flow, keeping cause, epc, and status registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
AudioXtreamer stream-trap controller: traps I2S/USB-FIFO faults (overrun, underrun, clock-slip) raised by a 32-channel PCM streaming engine, pausing the stream and redirecting the host to a handler.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), fault_valid, fault_cause[63:0], frame_addr[63:0], mret, resume, host_arm, host_disarm.

State registers:
- cause[63:0]: last fault cause.
- epc[63:0]: sample-frame address of the fault.
- status[63:0]: bit0 PIE, the saved stream_active.
- trap_depth[63:0]: nesting counter, saturating.
- in_trap (1): handler owns the bus.
- stream_active (1): stream engine owns the bus.
- log_mem[32][63:0] and log_ptr[4:0]: ring log of causes.
- win (1): property window.

Behavior when en is high. Priority is fault, then mret, then resume.
- Fault: cause <= fault_cause, epc <= frame_addr, status[0] <= stream_active, log_mem[log_ptr] <= fault_cause, log_ptr++, trap_depth++, in_trap <= 1, stream_active <= 0.
- mret with trap_depth != 0: trap_depth--. If trap_depth == 1, then in_trap <= 0 and stream_active <= status[0].
- resume: if trap_depth == 0, stream_active <= 1. The guard tests the counter, not the in_trap flag.
- Window: host_arm sets win and host_disarm clears it, with disarm winning. The window can open and close repeatedly.
- Reset: all registers are cleared.

Relation R (holds by construction):
(in_trap == (trap_depth != 0)) && (stream_active -> trap_depth == 0) && (status[0] -> !in_trap || trap_depth == 1 || !stream_active)
In practice the key conjunct is in_trap <-> trap_depth != 0.

Property P (absence, edge style, scoped between host_arm and host_disarm; antecedents include win):
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) (win && $rose(stream_active)) |-> !in_trap);
In words, the handler and the stream never both own the bus when the stream restarts inside the window.

Why induction needs R: consider the state win=1, in_trap=1, trap_depth=0, stream_active=0, status=0, en=0.
- It satisfies P, since stream_active is not rising.
- It violates R, because in_trap=1 while trap_depth=0.
- It is held indefinitely while en=0, so it is reachable in any k-step induction prefix.
- It then steps to a violation: raise en and pulse resume with no fault or mret. Since trap_depth==0, stream_active rises while in_trap is still 1, falsifying P.

Given R, in_trap=1 forces trap_depth!=0, which blocks resume. The only path that raises stream_active from mret clears in_trap in the same cycle, so P becomes 1-inductive. The 64-bit trap_depth plus the 32x64 log make the state space too large for a bounded unrolling to substitute for R.

What it is: Johnson ring counter: Circulates a pattern through a shift register whose last bit is inverted back into the first stage.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module yat_phase_ring: the phase sequencer of a toy 3-stage RISC-V pipeline (fetch/decode/execute, YatCPU-style). It keeps two 32-bit Johnson ring counters that should always agree. One is the fetch-side phase token and the other is the execute-side shadow that the hazard unit checks.

Ports: clk, rst (synchronous, active high), advance (enable; when low, all state holds), and outputs fetch_phase[31:0] and exec_phase[31:0].

State registers:
- fetch_ring [31:0]
- exec_ring [31:0]

Behaviour:
- On reset both registers become 32'h0.
- When advance is high, both take the Johnson step: ring <= {ring[30:0], ~ring[31]}. The inverted MSB feeds back into bit 0, giving a 64-state cycle.
- When advance is low, both hold.
- The two rings use separate but identical update logic, with no cross-coupling.

Relation R (holds by construction): fetch_ring == exec_ring, all 32 bits equal in every reachable state. Both start at 0 and always apply the same deterministic step under the same enable.

Property P (universality, global, unclocked module-level form):
assert property (fetch_ring[31] == exec_ring[31]);
The MSBs of the two rings always match. This is the bit the hazard unit samples to tell first-half phases from second-half phases.

Why P needs R: P only constrains bit 31, but the next value of bit 31 is the current bit 30. P alone therefore cannot rule out a disagreement in a lower bit that later shifts up into bit 31.

Counterexample to induction (CTI):
- State: fetch_ring = 32'h00000000 and exec_ring = 32'h40000000.
- It satisfies P, since both have bit31 = 0.
- It violates R, since bit 30 differs.
- With advance = 0 this state can be held for any number of cycles, so every prefix of a k-induction trace satisfies P. This defeats induction at any depth k.
- On the next cycle with advance = 1, fetch_ring becomes 32'h00000001 and exec_ring becomes 32'h80000001. Now fetch_ring[31] = 0 and exec_ring[31] = 1, which violates P.

With R supplied as a strengthening invariant, P follows immediately, and R itself is 1-inductive: equal rings under the same update stay equal.

What it is: Timer event queue: Holds several software-programmed absolute deadlines and fires an event when the free-running time reaches the earliest, keeping a deadline array, per-entry valid bits and a register for the current earliest-deadline index.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module tx_pace_tq: a NIC TX packet-pacing timer event queue. Software programs 128-bit absolute launch timestamps for queued Ethernet frames; the shell fires a 'launch' event when the free-running PTP-style clock reaches the earliest deadline, and the user box acknowledges completion of the transmit.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (global enable; when en=0 every register holds), wr, wr_idx (1b), wr_data (128b), ack, clr. Outputs: fire, done.

State registers:
- now (128b), the free-running time, incremented when en=1.
- dl[0:1] (2 x 128b), the deadline array.
- vld (2b), per-entry valid bits.
- eidx (1b), the earliest valid entry: the one with the smaller deadline among the valid entries.
- phase (2b): 0 IDLE, 1 ARMED, 2 RUNNING, 3 DONE.
- started (1b), sticky.
- finished (1b), sticky.
- win (1b), the after-Q-until-R window.

Behavior (only when en=1):
- Arm (Q): wr writes dl[wr_idx] and sets vld[wr_idx]. If phase==IDLE, phase goes to ARMED and win is set to 1.
- Start: if phase==ARMED and vld[eidx] and now>=dl[eidx], then phase goes to RUNNING, started is set to 1, and fire pulses.
- Finish: if phase==RUNNING and ack, then phase goes to DONE, finished is set to 1, vld[eidx] is cleared, and done pulses.
- Close (R): clr returns phase to IDLE and clears started, finished and win. clr may never be asserted.
- rst behaves like clr and also zeroes vld and now.

Relation R (holds by construction, since started and finished change only on the transitions above):
(phase>=RUNNING -> started) && (phase==DONE -> finished) && (finished -> started) && (started -> phase!=IDLE) && (started -> win).

Property P, with guarded style and chain precedence inside the window:
always @(posedge clk) if (win && finished) assert (started);
Once armed, finish can never be observed without start having happened, whether or not clr ever closes the window.

Why k-induction fails without R (counterexample to induction):
- The state is win=1, phase=RUNNING, started=0, finished=0, vld=2'b01, eidx=0.
- It satisfies P because finished=0.
- It violates R because phase==RUNNING but started=0.
- With en=0 this state is held unchanged for any k cycles, so every step satisfies P.
- Then en=1 and ack=1, clr=0: the finish transition gives phase=DONE, finished=1, started=0, win=1, which violates P.

Given R as a strengthening invariant, P is 1-inductive. Phase can reach RUNNING only through the start transition, which sets started in the same cycle. Only clr or rst can lower started, and they also clear finished and win.

What it is: JK flip-flop: Keeps one state bit that on each clock edge holds, sets, resets, or toggles according to the J and K inputs.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module hadesv_mie_jk: a HaDes-V-style CSR interrupt-enable bit (mstatus.MIE) built as a JK flip-flop, with a 32-bit history counter and a trap window. Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle input; when low ALL state holds), j (csrrs sets MIE), k (csrrc clears MIE), trap_enter, mret. On a clock edge with en=1, the JK rules apply: j&~k sets, ~j&k resets, j&k toggles, ~j&~k holds.

State registers:
- q (1 bit): the MIE JK flop, reset 0.
- tcnt (32 bits): shadow history counter, reset 0. It increments, wrapping at 2^32, whenever en=1 and the next q differs from the current q. It records how many past changes of MIE occurred.
- in_trap (1 bit): window register, reset 0. With en=1 it is set by trap_enter and cleared by mret (mret wins if both). The window can open and close repeatedly.

Relation R, which holds by construction: q == tcnt[0]. MIE starts at 0, and every change of q flips tcnt's LSB. The wrap at 2^32 is even, so parity is preserved.

Property P (precedence, scope, edge style):
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) (in_trap && $rose(q)) |-> tcnt[0] == 1'b1);
Meaning: inside a trap window, whenever MIE rises, an odd number of MIE changes must already be on record in the shadow counter, counting the change that just happened. The shadow register thus witnesses that an earlier set event occurred.

Why P needs R: P alone is not k-inductive.
- Counterexample-to-induction state: q=0, tcnt=32'h0000_0001, in_trap=1.
- This state satisfies P, because q is not rising.
- It violates R, because q != tcnt[0].
- With en=0 it can be held for any number of cycles, so every finite k-step induction trace is consistent.
- Next apply en=1, j=1, k=0. Then q becomes 1, tcnt becomes 2, and tcnt[0] becomes 0.
- That cycle has in_trap=1 and $rose(q), but tcnt[0]==0, so P is violated.

Given R as a lemma, P follows in one step. If q rose, it is now 1, so R forces tcnt[0]=1.

What it is: RGMII adapter: Converts between double-data-rate PHY signaling and single-rate internal buses using DDR capture and launch registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
RGMII RX adapter feeding an AutoBridge-style 4-entry relay-station FIFO, which buffers data across a floorplan boundary. Inputs: clk, rst, en (holds ALL state when low), rgmii_rxd[3:0], rgmii_rx_ctl, rd_en (consumer pop). DDR capture is modeled at the single-rate clock: each cycle the inputs supply rise_d[3:0]/rise_ctl and fall_d[3:0]/fall_ctl. State registers: cap_rise[4:0] and cap_fall[4:0] (DDR capture registers); byte_ph[1:0] (byte lane inside the current word); shift[23:0] (assembled bytes 0-2); mem[0:3][31:0] (relay FIFO); wr_cnt[31:0] and rd_cnt[31:0] (free-running push/pop totals, indexed by bits [1:0]); occ[31:0] (separately maintained occupancy counter); armed (1 bit, sticky). When en=1: rx_dv = cap_rise[4]; byte = {cap_fall[3:0], cap_rise[3:0]}. A valid byte advances byte_ph and fills shift. On byte_ph==3, the module forms the word {byte, shift} and pushes it if !full, where full = ((wr_cnt - rd_cnt) == 4). push writes mem[wr_cnt[1:0]] and increments wr_cnt. pop = rd_en && (wr_cnt != rd_cnt); it increments rd_cnt. occ <= occ + push - pop. armed <= armed | rx_dv, so it is set by the first valid RGMII byte (event Q) and is never cleared. rst zeroes everything. Relation R (holds by construction): occ == wr_cnt - rd_cnt, and (wr_cnt - rd_cnt) <= 4. Property P (bounded existence, at most 4, which is far below the 32-bit range): always @(posedge clk) assert (!armed || occ <= 32'd4); Why induction fails without R: full is computed from the pointer difference, not from occ, so the inductive step admits states where occ disagrees with the pointers. Counterexample-to-induction state: armed=1, occ=4, wr_cnt=rd_cnt=7 (difference 0, so not full), byte_ph=3, cap_rise[4]=1. This state satisfies P (occ=4) and violates R (occ != 0). It can be held indefinitely with en=0. Then, with en=1 and rd_en=0, a word push occurs because full=0, so occ becomes 5 and P is violated. Supplying R as a lemma makes P 1-inductive: occ tracks the pointer difference, and pushes are blocked exactly when that difference is 4.

What it is: Tapped delay line: Propagates a signal through a chain of buffers and exposes intermediate taps, with optional sampling flops on each tap.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module gf180_tapline_cal: an 8-tap delay line modeled on a chain of gf180mcu 7-track buffer cells, with sampling flops on each tap and a one-shot calibration marker that measures propagation.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle/enable: when low ALL state holds), din[63:0], cal_start (Q), cal_done (R, may never arrive).

State registers:
- tap[0:7] : 8 x 64-bit data stage flops. When en is high, tap[0]<=din and tap[i]<=tap[i-1].
- samp[0:7] : 8 x 64-bit sampling flops. When en is high, samp[i]<=tap[i].
- tok[7:0] : marker bits riding alongside the taps.
- win : 1-bit calibration window register.
- cal_cnt[63:0] : cycles since the marker was injected.

Behavior (only when en=1):
- On cal_start: win<=1, tok<=8'b0000_0001, cal_cnt<=0.
- Else if cal_done: win<=0, tok<=0.
- Else if win: tok<=tok<<1, so the marker falls off past tap 7, and cal_cnt<=cal_cnt+1.
- Else: tok<=0.

Relation R, which holds by construction:
- win implies tok == ((cal_cnt < 8) ? (8'b1 << cal_cnt) : 8'b0).
- !win implies tok == 0.
- Consequently tok is always one-hot or zero.

Property P (absence, scope after Q until R): while the calibration window is open, the marker is never seen at tap 6 and tap 7 at the same time.

always @(*) assert (!(win && tok[6] && tok[7]));

The window opened by cal_start may stay open forever, and P must still hold.

Why k-induction fails without R: consider the state win=1, tok=8'b0110_0000 (bits 5 and 6 set), cal_cnt=5, with arbitrary taps.
- It satisfies P, because tok[7]=0.
- It violates R, because tok is not one-hot and does not equal 1<<cal_cnt.
- With en=0 it is held unchanged for any number of cycles, so it forms an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix.
- On one cycle with en=1 and cal_start=0, cal_done=0, tok shifts to 8'b1100_0000. Now win && tok[6] && tok[7] holds, violating P.

Supplying R as a helper invariant excludes this state and makes P inductive.

What it is: Trace cache: Stores dynamic instruction sequences that span taken branches as single lines, keeping per-line start address, branch outcome flags, instruction slots and the next fetch address.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module tc_trace_cache: a 16-line trace cache. Each line holds a dynamic instruction trace spanning taken branches.

Inputs:
- clk, rst_n.
- en: global enable. When en=0, every register holds.
- op[1:0]: 0=nop, 1=fill, 2=invalidate, 3=flush.
- idx[3:0], fill_start[31:0], fill_flags[3:0], fill_instr[3:0][31:0], fill_next[31:0].
- trace_begin (Q) and trace_end (R).

State registers:
- valid[15:0]
- start_addr[0:15][31:0]
- br_flags[0:15][3:0]
- slot[0:15][0:3][31:0]
- next_fa[0:15][31:0]
- occ[31:0]: occupancy counter.
- win (1 bit): window register.

Behaviour (only when en=1, one op per cycle):
- fill writes line idx and sets valid[idx]. occ increments only if valid[idx] was 0; overwriting a valid line keeps occ.
- invalidate clears valid[idx]. occ decrements only if valid[idx] was 1.
- flush clears valid and occ.
- The window register win is updated in the same cycle as the op:
  - set on trace_begin, which opens a trace-build window;
  - cleared on trace_end or flush;
  - trace_begin has priority if both are asserted.
  - The window can open and close any number of times.
- Lookup is combinational: compare fetch_pc against start_addr of valid lines; output slots, flags and next_fa. Lookup does not affect state.

Relation R (by construction): occ == $countones(valid). Every change to occ is paired with exactly one 0->1 or 1->0 flip of a valid bit, and flush zeroes both.

Property P (bounded existence, between trace_begin and trace_end, $stable style). Assertions are clocked; antecedents include win:
- A1: win && $stable(valid) |-> $stable(occ). While the window is open, if the valid vector did not change, the occupancy did not change.
- A2: win |-> occ <= 32'd16. Inside the window, occupancy never exceeds 16, far below the 2^32-1 the counter width allows.

P is true because R holds and popcount of 16 bits is at most 16.

Counterexample to induction without R:
- State: win=1, valid=16'h0000, occ=32'd16. This violates R (popcount is 0).
- P holds in this state. A2 holds since occ=16. A1 holds while idle: with en=0 nothing changes, so both valid and occ are stable. The state can therefore be held for any number of cycles, defeating every induction depth k.
- Step: en=1, op=fill, idx=0. Then valid[0] becomes 1 and occ becomes 17 while win stays 1, so A2 fails.

Given R as a lemma, occ=16 forces valid=16'hFFFF. A fill then only overwrites a valid line and leaves occ unchanged, so P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Power domain dependency tracker: Keeps parent domains powered while any child domain or requester needs them, holding per-domain usage reference counts and a domain-on vector.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Zynq PS power-domain tracker (GenZ-inspired: FCLK root domain feeding 128 PL/PS peripheral child domains). Inputs: en (when low ALL state holds), req_on, req_off, idx[6:0]. State: dom_on[127:0] (child-domain-on vector, 128 entries), refcnt[7:0] (root usage count, 0..128), root_on (1b), pend (1b, root power-up request outstanding), prog[7:0] (PLL-lock ramp progress), cd[7:0] (response-deadline countdown), first_n (1b, resets to 1; cleared the first time the root domain shuts down). Reset: all zero except first_n=1. Behaviour when en=1: req_on with !dom_on[idx] sets the bit and increments refcnt; if refcnt was 0 and !root_on && !pend, the request is accepted: pend<=1, prog<=0, cd<=24. While pend: prog<=prog+1, cd<=cd-1; when prog==19, pend<=0 and root_on<=1 (lock reached at 20). req_off (ignored while pend or if both req signals high) with dom_on[idx] clears the bit and decrements refcnt; if refcnt becomes 0 and root_on, root_on<=0 and first_n<=0. Relation R (by construction): pend -> (cd + prog == 24 && prog <= 19); also refcnt == popcount(dom_on) and (refcnt!=0) == (root_on||pend). Property P (bounded response, safety, before-R scope, $stable style): antecedents first_n && pend && $stable(pend); consequent $stable(cd == 8'd0) && cd != 8'd0, i.e. before the root has ever been shut down, whenever the outstanding-request flag did not change (still outstanding) the expired indication did not change and the countdown has not expired. True: under R, cd = 24 - prog >= 5 while pend. Not k-inductive alone: CTI state pend=1, prog=5, cd=1, first_n=1, refcnt=1, dom_on one bit set, root_on=0. It satisfies P (cd!=0) but violates R (cd+prog=6!=24); with en=0 it is held indefinitely (all registers stable, P keeps holding for any k), then one cycle with en=1 steps to prog=6, cd=0 with pend still 1, violating P. Supplying R as a lemma (cd+prog==24 under pend) makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: Memory-map address decoder: Compares an incoming address against programmed region descriptors and selects a target slave.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
PyMTL-themed 'TestHarness MMIO router': a 64-region memory-map decoder with one outstanding-transaction timeout tracker. Storage: base[0:63] and limit[0:63] (64-bit each), written through a config port (cfg_we, cfg_idx[5:0], cfg_base, cfg_limit). An incoming 64-bit req_addr hits region i if base[i] <= addr <= limit[i]; a priority encoder picks the lowest i. State registers: busy (1b), win (1b, scope window), sel (6b, chosen slave), cnt (64b countdown), age (64b elapsed cycles), plus the region table. Input en is the idle control: when en=0 every register, including the table, holds. Constant K=16. Reset: busy=0, win=0, cnt=0, age=0. When en=1: (a) Accept (Q): req && hit && !busy sets busy=1, win=1, sel=index, cnt=K, age=0. (b) While busy: cnt<=cnt-1 and age<=age+1. When age==K-1, the slave is force-completed: busy<=0, cnt<=0, age<=0. (c) The window close (R-event) is the input win_clr, which clears win. It may never be asserted, so win can stay high across later transactions; win_clr takes priority over (a). Relation R, which holds by construction: busy -> (cnt + age == K && age < K && cnt >= 1), and !busy -> (cnt == 0 && age == 0). Property P (scope after Q until R; win and busy are listed in both antecedents), two assertions: A1 (bounded response, safety form): (win && busy) -> cnt != 0. This means the countdown never expires while the request is outstanding. A2: (win && busy) -> cnt <= K. This means the countdown never wraps above its programmed budget. Neither assertion is inductive alone. For A2, the state busy=1, cnt=0, age=0 satisfies A2 but the decrement wraps cnt to 2^64-1. For A1, the state busy=1, cnt=1, age=0 satisfies A1 and steps to cnt=0. Even their conjunction is not inductive, and R closes both. Counterexample to induction: busy=1, win=1, cnt=1, age=0, sel=0, any table contents, en=0. This state satisfies A1 (cnt!=0) and A2 (1<=16). It violates R because cnt+age=1 != 16. It is held indefinitely while en=0, so a k-step induction trace can sit in it for any depth. When en rises with win_clr=0, age=0 != K-1, so no completion fires and cnt decrements to 0 while busy=1 and win=1. This violates A1, and a further step wraps cnt and violates A2. Given R, cnt reaches 1 exactly when age==K-1, and completion clears busy in that same step, so both assertions become k-inductive.

What it is: AXI-Stream switch: Routes AXI-Stream packets from several input ports to output ports according to TDEST, holding per-output current-input selection and a packet-in-progress lock cleared on TLAST.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module hft_feed_switch: a 4x4 AXI-Stream switch routing 128-bit market-data beats from four exchange feed ports to four order-book ports by 2-bit TDEST. Input en: when low, all state holds and no handshakes occur (all tready=0).

Ports: s_tvalid[4], s_tdata[4][128], s_tdest[4][2], s_tlast[4], s_tready[4]. m_tvalid[4], m_tdata[4][128], m_tlast[4], m_tready[4].

State registers:
- sel_o[0..3], 2 bits each: the input currently selected by output j.
- lock_o[0..3], 1 bit each: output j has a packet in progress.
- busy_i[0..3], 1 bit each: input i is owned by some output.
- dst_i[0..3], 2 bits each: the output that owns input i.
- win, 1 bit: the scope window.

Behaviour, when en=1:
- Combinational path: m_tvalid[j] = lock_o[j] && s_tvalid[sel_o[j]], and m_tdata and m_tlast are muxed from sel_o[j]. s_tready[i] = busy_i[i] && m_tready[dst_i[i]].
- Grant: an unlocked output j grants the lowest i with s_tvalid[i] && s_tdest[i]==j && !busy_i[i]. The grant sets lock_o[j]=1, sel_o[j]=i, busy_i[i]=1 and dst_i[i]=j. TDEST is unique per input, so two outputs never grant the same input in one cycle.
- Release: a TLAST handshake on output j clears lock_o[j] and busy_i[sel_o[j]].
- Window: win is set when output 0 grants (Q). It is cleared by the TLAST handshake on output 0 (R). That handshake may never come.

Relation R (holds by construction), for every j:
- lock_o[j] -> (busy_i[sel_o[j]] && dst_i[sel_o[j]]==j).
- win -> lock_o[0].

Property P, at module level and unclocked:
assert property (!(win && lock_o[0]) || ((!lock_o[1] || sel_o[1]!=sel_o[0]) && (!lock_o[2] || sel_o[2]!=sel_o[0]) && (!lock_o[3] || sel_o[3]!=sel_o[0])));
From output 0's grant onward, whether or not its packet ever ends, no other order book is locked onto the same feed as book 0.

Why P is not inductive alone, shown by a state s:
- s has win=1, lock_o[0]=1, sel_o[0]=2, busy_i[2]=0, dst_i[2]=0. All other locks and busy bits are 0.
- s satisfies P, since no other output is locked.
- s violates R, since busy_i[2] should be 1.
- With en=0, s is held indefinitely.
- Then en=1 arrives with s_tvalid[2]=1, s_tdest[2]=1 and s_tlast[2]=0. Output 1 sees input 2 as not busy and grants it, so lock_o[1]=1 and sel_o[1]=2.
- Output 0 sees no TLAST, so win stays 1.
- The next state violates P.

With R supplied, busy_i[2]=1 blocks this grant, so P becomes inductive.

What it is: Matrix tile register file: Holds two-dimensional tiles of rows by columns accessed row-wise for loads and stores and as whole operands by a matrix engine, keeping the tile data and a per-tile shape configuration register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module tile_rf_led: a matrix tile register file in the style of a hobby FPGA gateware block (think ice40 demo). Storage mem[0:15] holds 64-bit rows. Row-wise stores fill rows; a matrix engine 'consume' reads the whole tile as one operand; a per-tile shape config limits how many rows may be filled.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (idle/enable: when low, every state register holds its value), ld, ld_data[63:0], consume, reshape, new_rows[4:0].

State registers:
- mem[16][63:0]: tile data.
- wptr[4:0]: next row index.
- fill_cnt[63:0]: rows loaded since the last consume.
- shape_rows[4:0]: configured row count. Resets to 12.
- pristine (1 bit): resets to 1.

Behavior when en is high:
- ld with wptr != shape_rows: write mem[wptr] = ld_data, then wptr++ and fill_cnt++. Saturation is decided only by wptr.
- consume: wptr = 0 and fill_cnt = 0. The engine reads mem as the operand.
- reshape (only accepted when wptr == 0): shape_rows = min(new_rows, 16) and pristine = 0. The scope event R_evt is the first reshape.
- Reset: wptr = 0, fill_cnt = 0, shape_rows = 12, pristine = 1.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- fill_cnt == {59'b0, wptr}
- wptr <= shape_rows
- pristine -> (shape_rows == 12)

Property P (pattern: bounded existence, at most 12; scope: before the first reshape; pristine is listed in the antecedents):
always @(posedge clk) assert (!pristine || fill_cnt <= 64'd12);
The bound 12 is far below the 2^64 range of fill_cnt, so it is a genuine reachability fact. It also holds only before reshape, since afterwards shape_rows may be 16.

Why k-induction fails without R: P constrains only fill_cnt, while the saturation guard uses wptr. Counterexample-to-induction state:
- pristine = 1, shape_rows = 12, wptr = 5, fill_cnt = 12.
- It satisfies P (12 <= 12) but violates R (fill_cnt != wptr).
- It can be held indefinitely with en = 0, so any length of P-satisfying prefix exists.
- Then en = 1, ld = 1: wptr = 5 != 12, so the store is accepted. fill_cnt becomes 13 while pristine is still 1, which violates P.

With R supplied, fill_cnt equals wptr, which is at most shape_rows = 12 while pristine, so P is 1-inductive.

What it is: Distributed-arithmetic multiplier: Computes a sum of products with fixed coefficients by using the input bits, one bit position per cycle, to address a precomputed table and shift-accumulating the outputs; it keeps the coefficient-sum ROM, input shift registers, an accumulator and a bit counter.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Theme: a fixed-coefficient 4-tap distributed-arithmetic (DA) filter coprocessor beside a RISC-V core. It post-processes 32-bit words fetched in a PSRAM burst, one bit slice per cycle, like an ad-hoc multi-cycle pipeline stage.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), start, d0..d3[31:0].

State registers:
- x0, x1, x2, x3 [31:0]: input shift registers.
- acc [63:0]: accumulator.
- cnt [31:0]: bit counter, counts up.
- rem [31:0]: shadow down-counter of remaining bit slices.
- busy (1 bit).
- win (1 bit): the property window.
- rom: a constant 16x32 table where rom[a] is the sum of coefficients C_i over all i with a[i]=1.

Behaviour (all updates only when en is high):
- Reset: cnt=0, rem=32, busy=0, win=0, acc=0.
- Q (start while !busy): load x_i<=d_i, acc<=0, cnt<=0, rem<=32, busy<=1, win<=1.
- Each busy cycle:
  - acc <= acc + (rom[{x3[0],x2[0],x1[0],x0[0]}] << cnt).
  - Each x_i shifts right by one.
  - cnt <= cnt+1 and rem <= rem-1.
  - When cnt==31 this is the final slice. It sets busy<=0 and win<=0; this is event R (done).
- The window reopens on every later start, so it opens and closes many times.

Relation R (holds by construction):
(cnt + rem == 32) && (cnt <= 32) && (busy -> cnt <= 31)

Property P (bounded existence, at most k), as two assertions that use the window in their antecedents:
- A1: win -> cnt <= 32
- A2: win -> rem <= 32

Both bounds are far below the 2^32 range of the registers.
- A1 alone is not inductive: a busy state with cnt=32 satisfies it but steps to 33.
- A2 alone is not inductive: a busy state with rem=0 satisfies it but wraps to 0xFFFFFFFF.
- R closes both:
  - busy implies cnt<=31, so cnt+1<=32.
  - busy implies rem = 32-cnt >= 1, so rem-1 does not wrap.
  - When idle, cnt and rem hold; on start they reset to 0 and 32.

Counterexample to induction without R: win=1, busy=1, cnt=32, rem=0.
- It satisfies A1 (32<=32) and A2 (0<=32).
- It violates R (busy with cnt=32).
- It is held indefinitely while en=0, since all state freezes.
- On the next cycle with en=1 (cnt is 32, not 31, so busy stays high and the window stays open), cnt becomes 33 and rem becomes 0xFFFFFFFF. That violates both A1 and A2 inside the window.

What it is: Thermometer-to-binary encoder: Converts a thermometer-coded input vector into the binary count of its asserted lines, optionally latching the result in an output register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Dual-adder thermometer totalizer (ripple vs. lookahead). Inputs: clk, en (when low all state holds), therm[63:0] (thermometer code, lines asserted from bit 0 upward). A combinational encoder produces cnt[6:0] = number of asserted lines (popcount, 0..64, valid for any input). Each enabled cycle the count is added into two redundant 64-bit accumulators built from different adder structures, echoing the README's adder comparison.

State registers:
- rca_sum[63:0]: updated through a 64-bit carry-ripple adder, rca_sum <= rca_sum + cnt.
- cla_sum[63:0]: updated through a 64-bit carry-lookahead adder (4-bit generate/propagate groups), cla_sum <= cla_sum + cnt.
- armed (1 bit): sticky, armed <= armed | (en && therm[63]). Event Q is the first full-scale (all-64-lines) sample; armed is never cleared.
- pv (1 bit): past-valid, reset 0, pv <= 1.
All of these reset to 0, and rca_sum, cla_sum and armed update only when en=1. The output register is out = rca_sum.

Relation R (by construction): rca_sum == cla_sum. Both reset to 0 and always add the same cnt under the same enable. The two adder structures are functionally identical.

Property P (precedence, after Q, $past style): the ripple total seen now must equal the lookahead total from the previous cycle plus the count sampled then.
always @(posedge clk) if (pv && armed && $past(en)) assert (rca_sum == $past(cla_sum) + $past(cnt));
The $past(cla_sum) and $past(cnt) values act as the shadow of the earlier event.

Why induction fails without R: take the state rca_sum=1, cla_sum=0, armed=1, pv=1. Hold it with en=0, so $past(en)=0 and P is vacuous; R is violated and P holds, and the state persists indefinitely while idle. Next, raise en=1 with therm=0, so cnt=0. In the following cycle rca_sum=1 but $past(cla_sum)+$past(cnt)=0, so P fails. An arbitrarily long idle prefix defeats any fixed k. Supplying R (rca_sum == cla_sum) as a strengthening invariant makes P inductive. R is itself inductive, because both registers start equal and receive identical increments under identical enables.

What it is: Failover source multiplexer: Forwards a primary source and switches to a backup when the primary is reported faulty, keeping a health-status register and an active-source flag.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module dbg_failover_mux: a debug-transport source selector that forwards 8-bit DMI data from a primary JTAG DTM and fails over to a backup DTM. Inputs are clk, rst_n, en, pri_data[7:0], bak_data[7:0], pri_fault and pri_ok. The input en is the idle/enable control: when en is low, every register holds its value. Output is out_data = active_src ? bak_data : pri_data.

State registers:
- health[7:0]: saturating fault counter. It increments on pri_fault and clears on a completed recovery.
- arm_f (1 bit): the arm step of the failover chain.
- start_f (1 bit): the start step.
- fin_f (1 bit): the finish step.
- active_src (1 bit): 0 selects primary, 1 selects backup.

Update rules, applied only when en is high:
- arm_f <= 1 when health >= 8'd3 and !arm_f.
- start_f <= 1 when arm_f && pri_fault && !start_f.
- fin_f <= 1 when start_f && !fin_f.
- active_src <= 1 when start_f && arm_f && !active_src.
- Recovery: when pri_ok && fin_f && active_src, clear arm_f, start_f, fin_f, active_src and health together.

From reset (all zero), active_src and fin_f always rise in the same cycle (start_f implies arm_f) and clear in the same cycle.

Relation R (holds by construction): (active_src == fin_f) && (start_f -> arm_f) && (fin_f -> start_f).

Property P (global, no arming register, $stable style): assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) $stable(fin_f) |-> $stable(active_src)). In words: whenever the finish flag of the arm->start->finish chain did not change, the active-source flag must not have changed either. This means the source can never be switched unless the finish step is observed in the same cycle, and finish itself is reachable only after arm and start.

Counterexample to induction without R: take the state arm_f=1, start_f=1, fin_f=1, active_src=0, health=8'd3.
- It violates R because active_src != fin_f.
- With en low, all state is held, so fin_f and active_src are both stable and P holds for any number of idle cycles.
- On the next cycle with en high, the condition start_f && arm_f && !active_src fires, so active_src rises from 0 to 1. Meanwhile fin_f stays at 1 because !fin_f is false.
- So $stable(fin_f) is true while $stable(active_src) is false, and P is violated.

The induction step therefore fails unless the prover is given active_src == fin_f, which makes the k-induction proof of P go through.

What it is: Mode register programming unit: Issues MRS/MRW commands that load CAS latency, burst length, ODT and drive-strength settings into the DRAM, keeping shadow copies of each mode register and a pending-update flag set.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module orbit_mrs_unit: a DRAM mode-register programming unit, framed as an Orbit-style 'package installer' that installs one configuration word (CAS latency, burst length, ODT, drive strength, etc.) into one of 8 mode registers at a time.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en, req_valid, req_idx[2:0], req_data[15:0], cfg_lock. When en is low, every state register holds its value.

State registers:
- shadow[0:7], each 16 bits: shadow copies of the mode registers.
- pend[7:0]: pending-update flags.
- cur_idx[2:0]: index of the register being updated.
- cur_data[15:0]: data being written.
- cnt[15:0]: tMRD/tMOD countdown.
- win (1 bit): observation window.

Output: busy = |pend.

Behavior on each clock edge with en=1:
- Accept: if req_valid && !busy, the unit accepts the request. It sets pend[req_idx], latches cur_idx and cur_data, loads cnt=16'd8, and drives mrs_cmd_valid with {req_idx, req_data}.
- Count down: else if busy && cnt>1, cnt decrements.
- Complete: else if busy && cnt==1, then shadow[cur_idx]<=cur_data, pend[cur_idx]<=0 and cnt<=0.
- Window: win is set on an accept (Q). It is cleared when cfg_lock is asserted (R). cfg_lock may never arrive.
- Reset clears all registers.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- pend is either zero or exactly the one-hot vector (8'b1 << cur_idx).
- (pend != 0) == (cnt != 0).
- cnt <= 8.

Property P (bounded response, safety form, scope 'after Q until R'): the countdown never expires while the request is still outstanding inside the window.
always @(posedge clk) assert (!(win && busy) || (cnt != 16'd0));

Counterexample to induction (CTI):
- State: win=1, pend=8'b0000_0011, cur_idx=0, cnt=16'd1, other registers arbitrary.
- P holds: busy=1 and cnt!=0.
- R is violated: two pending bits are set, which is not one-hot.
- With en=0 the state is frozen indefinitely, so it can be held while idle.
- Next step with en=1 and cfg_lock=0: completion fires because cnt==1. It clears only pend[0] and sets cnt=0. pend becomes 8'b0000_0010, so busy is still 1 while cnt=0 and win=1. P fails.

Why R is needed: from reachable states, only one bit of pend is ever set, so completion always drops busy in the same cycle cnt reaches 0. k-induction on P alone cannot exclude the multi-pending CTI, because the en=0 stall lets it persist for any k. Supplying R (one-hot pend tied to cur_idx, busy iff cnt nonzero, cnt bounded by 8) makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: Bipartite table function unit: Approximates a smooth function by adding outputs of a coarse table-of-initial-values and a smaller table-of-offsets indexed by different input bit fields, keeping both tables and the sum register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
DRAM retention-time estimator, a bipartite table unit themed on DRAM Bender. A 4-bit temperature code x selects entries in two tables: x[3:2] indexes a coarse table-of-initial-values (TIV) and x[1:0] indexes a table-of-offsets (TO). The unit outputs an 8-bit refresh-interval estimate through a 2-stage pipeline.

Ports: clk, rst, en (idle input: when en=0 every register holds), x[3:0], and output est[7:0]=sum_q.

Constants: TIVc={200,150,100,60} and TOc={0,12,24,36}.

State:
- tiv[0:3] (8b each) and to[0:3] (8b each): table registers loaded with TIVc/TOc at reset and never written.
- Stage 1: idx1 (4b), the shadow of the accepted input; tiv_r (8b); to_r (8b).
- Stage 2: idx2 (4b), the shadow carried from idx1; sum_q (8b), the sum register.
- arm (1b): sticky; set on the first en-high cycle after reset (Q = first lookup accepted) and never cleared.

Reset values: idx1=0, tiv_r=200, to_r=0, idx2=0, sum_q=200, arm=0.

On an en-high cycle:
- idx1<=x; tiv_r<=tiv[x[3:2]]; to_r<=to[x[1:0]].
