- idx2<=idx1; sum_q<=tiv_r+to_r.
- arm<=1.

Relation R (holds by construction), with i ranging over 0..3:
arm -> (tiv[i]==TIVc[i] && to[i]==TOc[i] && tiv_r==TIVc[idx1[3:2]] && to_r==TOc[idx1[1:0]]).

Property P (precedence, after-Q scope): an estimate observed now must equal the table sum for the input recorded earlier in the shadow idx2.
always @(posedge clk) assert (!arm || sum_q == TIVc[idx2[3:2]] + TOc[idx2[1:0]]);

Why induction needs R: P constrains only stage 2. A stage-1 corruption can sit indefinitely while en=0, so no k-step window rules it out unless R is given.

Counterexample-to-induction state:
- arm=1; tables correct.
- idx2=4'b0000, sum_q=200, so P holds.
- idx1=4'b0101, which requires tiv_r=150 and to_r=12.
- But tiv_r=0, so R is violated.

With en=0 the state is held for any number of cycles while P keeps holding. On the next en=1 cycle, idx2 becomes 0101 and sum_q becomes 0+12=12, whereas P requires 150+12=162. P is violated.

What a strengthened proof uses: given R, stage 1 always holds the correct table values for idx1. Its sum therefore always moves into sum_q together with idx1 moving into idx2, so P is preserved.

What it is: UART receiver: Samples an asynchronous serial line at mid-bit and assembles a byte in a shift register with bit counter and framing-error flag.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
SD-link line-fill UART: a UART receiver that collects 16-bit words from a serial 'secondary storage' link into an 8-entry cache-line fill buffer, mimicking a main-memory-to-cache line refill.

Ports: clk, rst (sync), en (when low every state register holds its value), rx (serial line), flush (pulse: empties the line, valid only when en is high). Parameter CLKS_PER_BIT = 16.

State registers: st[1:0] (IDLE, START, DATA, STOP); baud_cnt[15:0], which counts toward a mid-bit sample point; bit_cnt[15:0] (0..15 data bits); shreg[15:0], which shifts in data LSB-first; line[0:7][15:0] (fill buffer); wr_ptr[2:0]; occ[15:0] (words held in the line); line_full (1 bit); frame_err (1 bit, sticky until flush); armed (1 bit, sticky, never cleared, not even by flush).

Behaviour (only when en=1):
- IDLE: a falling edge on rx enters START.
- START: re-checks rx at mid-bit and enters DATA if rx is still low.
- DATA: samples 16 bits at mid-bit.
- STOP: samples the stop bit at mid-bit.
  - Stop bit = 0 sets frame_err and drops the word.
  - Stop bit = 1 with !line_full commits the word: line[wr_ptr] <= shreg, wr_ptr++, occ++, line_full <= (occ+1 == 8), armed <= 1.
  - Stop bit = 1 with line_full drops the word as an overrun.
- flush clears occ, wr_ptr, line_full and frame_err.
- rst clears everything, including armed.

Relation R (by construction): line_full == (occ == 8) && occ <= 8 && wr_ptr == occ[2:0].

Property P (bounded existence, at most 8, out of a 16-bit range; scope after the first committed word):
always @(posedge clk) if (armed) assert (occ <= 16'd8);

Why induction fails without R: consider the state where
- armed=1, occ=8, line_full=0, wr_ptr=0;
- st=STOP, baud_cnt one tick before the mid-bit sample point.

This state satisfies P (occ=8) but violates R, because line_full should be 1. With en=0 it can be held for any number of cycles, so the k-induction prefix is a constant stutter that obeys P. Then raise en=1 with rx=1: the stop bit is sampled valid, and because !line_full the word commits. occ becomes 9 while armed=1, so P fails. With R, occ==8 forces line_full=1, which blocks the commit, while occ<8 gives at most 8 after an increment; flush only lowers occ. So P together with R is 1-inductive.

What it is: Device identification ROM: Exposes read-only vendor, part, revision, and feature-capability words at fixed register addresses, keeping the hardwired ID constants and a read-data output register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module perfect_id_rom: a PERFECT-themed device identification ROM that auto-scans six hardwired 32-bit ID words. Each word is presented on a registered read-data output, like a Chisel ID-chain walker.

Constants (localparam, 6 entries x 32 bits):
- ROM[0] VENDOR = 0x49424D00 ("IBM")
- ROM[1] PART = 0x50455246 ("PERF")
- ROM[2] REVISION = 0x00000003
- ROM[3] FEAT0 = 0x0000C3A5
- ROM[4] FEAT1 = 0x00000011
- ROM[5] SIGNATURE = 0x43484933 ("CHI3")

Ports: clk, rst (synchronous), en (scan enable / idle when low), rdata[31:0], last.

State registers:
- ptr [31:0]: current ROM index.
- remaining [31:0]: words left before wrap.
- rdata_q [31:0]: read-data output register.

Reset values: ptr = 0, remaining = 5, rdata_q = 0.

When en is low, all three registers hold. When en is high, the update is deliberately cross-coupled:
- rdata_q <= ROM[ptr], or 0 if ptr > 5.
- ptr <= (remaining == 0) ? 0 : ptr + 1. The pointer wraps on the other counter.
- remaining <= (ptr == 5) ? 5 : remaining - 1. The countdown reloads on the pointer.
- last = (remaining == 0).

Relation R (holds by construction): ptr <= 5 && remaining == 5 - ptr. The two counters always sum to 5, so ptr hits 5 exactly when remaining hits 0, and both branches fire together.

Property P (Bounded Existence, at most k, global, two assertions, no arming register):
- A1: assert property (ptr <= 5). The index never exceeds 5 even though 32 bits allow about 4e9.
- A2: assert property (remaining <= 5). The countdown never exceeds 5.

Why neither is inductive alone:
- A1 alone, state ptr=5, remaining=3: remaining != 0, so ptr steps to 6.
- A2 alone, state ptr=2, remaining=0: ptr != 5, so remaining underflows to 0xFFFFFFFF.
- Even A1 && A2 together are not inductive; the counterexample to induction (CTI) below satisfies both.
- Adding R closes both: the wrap and the reload are then simultaneous, so ptr stays in 0..5 and remaining = 5 - ptr stays in 0..5.

CTI (satisfies P, violates R, holdable while idle, steps to a P violation):
- State: ptr = 5, remaining = 3, rdata_q = 0.
- P holds: 5 <= 5 and 3 <= 5.
- R is violated: 5 - 5 = 0, not 3.
- With en = 0 the state is held indefinitely, so it survives any induction depth k.
- With en = 1, remaining != 0 so ptr becomes 6, violating A1. Meanwhile ptr == 5 reloads remaining to 5.

The mirror state ptr = 3, remaining = 0 is also held while idle. It steps to remaining = 0xFFFFFFFF, violating A2.

So k-induction on A1 and A2 fails for every k without R and succeeds at k = 1 once R is supplied as a strengthening invariant.

What it is: Hamming-distance threshold comparator: Counts the bit positions in which two words differ and compares that count to a programmable tolerance, holding the tolerance register and a registered near-match flag.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
JSON key fuzzy matcher: a stored 8-bit query key token is compared against incoming 8-bit key tokens streamed from a JSON parser, and a key is accepted as a 'near match' when the Hamming distance is within a programmable tolerance (for tolerant path lookup).

Inputs: clk, rst, en (enable; when low ALL state below holds), key_in[7:0], query[7:0], ld_tol, tol_in[3:0], q_open (Q: path query starts), q_close (R: query ends; may never arrive).

State registers:
- tol[3:0]: tolerance, loaded from tol_in when en && ld_tol. Reset 0.
- near (1b): registered near-match flag. When en: near <= (popcount(key_in ^ query) <= tol). Reset 0.
- far (1b): redundant mismatch flag. It is not computed directly. When en it toggles exactly when near toggles: far <= far ^ (near ^ near_nxt). Reset 1.
- win (1b): query window. When en: win <= q_open ? 1 : (q_close ? 0 : win). Reset 0.
- pv (1b): past-valid checker register, pv <= 1 every cycle. Reset 0.

popcount(key_in ^ query) is a 4-bit combinational distance (0..8).

Relation R (by construction): far == !near. It holds at reset (0/1). Every enabled update flips both or neither, and idle holds both.

Property P (absence, after q_open until q_close, previous-cycle style):
always @(posedge clk) if (pv && $past(win)) assert (!($past(near) && $past(far)));
Near-match and mismatch are never asserted together while the query window is open. This must hold even if q_close never arrives.

Why k-induction fails without R: consider the state near=0, far=0, win=1, tol=8, with pv=1.
- It satisfies P, since near && far is false.
- It violates R, since far is not !near.
- With en=0 it can be held for any number of cycles, so it supplies an arbitrarily long P-satisfying induction prefix.
- Then raise en with any key_in. The distance is at most 8, which is within tol=8, so near_nxt=1. near toggles 0->1, and far toggles 0->1, giving near=far=1 with win still 1.
- On the next cycle the assertion sees $past(win)=1, $past(near)=1 and $past(far)=1, so P fails.

Once far == !near is supplied as an invariant, P follows immediately, because near && far contradicts far == !near.

What it is: Boundary-scan register chain: Captures and drives chip pin values through a serial chain of boundary cells with capture and update latches.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module monocle_bscan: a 24-cell boundary-scan chain for the Monocle FPGA's camera, display and SPI pins.

Ports: clk, rst_n, en (idle input; when low, every register holds), capture, update, shift, tdi, pins_in[23:0]. Outputs: tdo = shift_reg[0] and pins_out[23:0] = update_reg.

State registers:
- shift_reg[23:0]: the capture/shift latches.
- update_reg[23:0]: the update latches that drive the pins.
- shifted_cnt[15:0]: bits shifted in during the current frame.
- remain_cnt[15:0]: bits still needed to complete the frame.
- armed (1 bit): sticky flag.

Reset values: shift_reg=0, update_reg=0, shifted_cnt=0, remain_cnt=24, armed=0.

Behavior when en=1, with priority capture > update > shift:
- capture: shift_reg<=pins_in; shifted_cnt<=0; remain_cnt<=24; armed<=1.
- update: update_reg<=shift_reg; shifted_cnt<=0; remain_cnt<=24.
- shift, only when remain_cnt!=0: shift_reg<={tdi,shift_reg[23:1]}; shifted_cnt<=shifted_cnt+1; remain_cnt<=remain_cnt-1.

The chain reports two status flags:
- frame_full = (remain_cnt==0), meaning the chain is fully loaded.
- frame_empty = (shifted_cnt==0), meaning nothing has been shifted yet.

Relation R, which holds by construction: shifted_cnt + remain_cnt == 16'd24, computed with a 16-bit sum. Both reloads set the pair to (0,24). Each shift moves one unit from remain_cnt to shifted_cnt, so the sum never changes.

Property P uses the absence pattern with the after-capture scope. The event Q is a capture with en high, and it sets armed, which is never cleared. The check is a plain combinational assertion:
always @(*) assert (!armed || !(shifted_cnt==16'd0 && remain_cnt==16'd0));
In words, once armed, the chain is never flagged full and empty at once. Under R the two counters sum to 24, so they cannot both be zero.

Counterexample to induction without R: armed=1, shifted_cnt=16'hFFFF, remain_cnt=16'd1, with any shift_reg and update_reg values.
- It satisfies P, because remain_cnt is not zero.
- It violates R, because the 16-bit sum is 0, not 24.
- It is held indefinitely while en=0, so an idle prefix of any length k passes P.
- One step with en=1, shift=1, capture=0 and update=0 wraps shifted_cnt to 0 and decrements remain_cnt to 0. Both flags are then set while armed is high, which violates P.

Longer variants defeat larger k without any idle cycles. For example, armed=1, shifted_cnt=65535-j, remain_cnt=j+1 satisfies P for j+1 consecutive shifts and then fails. k-induction therefore needs R, which together with P is inductive.

What it is: Reset synchronizer: Asserts reset asynchronously and releases it synchronously using a short chain of flip-flops.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module friscv_hart_rst_sync: a reset synchronizer for a RISC-V platform's hart. It asserts the hart reset asynchronously and releases it synchronously through a 4-entry flop chain. Software can also request a hart reset (e.g. through a CLINT-style write), and each request is bounded by a 64-bit release watchdog.

Ports: clk, arst_n (asynchronous, active low), en (enable; when low, every register holds), soft_req, and output hart_rst_n = sync[3].

State registers:
- sync[3:0]: 4-entry synchronizer chain.
- cnt[63:0]: release countdown.
- pend (1 bit): request outstanding.
- win (1 bit): property window.

Behavior:
- arst_n low asynchronously clears sync, cnt, pend and win.
- Accept (en && soft_req && !pend): sync<=4'b0000, cnt<=64'd6, pend<=1, win<=1. This accept is Q.
- While en && pend && sync!=4'b1111: sync<={sync[2:0],1'b1}, cnt<=cnt-1.
- When en && pend && sync==4'b1111: pend<=0, win<=0. This completion is R.
- When en is low, nothing changes.
- Trace of one request: 0000/6, 0001/5, 0011/4, 0111/3, 1111/2, then pend drops.
- The window opens on every new soft_req after completion, so it opens and closes repeatedly.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- win == pend.
- pend implies sync is a thermometer code (sync is one of 0000, 0001, 0011, 0111, 1111).
- pend implies cnt == 6 - popcount(sync).

Property P (bounded response, safety form, edge style, window in antecedent): assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!arst_n) (win && $rose(sync[3])) |-> (cnt != 64'd0)). In words: when the synchronized reset is released inside the window, the countdown has not expired while the request is still outstanding.

Counterexample to induction:
- State: pend=1, win=1, sync=4'b0111, cnt=64'd1.
- P holds in this state, because sync[3] has not risen.
- R is violated, because R requires cnt=3.
- With en=0 the state is held for any number of cycles, so k-induction cannot rule it out using P alone.
- With en=1 it steps to sync=4'b1111 and cnt=0 with win still 1, so $rose(sync[3]) fires with cnt==0 and P fails.
- Given R, cnt is 2 whenever sync[3] rises, so P is k-inductive.

What it is: Redundancy-steering row decoder: Decodes a row address but compares it against fuse-loaded repair addresses and activates a spare row instead on a match, keeping the repair address registers and their enable bits.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module hack_rowfix: a Hack-RAM (nand2tetris) row decoder with fuse-based row repair. Each lookup scans a 16-entry repair table, 4 entries per cycle. If any enabled fuse address equals the latched row, the decoder selects that spare row; otherwise it selects the normal decoded row.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), req, row_addr[63:0], fuse_load, fuse_idx[3:0], fuse_val[63:0], fuse_reload.

State registers:
- fuse_addr[0:15] (64-bit each) and fuse_en[0:15] (1-bit each).
- lat_addr (64-bit) holds the latched request row.
- busy (1-bit) marks a request as outstanding.
- idx (5-bit) is the scan pointer.
- cnt (64-bit) is the response countdown.
- hit (1-bit) and hit_slot (4-bit) record a spare match.
- spare_sel (5-bit) and row_out (64-bit) are the outputs.
- pre_ev (1-bit) resets to 1.

Behaviour, applied only when en is high:
- A fuse_load writes fuse_addr[fuse_idx] = fuse_val and sets fuse_en.
- If req && !busy, the request is accepted: lat_addr = row_addr, busy = 1, idx = 0, cnt = 4, hit = 0.
- While busy, the module compares entries idx..idx+3 against lat_addr and records the first enabled match. It then sets idx += 4 and cnt -= 1.
- When busy && idx == 12, the request completes: busy = 0, and the outputs are driven (spare row on hit, else decoded lat_addr).
- fuse_reload is the scope event. It restarts the scan (idx = 0) without reloading cnt, and clears pre_ev forever.

Relation R, which holds by construction before any reload:
pre_ev && busy -> (idx[1:0] == 0 && idx <= 12 && cnt == 4 - idx[4:2])

This means the countdown stays exactly locked to the scan progress.

Property P (bounded response, before-event scope; antecedent is pre_ev):
- A1: pre_ev && busy -> cnt != 0. The countdown never expires while a request is outstanding, so completion occurs within 4 cycles.
- A2: pre_ev && busy -> idx < 16. The scan never overruns the 16-entry repair table.

Neither assertion is inductive alone:
- A1 fails induction from the state busy, idx = 4, cnt = 1.
- A2 fails induction from the state busy, idx = 13: the scan skips the completion point and reaches 17.

Given R, both assertions become inductive. Completion happens exactly when cnt == 1 and idx == 12, and before completion cnt never reaches 0 and idx never exceeds 12.

Counterexample to induction:
- State: pre_ev = 1, busy = 1, idx = 4, cnt = 1, other registers arbitrary.
- It satisfies A1 (cnt != 0) and A2 (idx < 16).
- It violates R, which requires cnt = 3 at idx = 4.
- With en low, the state is held indefinitely.
- With en high and no fuse_reload, idx != 12, so the request stays busy and cnt steps to 0, giving busy && cnt == 0 and violating A1.
- The companion state idx = 13, cnt = 4 steps to idx = 17, violating A2.
- Neither state is reachable from reset, because acceptance always sets idx = 0, cnt = 4, and each step moves both in lockstep.

What it is: Golay code encoder/decoder: Encodes 12-bit words into 24-bit extended Golay codewords and corrects up to three bit errors via syndrome lookup, keeping a syndrome register and a decode lookup table.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Clio-style memory-node Golay scrubber (golay_scrub). A 16-entry store mem[0:15] holds 24-bit extended Golay codewords; host writes encode 12-bit data via the generator matrix. A scrub engine walks entries, computes a 12-bit syndrome, and corrects up to 3 errors through a decode lookup table.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), wr, wr_addr[3:0], wr_data[11:0], inj, inj_addr[3:0], inj_mask[23:0] (fault injection, models link/DRAM upset), scrub_start, scrub_done.

State: mem[0:15] (24b each); err_flag[15:0] (per-entry 'possibly corrupted' bit); syn_reg[11:0]; scan_ptr[3:0]; inj_cnt[31:0]; corr_cnt[31:0]; inj_seen (1b, shadow, sticky, set on any accepted inj); win (1b, set by scrub_start, cleared by scrub_done, can reopen repeatedly). On rst, all of these are cleared and mem is reset to encode(0).

Behavior when en=1: inj XORs inj_mask into mem[inj_addr], sets err_flag[inj_addr], increments inj_cnt and sets inj_seen. wr stores encode(wr_data) and clears err_flag[wr_addr]. While win=1, each cycle the engine latches syn_reg = syndrome(mem[scan_ptr]). If err_flag[scan_ptr] is set, it decodes only that entry, writes back the corrected codeword, clears the flag, and increments corr_cnt. It then advances scan_ptr. Gating the correction on err_flag means corr_cnt can only grow on an entry that was earlier injected.

Relation R (holds by construction): !inj_seen -> (corr_cnt == 0 && err_flag == 16'h0).

Property P (precedence, between scrub_start and scrub_done, unclocked module-level form):
assert property (!(win && corr_cnt != 32'd0) || inj_seen);
In words: inside a scrub window, an observed nonzero correction count requires that an injection was recorded earlier. The window register win is listed in the antecedent. inj_seen is sticky, so 32-bit wraparound of corr_cnt is harmless.

Why k-induction needs R: an unreachable state can satisfy P only because win is closed. It can then be held arbitrarily long with en=0, and it violates P one step after the window opens.

Counterexample-to-induction state: win=0, inj_seen=0, inj_cnt=0, corr_cnt=32'd5, err_flag=16'h0001, scan_ptr=0, mem arbitrary.
- P holds because win=0.
- R is violated because corr_cnt!=0 and err_flag!=0 while inj_seen=0.
- With en=0, all state is frozen, so the state persists for any k.
- Then en=1 with scrub_start=1 sets win=1 while corr_cnt stays 5 and inj_seen stays 0, so P fails.

Given R as an invariant, any state with inj_seen=0 has corr_cnt=0 and no flags. corr_cnt therefore cannot become nonzero without a prior inj, and P becomes inductive.

What it is: Window function multiplier: Scales incoming samples by coefficients read from a window ROM addressed by a sample-index counter.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module hdmi_line_window: a per-scanline window-function multiplier that tapers the 32-bit pixel-intensity stream before it goes to an ADV7513-style video path. A 256-entry, 32-bit coefficient ROM, win_rom[0:255], holds a symmetric Hann-like taper and is initialized at elaboration. Each sample is scaled by that ROM's coefficients.

Inputs: clk, rst, en, line_start (Q), line_stop (R), and sample_in[31:0]. The en input is the enable: when en is low, every register holds its value.

State registers:
- idx[31:0]: up-counting sample index.
- dn[31:0]: down-counting mirror index, used to address the symmetric half of the taper.
- win: 1-bit observation window register.
- y[31:0]: scaled output register.

Reset values are idx=0, dn=255, win=0 and y=0.

When en=1, the next state is:
- Counters: if dn==0, then idx<=0 and dn<=255. Otherwise idx<=idx+1 and dn<=dn-1. The wrap decision looks only at dn, never at idx.
- Window: win <= line_start ? 1 : (line_stop ? 0 : win).
- Output: y <= sample_in * ((win_rom[idx[7:0]] + win_rom[dn[7:0]]) >> 1), keeping the low 32 bits.

Because line_start and line_stop are free inputs, the window can open and close any number of times. Each line is one 256-sample sweep of the index counters.

Relation R, which holds by construction: idx + dn == 255, and therefore idx <= 255 and dn <= 255. Both counters start consistent, move in lockstep in opposite directions, and wrap together exactly when dn reaches 0, which is exactly when idx reaches 255.

Property P (universality restricted to the Q-to-R window, with win as the antecedent), written at module level and unclocked:
assert property (!win || idx <= 32'd255);

Why k-induction fails without R: idx is bounded only through dn's wrap condition. Consider the state idx=255, dn=5, win=1, y=0.
- It satisfies P, since 255 <= 255.
- It violates R, since 255 + 5 = 260.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0, so a length-k run of P-satisfying states exists for every k.
- Stepping once with en=1 and line_start=1 (so the window stays open) gives dn!=0, so idx becomes 256 and dn becomes 4 with win=1. That state violates P.

Supplying R, i.e. assuming idx + dn == 255 && dn <= 255, rules this state out and makes P 1-inductive. The intended aids are the helper assertion assert property (idx + dn == 32'd255); and assert property (dn <= 32'd255);.

invariants: phase != 2'd1 || (arm_cnt == start_cnt + 32'd1 && start_cnt == fin_cnt && clk_en && hs_latch)
description:
What it is: Pausible clock controller: Stretches or pauses a local ring-oscillator clock while an asynchronous handshake is resolved by a mutual-exclusion element, keeping the clock-enable state and the handshake latch.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module jls_pausible_clkctl: a pausible-clock controller that lets an async JPEG-LS pixel-word producer hand 32-bit words into a locally clocked encoder line buffer. Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (all state holds when en=0), areq (async request, pre-synchronized), mutex_gnt (mutex grant), din[31:0], sof, eof. State: phase[1:0] (IDLE=0, ARMED=1, STARTED=2), hs_latch (1, captured request), clk_en (1, local ring clock enable; 0 while paused), arm_cnt[31:0], start_cnt[31:0], fin_cnt[31:0], wptr[7:0], linebuf[0:255][31:0], win (1, observation window).

Behavior when en=1: IDLE and areq: hs_latch<=1, phase<=ARMED, arm_cnt++. ARMED and mutex_gnt: clk_en<=0 (clock paused), phase<=STARTED, start_cnt++. STARTED: linebuf[wptr]<=din, wptr++, hs_latch<=0, clk_en<=1, phase<=IDLE, fin_cnt++. Encoding 3 never entered (maps to IDLE). win<=1 on sof, win<=0 on eof (eof priority); sof/eof recur, so the window opens and closes many times; win does not affect the handshake. When en=0 every register holds.

Relation R (by construction): (phase==IDLE -> arm_cnt==start_cnt && start_cnt==fin_cnt && clk_en && !hs_latch) && (phase==ARMED -> arm_cnt==start_cnt+1 && start_cnt==fin_cnt && clk_en && hs_latch) && (phase==STARTED -> arm_cnt==start_cnt && start_cnt==fin_cnt+1 && !clk_en && hs_latch) && phase!=3.

Property P (chain precedence arm->start->finish, scoped between sof and eof):
always @(posedge clk) if (win && phase==2'd2) assert (arm_cnt == start_cnt && start_cnt == fin_cnt + 32'd1 && !clk_en);
It says inside the window a started (clock-paused) transfer is always matched by exactly one prior arm and is the one unfinished start. True because every STARTED entry is preceded by ARMED, which is preceded by an arm increment.

CTI state (satisfies P, violates R): win=1, phase=ARMED, hs_latch=1, clk_en=1, arm_cnt=5, start_cnt=5, fin_cnt=5. P holds vacuously (phase!=STARTED); R fails because ARMED requires arm_cnt==start_cnt+1. With en=0 it is held indefinitely. Then en=1, mutex_gnt=1, no eof: phase<=STARTED, clk_en<=0, start_cnt<=6 while arm_cnt=5, so arm_cnt!=start_cnt with win=1 and phase==STARTED, violating P. k-induction alone cannot exclude this since the en=0 hold yields arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefixes; supplying R as a lemma makes P inductive.

What it is: Ring stop interface: Inserts and removes flits on a unidirectional ring, giving through-traffic priority over injection, and keeps a ring slot register, an injection queue head and a starvation counter that triggers slot reservation.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module neo_ringstop: a Neo Geo themed ring stop where the LSPC sprite-fetch engine injects 64-bit tile-request flits onto a unidirectional video ring. Through-traffic always has priority over injection.

Inputs:
- clk, rst.
- en: the idle/enable input. When en=0, every register holds.
- ring_in_vld, ring_in_data[63:0], ring_in_dst[3:0].
- push, push_data[63:0], my_id[3:0].

State registers:
- slot_vld (1), slot_data (64), slot_dst (4): the ring slot register.
- fifo[16] x 64: the injection queue storage.
- q_head (5) and q_tail (5): 4-bit index plus a wrap bit.
- q_count (5).
- starve_cnt (64).
- rsv (1): the slot-reservation flag.
- inj_total (64).
- pre_rsv (1): resets to 1.

Behaviour when en=1:
- An incoming flit addressed to my_id is ejected. Any other valid incoming flit is forwarded into the slot.
- Injection is pop = (q_head != q_tail) && free slot. The free-slot condition is that there is no non-ejected through flit, or rsv=1, in which case the upstream stop is told to hold via ring_hold.
- On pop: fifo[q_head[3:0]] goes to the slot, q_head increments, and inj_total increments.
- On push when q_count<16: write fifo[q_tail[3:0]] and increment q_tail.
- q_count <= q_count + push_ok - (pop && q_count!=0). The decrement saturates at zero.
- starve_cnt increments while the queue is nonempty and pop is blocked, and clears on pop.
- When starve_cnt reaches 64'd1000: rsv is set and pre_rsv is cleared permanently. rsv clears after the next pop.

Relation R (holds by construction, since push and pop move the pointers and the count in lockstep):
- q_count == (q_tail - q_head) mod 32.

Property P (universality over every reachable state, before-reservation scope, no-change style):
- assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) pre_rsv && $stable(q_tail) && $stable(q_count) |-> $stable(q_head));
- Meaning: before any reservation has ever happened, if no flit was enqueued and the occupancy count did not change, then no injection occurred.
- In reachable states this is true. A pop with no push always changes q_count, because R makes q_count nonzero whenever the pointers differ.

Counterexample to induction:
- State: q_head=0, q_tail=1, q_count=0, slot_vld=0, starve_cnt=0, rsv=0, pre_rsv=1.
- This violates R, since 1-0 != 0.
- It satisfies P: holding with en=0 keeps every register $stable, so the implication holds for any number of idle cycles.
- Next step with en=1, push=0, ring_in_vld=0: pointer-based pop fires because q_head != q_tail.
- q_head becomes 1, while q_count stays 0 by saturation and q_tail is unchanged. pre_rsv is still 1.
- So the antecedent holds but $stable(q_head) fails, violating P.

k-induction without R can always prepend arbitrarily long idle stretches in this inconsistent state, so it fails. With R supplied as an invariant, P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: One-hot AND-OR multiplexer: Combines inputs by ANDing each with its own bit of a one-hot select register and ORing the results into the output, holding only that one-hot select register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module hfrisc_ctx_save_mux: the context-save sequencer of an HF-RISC-style core. On an interrupt it streams the 32 x 32-bit register file out through a one-hot AND-OR read multiplexer, one register per cycle.

Ports: clk, rst, en (enable; when low all state holds), rf_flat[1023:0] (32 entries of 32 bits each), dout[31:0].

State registers:
- sel[31:0]: the one-hot select, i.e. the word line of the register being saved.
- idx[4:0]: the binary register index, used to form the save-memory address.

Datapath: dout = OR over i of (rf[i] & {32{sel[i]}}). This is a pure AND-OR mux with no priority logic.

Update:
- On reset: sel = 32'h1, idx = 0.
- When en is high, the word line advances with a cheap XOR move indexed by the binary pointer: sel <= sel ^ (32'h1 << idx) ^ (32'h1 << (idx+5'd1)), and idx <= idx + 5'd1 (mod 32, so the move from 31 wraps to bit 0).
- When en is low, sel and idx both hold.

Relation R (holds by construction): sel == (32'h1 << idx). Reset establishes it. Each enabled step clears exactly bit idx, the only set bit, and sets bit idx+1 while idx increments. So R is re-established every cycle.

Property P (universality, global, combinational):
always @(*) assert ($onehot(sel));
The AND-OR mux must never OR two registers together onto dout. P holds in every reachable state because it is implied by R.

Why P is not k-inductive alone: the update of sel depends on idx, but P constrains only sel. Consider the state sel = 32'h20, idx = 0, i.e. sel = 1 << (idx+5).
- It satisfies P, since sel is one-hot.
- It violates R, since 32'h20 != (32'h1 << 0).
- It can be held forever with en = 0, so a P-satisfying trace of any length k ends in it, and plain k-induction has no depth at which it succeeds.
- With en = 1 it steps to sel = 32'h20 ^ 32'h1 ^ 32'h2 = 32'h23, idx = 1. Three bits are set, so P is violated.

Supplying R (sel == 1 << idx) as a strengthening invariant makes P 1-inductive. Under R the XOR clears the single set bit and sets the next one, so sel stays one-hot.

What it is: Pin mux controller: Selects which internal function drives each physical pad using per-pin function-select registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
BabySoC pad mux: an 8-pad pin-mux controller for a VSDBabySoC-style chip. It routes RVMYTH GPIO, the PLL clock-out, the DAC serial bit or the UART TX onto each physical pad.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, every register holds), wr (write strobe), wr_idx[2:0], wr_func[2:0], lock_req (firmware freezes the pad configuration after the PLL locks), plus function sources gpio_out[7:0], pll_clk, dac_bit, uart_tx.

State registers:
- func_sel[0:7], 3 bits each: per-pad function select, reset to 0 (GPIO).
- wr_cnt[31:0]: count of accepted writes, incremented when en && wr && !locked.
- cm_cnt[31:0]: commit counter, incremented by the same condition in the same always block, so it shadows the write path.
- err (1 bit): sticky; err <= err | (wr_cnt != cm_cnt) whenever en is high.
- locked (1 bit): reset 0; set by en && lock_req.
- pre_lock (1 bit): reset 1; cleared the first time en && lock_req occurs. This is the 'before R' scope register.

Output: pad_out[i] is selected by func_sel[i]:
- 0: gpio_out[i]
- 1: pll_clk
- 2: dac_bit
- 3: uart_tx
- any other value: 0

Relation R (holds by construction): wr_cnt == cm_cnt. Both counters reset to 0 together and are always incremented under the identical condition. Because R holds, err stays 0 in every reachable state.

Property P (universality, guarded by the before-lock scope; antecedent: pre_lock):
always @(posedge clk) if (pre_lock) assert (!err);

Why induction fails without R: consider the state wr_cnt=5, cm_cnt=4, err=0, pre_lock=1, locked=0, with func_sel arbitrary.
- It satisfies P, since err=0.
- It violates R, since 5 != 4.
- It is stable under en=0, because all registers hold. An induction trace of any length can therefore sit in it while satisfying P.
- From it, one cycle with en=1, lock_req=0, wr=0 sets err=1 while pre_lock stays 1. P is then violated.

k-induction therefore cannot prove P for any k. Supplying R (wr_cnt == cm_cnt) as a strengthening lemma makes P 1-inductive: R is preserved by the lock-step increments, and R together with !err implies !err at the next step.

What it is: Pipelined CAM: Splits the key comparison across pipeline stages so each stage narrows a partial match vector, keeping the key array, valid bits and per-stage partial-match and key registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
HDLBits 'problem-ID lookup' pipelined CAM: a 2-entry, 64-bit-key CAM that maps a 64-bit problem hash to a solution slot. The key comparison is split over two pipeline stages, and an in-flight occupancy counter tracks how many lookups are currently in the pipe.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when en=0 every register holds its value), lookup, lookup_key[63:0], wr_en, wr_idx, wr_key[63:0].
Outputs: hit, hit_vec[1:0].

State registers:
- key_mem[0:1], 64-bit each.
- valid[1:0].
- Stage 1: s1_vld (1), s1_key_hi[31:0], s1_pm[1:0], the partial match on the low 32 bits.
- Stage 2: s2_vld (1), s2_match[1:0].
- inflight[63:0].
- armed (1).
Reset clears everything to 0.

Behaviour, only when en=1:
- Write: if wr_en, then key_mem[wr_idx]<=wr_key and valid[wr_idx]<=1.
- Stage 1: s1_vld<=lookup; s1_key_hi<=lookup_key[63:32]; s1_pm[i]<=valid[i] & (key_mem[i][31:0]==lookup_key[31:0]).
- Stage 2: s2_vld<=s1_vld; s2_match[i]<=s1_pm[i] & (key_mem[i][63:32]==s1_key_hi).
- Outputs: hit_vec=s2_vld?s2_match:0 and hit=|hit_vec.
- inflight<=inflight + lookup - s2_vld. A lookup enters every cycle that lookup=1, and stage 2 drains every cycle.
- armed<=armed | lookup. This is sticky: it is set by the first lookup issued (event Q) and never cleared.

Relation R (holds by construction): inflight == s1_vld + s2_vld. It holds at reset (all zero) and is preserved by every update, because the next inflight equals lookup + s1_vld, which is exactly next s1_vld + next s2_vld. Holding with en=0 also preserves it.

Property P (bounded existence, after Q):
always @(*) assert (!armed || inflight <= 64'd2);
The bound 2 is far below what the 64-bit counter can represent, so it is a real fact about reachable states. It holds only because the pipeline has exactly two stages.

Why k-induction fails without R: take the state armed=1, inflight=2, s1_vld=0, s2_vld=0, with the other state arbitrary.
- It satisfies P, since 2 <= 2.
- It violates R, since 2 != 0+0.
- With en=0 it can be held unchanged for any number of cycles, giving an arbitrarily long P-satisfying prefix.
- Then step with en=1 and lookup=1. Because s2_vld=0, nothing drains, so inflight becomes 3 while armed stays 1, violating P.

Adding R as a lemma excludes this state. Under R, inflight is at most 2 at all times, so the inductive step goes through.

What it is: Oversampling clock-data recovery: Samples a serial line several times per bit and picks the best phase, keeping phase-select and majority-vote registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module doomsday_cdr: a 4x-oversampling clock-data recovery front end. It recovers bits from a serial line and counts recovered bits toward a 'doomsday' frame length of 383 bits, a nod to the 383-bit counter. Inputs: clk, rst, en (idle input; when low every register holds), rx (serial line). State registers: samp[3:0] holds the last four oversamples; phase_sel[1:0] selects the sampling phase; vote[2:0] is the majority-vote window of the selected phase; os_cnt[1:0] is the oversample index; bit_cnt[15:0] counts recovered bits; armed, started, finished are 1-bit sticky flags; no_slip is 1 bit, reset to 1. Behaviour when en=1: samples shift into samp. At each os_cnt wrap, the selected phase is majority-voted into the recovered bit. An edge detected away from the current phase is a slip: phase_sel moves toward that edge and no_slip clears permanently. The chain runs arm, then start, then finish. armed sets on the first edge seen while idle-synced. started sets when armed is 1 and a start pattern 1-0 is recovered. While started, bit_cnt increments once per recovered bit. finished sets when started is 1 and bit_cnt == 383. All three flags are sticky until rst. Relation R, true by construction: (started -> armed) && (finished -> started) && (bit_cnt != 0 -> started). Property P uses the $past style with a past-valid register and the before-slip scope. Declare reg pv = 0; always @(posedge clk) pv <= 1; then always @(posedge clk) if (pv && no_slip) assert (!finished || $past(armed)); with no_slip listed as an antecedent. P holds because finished can only rise from a cycle where started was 1, hence armed was 1. Once finished is set, R keeps armed high, and armed is sticky. Counterexample to induction without R: armed=0, started=1, finished=0, bit_cnt=383, no_slip=1, pv=1, en=0. P holds here because finished=0, and this state persists for any number of idle cycles. R is violated because started=1 while armed=0. Raise en with rx causing no slip: the next cycle sets finished=1 while $past(armed)=0, so P fails. k-induction alone therefore cannot close P, but strengthening with R removes this unreachable state and P proves at k=1.

What it is: LED matrix scanner: Drives rows sequentially while presenting column data, keeping a row counter and a frame bitmap memory.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module metro_led_scan: a 64x64 LED matrix scanner for an FPGA panel. Its structure follows a clean coding style, with separate always_ff blocks per register and every name suffixed _r.

Ports: clk, rst, en (scan enable), wr_en, wr_addr[5:0], wr_data[63:0], and outputs row_drv[63:0] and col_drv[63:0].

State registers:
- frame_mem_r: 64 entries x 64 bits, the frame bitmap. It is written whenever wr_en is high, independent of en, and is not part of R.
- row_idx_r[63:0]: binary row counter. It counts 0..63 and wraps to 0.
- row_sel_r[63:0]: one-hot row strobe. It rotates left with wraparound: row_sel_r <= {row_sel_r[62:0], row_sel_r[63]}.
- col_r[63:0]: column data, loaded with frame_mem_r[row_idx_r[5:0]].
- armed_r (1 bit): sticky arm register.
- pv_r (1 bit): past-valid register. It resets to 0 and is then set to 1 every cycle.

Outputs: row_drv = row_sel_r, col_drv = col_r.

Reset values: row_idx_r = 0, row_sel_r = 64'h1, armed_r = 0.

When en is low, row_idx_r, row_sel_r, col_r and armed_r all hold. When en is high, the row counter and the strobe advance together each cycle.

Event Q is the first completed frame: en && row_idx_r == 63. On Q, armed_r is set, and it is never cleared afterwards except by rst.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- row_idx_r < 64, and
- row_sel_r == (64'h1 << row_idx_r[5:0]).
In words, the strobe is exactly one-hot and agrees with the counter.

Property P (absence: the top-row and bottom-row drivers are never on together, checked one cycle late):

always @(posedge clk) if (pv_r && $past(armed_r)) assert (!($past(row_sel_r[0]) && $past(row_sel_r[63])));

P is true because R makes row_sel_r one-hot, so bits 0 and 63 are never both high.

Counterexample to induction without R:
- State: pv_r = 1, armed_r = 1, row_idx_r = 5, row_sel_r = 64'hC000_0000_0000_0000 (bits 62 and 63 set, all others clear).
- This state satisfies P, since bit 0 is clear.
- It violates R, since the strobe is not one-hot and does not match the counter.
- With en low it is held indefinitely, so P keeps holding for any induction depth k.
- Raising en for one cycle rotates row_sel_r to bits 63 and 0. At the next clock the $past values show row_sel_r[0] and row_sel_r[63] both high with armed_r = 1, and P fails.

Supplying R as an invariant removes this unreachable state, after which P is proved 1-inductive.

What it is: Hardware semaphore block: Provides test-and-set lock cells that record the owning requester id and a locked flag per cell.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module isp_fb_sema is a frame-buffer semaphore for a mini-ISP. A demosaic or tonemap stage must lock a line-buffer cell before it uses that cell. The block has 48 test-and-set lock cells, and a 3-step transaction FSM (arm, start, finish) wraps them.

Inputs:
- clk, rst_n.
- en: global enable. When en is low, every register holds its value.
- req_id[31:0].
- cell_sel[5:0], valid range 0..47.
- arm_req, start_req, fin_req.

State registers:
- locked[47:0]: one locked flag per cell.
- owner[0:47][31:0]: owning requester id per cell.
- cur_cell[5:0]: the cell held by the current transaction.
- phase[1:0]: 0=IDLE, 1=ARMED, 2=STARTED.
- arm_cnt[31:0], start_cnt[31:0], fin_cnt[31:0]: transaction step counters.

Behaviour, only when en=1:
- Arm (test-and-set): if phase==0, arm_req is high, cell_sel<48 and !locked[cell_sel], then set locked[cell_sel]=1, owner[cell_sel]=req_id, cur_cell=cell_sel, phase=1 and arm_cnt++.
- Start (pixel processing begins): if phase==1 and start_req is high, set phase=2 and start_cnt++.
- Finish (buffer released): if phase==2 and fin_req is high, clear locked[cur_cell], set phase=0 and fin_cnt++.
- phase==3 is never entered; any other input is a no-op.

Relation R, which holds by construction:
- phase==0 implies arm_cnt==start_cnt and start_cnt==fin_cnt.
- phase==1 implies arm_cnt==start_cnt+1 and start_cnt==fin_cnt.
- phase==2 implies arm_cnt==start_cnt and start_cnt==fin_cnt+1.
- phase!=3.
All arithmetic is modulo 2^32.

Property P (chain precedence, global, no arming register):
No later step ever runs ahead of an earlier one. P is stated with modular differences so that counter wrap after 2^32 transactions stays correct:
  always @(*) assert ((arm_cnt - start_cnt) <= 32'd1 && (start_cnt - fin_cnt) <= 32'd1);
So a finish is never observed without a matching start, and a start is never observed without a matching arm.

Why P needs R: take the state
  phase=2, arm_cnt=start_cnt=fin_cnt=32'd5, cur_cell=0, locked[0]=1, owner[0]=7.
- It satisfies P, because both differences are 0.
- It violates R, because STARTED requires start_cnt==fin_cnt+1.
- With en=0 it can be held for any number of cycles, so it defeats k-induction for every k.
- When en=1 and fin_req=1, the FSM performs a finish and fin_cnt becomes 6. Then start_cnt - fin_cnt = 32'hFFFFFFFF > 1, so P fails.
Once R is supplied as a strengthening invariant, P together with R is 1-inductive. Every transition preserves the exact per-phase counter offsets, and those offsets imply both differences are 0 or 1.

What it is: 64b/66b gearbox: Repacks 64-bit payloads plus sync header into a continuous 66-bit serial framing, keeping a barrel buffer and bit-offset counter.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module: vid_gearbox_128b130b. A video line packer for camera pixels. Each 128-bit block carries 16 greyscale pixels, the payload word size. A 2-bit sync header is prepended: 01 for pixel data, 10 for control. The 130-bit blocks are repacked into a continuous stream of 128-bit output words.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (hold-all-state when low), sof, eof, in_v, in_data[127:0], in_ctl.
Outputs: out_v, out_word[127:0].

State registers:
- buf[255:0]: barrel buffer.
- occ[7:0]: residual bit count left in buf after each emit.
- ph[6:0]: gearbox phase, range 0..64.
- win[0:0]: frame window.
- acc_seen[0:0]: shadow flag meaning a block was accepted in this window.

Behaviour, only when en=1:
- On sof: buf, occ and ph are cleared, win<=1 and acc_seen<=0.
- On eof (without sof): win<=0.
- Stall cycle (ph==64): no input is accepted. The 128 residual bits are emitted (out_v=1), occ<=occ-128 and ph<=0.
- Otherwise, if in_v: the 130-bit block {hdr,in_data} is shifted into buf at offset occ. The low 128 bits are emitted (out_v=1). Then occ<=occ+2 (8-bit wrap), ph<=ph+1 and acc_seen<=1.
- With en=0, every register holds.
- Reset gives all zeros, so R holds.

Relation R (by construction): occ == {ph,1'b0}, i.e. occ == 2*ph. Each accepted block adds 130 bits and removes 128, adding 2. The stall removes 128 = 2*64 and resets ph to 0.

Property P: precedence with a shadow register, scope after sof until eof. eof may never arrive, so P must hold from sof onward whether or not the window closes. Two assertions, with win in both antecedents:
- A1: (win && !acc_seen) |-> (occ == 0). Leftover bits in the frame window require an earlier accepted block.
- A2: (win && acc_seen && ph != 0) |-> (occ != 0). A mid-cycle phase after an earlier acceptance requires buffered residue.

Neither assertion is inductive alone, nor together, without R.
- A1 alone, CTI: win=1, acc_seen=0, ph=64, occ=0, which violates R. The stall step gives occ=0-128=128 with acc_seen still 0, so A1 fails.
- A1∧A2 together, CTI: win=1, acc_seen=1, ph=0, occ=254. Both assertions hold (A1 vacuous, A2 vacuous since ph=0), but R is violated (2*0≠254). The state is held indefinitely while en=0. When en=1 and in_v=1, occ becomes 254+2=256, which wraps to 0, and ph becomes 1. That violates A2.
- With R: !acc_seen forces ph=0, so the stall branch is unreachable and A1 is preserved. Also ph∈1..64 forces occ=2*ph∈2..128, which is nonzero, so A2 is preserved. Therefore R∧A1∧A2 is 1-inductive.

What it is: Manchester decoder: Recovers data and clock from a Manchester-coded line by timing transitions against expected half and full bit periods, holding an edge-interval counter, the last line level and a decoded-bit shift register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module manch_h16_rx: a Manchester receiver for a serial line carrying IEEE binary16 (or 8.8 fixed-point) operands, as if feeding a half-precision adder or multiplier. Each frame is 16 Manchester bits, and each bit lasts exactly FULL=16 clocks. The line is sampled at the quarter-bit and three-quarter-bit points. A mid-bit level change decodes the bit (high-to-low = 1). A missing transition sets an err flag but does not stall timing, so frame length is fixed. Input en is the enable: when en is low, every register holds.

State registers:
- phase[31:0]: edge-interval counter within the current bit.
- last_lvl[0:0]: last sampled line level.
- shreg[31:0]: decoded-bit shift register; low 16 bits hold the binary16 word.
- bits_left[31:0]: bits remaining in the frame.
- deadline[31:0]: completion countdown, decrementing and saturating at 0.
- busy[0:0]: a frame is outstanding.
- err[0:0]: missing-transition flag.
- win[0:0]: property window.

Behaviour when en=1:
- Accept (Q): when sof=1 and busy=0, set busy=1, bits_left=16, phase=0, deadline=256, win=1.
- While busy, each cycle: deadline decrements and phase increments. At phase==15, phase wraps to 0 and bits_left decrements. When bits_left would reach 0, set busy=0 and pulse done.
- Close (R): win clears on done or on an abort input. abort also clears busy.
- Window reuse: the next sof reopens the window, so it can open and close any number of times.
- mid_strobe = busy && (phase==8) is the mid-bit sample point. It rises once per bit.

Relation R (holds by construction):
busy -> (bits_left>=1 && bits_left<=16 && phase<16 && deadline == bits_left*16 - phase).
Also win -> busy.

Property P (bounded response, safety form, scoped between sof and done/abort, edge style):
assert property (@(posedge clk) win && $rose(mid_strobe) |-> deadline != 0);
The countdown has not expired while a decoded word is still outstanding. P holds because, by R, deadline at a mid-bit sample is at least bits_left*16 - 8, which is at least 8.

Why induction fails without R:
Take the state win=1, busy=1, bits_left=3, phase=7, deadline=1, en=0. This state satisfies P, since mid_strobe is low. It violates R, which requires deadline=41. With en=0 it can be held for any number of cycles, so every k-step prefix satisfies P. Raising en steps it to phase=8 and deadline=0. mid_strobe then rises with win=1, which violates P. With R supplied, deadline is pinned to phase and bits_left, and P becomes inductive.

What it is: SPI chip-select sequencer: Asserts and deasserts individual slave-select lines with programmable setup, hold and inter-transfer delays, keeping a selected-slave register, a delay counter and a sequencing state register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module toast_spi_cs_seq: a memory-mapped SPI chip-select sequencer peripheral, as a Toast RV32I core would expose over MMIO. Software pushes transfer descriptors into a 24-entry queue. Each descriptor holds a 5-bit slave index (0..23) and a 128-bit data word. The sequencer pops a descriptor, asserts that slave's select line, waits a programmable setup delay, then shifts out 128 bits. It then waits a hold delay, deasserts the select line, and waits an inter-transfer gap.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when en is low every state register holds its value), push, push_slv[4:0], push_data[127:0], and the delay registers cfg_setup[7:0], cfg_hold[7:0], cfg_gap[7:0].

State registers:
- st[2:0]: IDLE, SETUP, XFER, HOLD, GAP.
- sel[4:0]: the selected slave.
- dly[7:0]: delay counter.
- bitcnt[6:0]: shift counter.
- cs_vec[23:0]: active-high select lines; the output is cs_n = ~cs_vec.
- shreg[127:0]: shift register.
- Queue: q_slv[0:23][4:0], q_dat[0:23][127:0], wptr[4:0], rptr[4:0], count[4:0] (24 entries, so the pointers wrap at 23).

Behaviour (all updates only when en is high):
- In IDLE or at the end of GAP, if count != 0: pop the head entry, set sel to q_slv[rptr], set cs_vec <= cs_vec | (24'b1 << q_slv[rptr]), load shreg and set dly <= cfg_setup, then go to SETUP.
- SETUP counts dly down to 0, then goes to XFER with bitcnt = 127.
- XFER shifts one bit per cycle until bitcnt reaches 0, then goes to HOLD with dly = cfg_hold.
- At the end of HOLD: cs_vec <= cs_vec & ~(24'b1 << sel), dly <= cfg_gap, then go to GAP.
- When GAP expires with an empty queue, go to IDLE.
- Reset clears everything.

The select update is a read-modify-write of cs_vec rather than a fresh one-hot assignment. This is why the invariant is only maintained by construction and is not locally evident.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- When st is SETUP, XFER or HOLD: cs_vec == (24'b1 << sel) and sel < 24.
- When st is IDLE or GAP: cs_vec == 24'b0.

Property P (absence of two simultaneous slave selects, global, guarded):
always @(posedge clk) if (st != ST_IDLE) assert ($onehot0(cs_vec));

Counterexample to induction (satisfies P, violates R):
- st = GAP, dly = 1, sel = 5, cs_vec = 24'h000008 (bit 3 stale), count = 1, and q_slv[rptr] = 7.
- P holds, because cs_vec is onehot0.
- R is violated, because cs_vec should be 0 in GAP.
- With en low this state is held indefinitely, so a k-induction prefix of any length satisfies P.
- When en rises, dly reaches 0, the queue pops slave 7, and st moves to SETUP with cs_vec = 24'h000088.
- Two select lines are now asserted with st != IDLE, so P fails.

Giving the prover R excludes the stale bit, and P then becomes inductive.

What it is: Brown-out detector filter: Digitally qualifies a comparator's low-voltage indication and raises a brown-out event or reset, keeping a debounce counter, a threshold-select register and a brown-out status flag.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module coyote_vfpga_bod: a brown-out filter guarding one vFPGA tenant region's power rail in an FPGA-OS shell. Before the shell isolates and resets the tenant slot, it requires a comparator low indication that is digitally qualified.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle input; when low, ALL state holds), cmp_low (rail comparator), clr (software acknowledge), sel_wr, sel_in[1:0].

Constant 4-entry threshold table THR[0..3] = {16'd4, 16'd16, 16'd256, 16'd4096}. Let thr = THR[thr_sel].

State registers:
- deb_cnt[15:0]: debounce counter.
- thr_sel[1:0]: threshold-select register.
- bo_flag: sticky brown-out status flag, which drives slot_reset.
- streak[15:0]: shadow register counting consecutive low cycles, saturating at 16'hFFFF.

Behavior (only when en=1; reset zeroes all registers):
- If !cmp_low: deb_cnt<=0 and streak<=0.
- Else: streak<=sat_inc(streak). If !bo_flag, then deb_cnt<=deb_cnt+1, and if deb_cnt+1 >= thr then bo_flag<=1.
- clr: bo_flag<=0 and deb_cnt<=0. streak is untouched.
- sel_wr: thr_sel<=sel_in, accepted only when deb_cnt==0. This means the threshold never changes during a qualification run.
- While bo_flag=1, deb_cnt freezes; it stays bounded by 4096.

Relation R (holds by construction): streak >= deb_cnt. Both registers are cleared together when cmp_low is deasserted. Both increment together while qualifying. streak keeps counting, or saturates far above 4096, while deb_cnt is frozen or cleared by clr.

Property P (global precedence, edge style): assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff(!rst_n) $rose(bo_flag) |-> streak >= thr). In words: a brown-out event may only rise if the comparator was observed low for at least thr consecutive cycles beforehand. P is true because at the rising step deb_cnt >= thr; by R, streak >= deb_cnt; and thr_sel could not have changed, since deb_cnt was nonzero.

Why k-induction fails without R: there is a counterexample-to-induction state that satisfies P, violates R, can be held while idle, and steps to a violation of P:
- The state: thr_sel=0 (thr=4), deb_cnt=3, streak=0, bo_flag=0, cmp_low=1.
- It satisfies P, because bo_flag is not rising.
- It violates R, because 0 < 3.
- With en=0, all state holds, so any k-length prefix of identical, P-satisfying states is legal.
- When en=1, deb_cnt+1=4 >= thr sets bo_flag, while streak becomes only 1.
- So $rose(bo_flag) occurs with streak=1 < 4, and P fails.

Supplying R as an invariant (streak >= deb_cnt, plus deb_cnt <= thr whenever bo_flag==0) makes P 1-inductive.

What it is: Decimation filter: Low-pass filters and downsamples an oversampled stream, keeping filter state registers and a decimation phase counter.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module wl_decim48: a boxcar/CIC-style decimator for an oversampled 64-bit 'routing-congestion' sample stream. It sums 48 consecutive placement-density samples and emits one averaged word per window. This is loosely themed on smoothing a placer's wirelength cost trace.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (sample-valid; when low every register holds), flush, din[63:0].

State registers:
- phase[5:0]: decimation phase, range 0..47.
- acc[63:0]: integrator.
- dout[63:0]: last decimated sum.
- in_cnt[63:0]: samples accepted.
- out_cnt[63:0]: words emitted.
- tick (1 bit): output strobe register.
- pre_flush (1 bit): resets to 1 and clears the first cycle en&&flush occurs.

Behavior on reset: all registers are 0 except pre_flush=1.

Behavior when en=1 and flush=0:
- in_cnt increments by 1.
- If phase==47: phase becomes 0, dout gets acc+din, acc becomes 0, out_cnt increments by 1, tick becomes 1.
- Otherwise: phase increments by 1, acc gets acc+din, tick becomes 0.

Behavior when en=1 and flush=1: phase becomes 0, acc becomes 0, tick becomes 0 and pre_flush becomes 0. in_cnt and out_cnt are left unchanged, which is deliberately unsafe for the count bookkeeping.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- phase<48.
- pre_flush implies in_cnt == 48*out_cnt + phase (mod 2^64).
- tick implies phase==0.

Property P (before-flush universality, edge style):
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (rst) (pre_flush && $rose(tick)) |-> (in_cnt == 48*out_cnt));
The pre_flush register is listed as an antecedent. In words: on every rising edge of the output strobe, before any flush has ever happened, exactly 48 input samples have been consumed per emitted word.

Why P is true: pre_flush means no flush has occurred, so the counters are consistent. tick only rises on a wrap, which leaves phase==0. R at that point gives in_cnt == 48*out_cnt.

Why k-induction fails without R: idle stuttering (en=0) lets any bad state persist for arbitrarily many cycles. Those cycles have no tick rise, so P holds vacuously along the way.

Counterexample-to-induction state:
- pre_flush=1, tick=0, phase=47, out_cnt=5, in_cnt=243 (that is 48*5+3, which violates R), acc and dout arbitrary.
- With en=0 the state holds indefinitely and P holds, since tick is not rising.

One step with en=1, flush=0:
- phase wraps to 0, tick rises 0→1, out_cnt becomes 6, in_cnt becomes 244.
- 48*6 = 288 ≠ 244, so P is violated.

Supplying R as a strengthening invariant makes P 1-inductive: the wrap step preserves in_cnt − 48*out_cnt − phase = 0.

What it is: FIR filter: Computes a weighted sum of recent samples using a tapped delay line of sample registers and a coefficient memory.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
SURF-style DSP block 'SsiFir8': an 8-tap, 32-bit FIR with a runtime-reloadable coefficient memory, like an AXI-Lite-reprogrammed filter in a SLAC DAQ chain. Inputs: clk, en, load_req, coef_in[31:0], s_valid, s_data[31:0], frame_end. Outputs: y[31:0] = sum over i of tap[i]*coef[i] (truncated to 32 bits) and y_valid = primed. All state holds when en=0.

State registers:
- tap[0:7] (8 x 32-bit): sample delay line.
- coef[0:7] (8 x 32-bit): coefficient memory.
- fill_cnt (32-bit): count of valid samples in the delay line, saturating at 8.
- primed (1-bit): output-valid flag.
- loading (1-bit): a coefficient reload is in progress.
- load_ptr (32-bit): coefficient write index.
- win (1-bit): property window.
- pv (1-bit): past-valid register.

Behaviour, when en=1:
- If load_req: loading<=1, load_ptr<=0, fill_cnt<=0, so the stale delay line is invalidated.
- Else if loading: coef[load_ptr]<=coef_in and load_ptr<=load_ptr+1; when load_ptr==7, loading<=0. Samples are ignored and fill_cnt is frozen.
- Else if s_valid: shift s_data into tap[0], and fill_cnt<=(fill_cnt<8)?fill_cnt+1:8.
- Every enabled cycle: primed<=(fill_cnt>=8). This deliberately does not gate on loading; safety relies on fill_cnt being 0 during a reload.
- Window: win<=1 on load_req (Q); otherwise win<=0 on frame_end (R), else it holds. frame_end may never arrive.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- loading -> (fill_cnt==0 && !primed)
- fill_cnt<=8
- load_ptr<=7

Property P (Absence, after Q until R, past style):
reg pv=0; always @(posedge clk) pv<=1;
always @(posedge clk) if (pv && $past(win)) assert(!($past(primed) && $past(loading)));
That is, from a reload request onwards, whether or not frame_end ever closes the window, the filter never claims valid output while its coefficients are being rewritten.

Counterexample to induction (CTI):
- State: win=1, loading=1, load_ptr=3, fill_cnt=8, primed=0, pv=1.
- P holds because primed=0. R is violated because fill_cnt!=0 while loading.
- With en=0 the state is held indefinitely, so k-induction cannot exclude it for any k.
- Step with en=1, load_req=0, frame_end=0: loading stays 1 (load_ptr<7) and primed<=(fill_cnt>=8)=1.
- The next state has win=1, loading=1, primed=1. One cycle later the $past assertion fires.
- Supplying R as an invariant blocks this CTI, and P becomes inductive.

What it is: ECC error logger: Captures details of detected memory errors for software, holding syndrome, failing-address and error-type capture registers plus correctable and uncorrectable error counters.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module ecc_err_logger: an opencores-style ECC error logger whose capture handshake runs arm, then start, then finish.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle/enable: when low every register holds), sw_arm, err_valid, err_ue, err_syn[31:0], err_addr[31:0], sw_ack.

State registers:
- phase[1:0]: IDLE=0, ARMED=1, CAPT=2, DONE=3.
- syn_q[31:0], addr_q[31:0], type_q[0:0] (1 means uncorrectable).
- ce_cnt[31:0], ue_cnt[31:0], both saturating.
- log_mem[0:127][31:0], an address history ring, with wp[6:0].
- History bits arm_seen, start_seen, fin_seen (1 bit each, sticky). All are cleared on reset.

Transitions (only when en=1):
- IDLE or DONE, with sw_arm: phase<=ARMED and arm_seen<=1.
- ARMED, with err_valid: phase<=CAPT and start_seen<=1. Also latch syn_q, addr_q and type_q, increment ue_cnt or ce_cnt according to err_ue, write log_mem[wp]<=err_addr, and increment wp.
- CAPT, with sw_ack: phase<=DONE and fin_seen<=1.
The finish step sets only fin_seen. It never touches arm_seen or start_seen.

Relation R (holds by construction):
(phase==ARMED -> arm_seen) && ((phase==CAPT || phase==DONE) -> (arm_seen && start_seen)).
This holds because ARMED is entered only while setting arm_seen, CAPT only from ARMED while setting start_seen, DONE only from CAPT, and the history bits are sticky.

Property P (chain precedence, global, unclocked module-level form):
assert property (!fin_seen || (start_seen && arm_seen));
A finish can never be observed unless both a start and an arm were recorded.

Why k-induction fails without R:
Take the state phase=CAPT, arm_seen=0, start_seen=0, fin_seen=0, with arbitrary capture, counter and log contents.
- It satisfies P, because fin_seen=0.
- It violates R, because phase is CAPT but start_seen=0.
- It is unreachable, yet it can be held for any number of cycles with en=0, so every induction window of length k is self-consistent and satisfies P.
- The next cycle with en=1 and sw_ack=1 moves to phase=DONE with fin_seen=1 while start_seen and arm_seen are still 0, which violates P.
Adding R as a strengthening invariant excludes this state. P && R is then 1-inductive, because every transition that sets fin_seen comes from CAPT, where R guarantees arm_seen and start_seen.

What it is: Normalizer: Left-shifts a mantissa by its leading-zero count and adjusts the exponent accordingly, holding the shift amount in an internal register.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
CSCvon8-style FP normalizer stage (as if bolted onto the ALU ROM path): `norm32` takes a 32-bit mantissa and a 32-bit exponent. It left-shifts the mantissa one bit per cycle until bit 31 is set (or the mantissa is zero), and holds the running shift count internally. A three-step handshake is enforced by an FSM: arm (operand latched), then start (shifting begins), then finish (result valid).

Inputs: clk, en (when low, ALL state holds), arm, load, start, ack, din[31:0], ein[31:0].

State registers:
- phase[1:0]: 0=IDLE, 1=ARMED, 2=SHIFT, 3=DONE.
- mant[31:0], exp[31:0].
- shamt[5:0], the held shift amount (0..32).
- armed_f[0], set on arm.
- started_f[0], set on start.
- q_seen[0], sticky.
- pv[0], the past-valid register.

Behavior, applied only when en=1:
- q_seen <= q_seen | load. It is never cleared.
- IDLE & arm: mant<=din, exp<=ein, shamt<=0, armed_f<=1, phase<=ARMED.
- ARMED & start: started_f<=1, phase<=SHIFT.
- SHIFT:
  - If mant[31] | (mant==0): exp<=exp-shamt, phase<=DONE.
  - Else: mant<=mant<<1, shamt<=shamt+1.
- DONE & ack: armed_f<=0, started_f<=0, phase<=IDLE.

Outputs: done=(phase==3), mant_o, exp_o.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- (phase==1) -> armed_f;
- (phase>=2) -> (armed_f && started_f);
- started_f -> armed_f;
- shamt <= 32.

Property P (chain precedence, after-Q scope, past style):
```
reg pv=0; always @(posedge clk) pv<=1;
always @(posedge clk) if (pv && q_seen && $past(q_seen) && $past(phase)==2'd3) assert($past(armed_f) && $past(started_f));
```
That is, once a load has been seen, finish was never observed without both arm and start having occurred.

Why P needs R (counterexample to induction):
Consider the state phase=2 (SHIFT), armed_f=1, started_f=0, mant=32'h8000_0000, shamt=0, q_seen=1.
- It satisfies P, because the phase is not DONE.
- It violates R, because phase>=2 requires started_f.
- With en=0 it is held unchanged for any number of cycles, so every induction prefix of length k satisfies P.
- When en=1, mant[31]=1, so phase steps to DONE while started_f stays 0.
- The next cycle, the assertion sees $past(phase)==3 with $past(started_f)==0, and P fails.

k-induction alone cannot exclude this unreachable state. Supplying R as a strengthening invariant makes P inductive. R itself is inductive: every transition into SHIFT sets started_f, and only the DONE->IDLE transition clears it.

What it is: NOR gate: Outputs the complement of the OR of its inputs, and holds no internal state.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
BoxLambda DFX bus-quiesce tracker. Before partial reconfiguration, BoxLambda must confirm the Harvard interconnect port to the reconfigurable region is idle. A 16-input NOR gate computes bus_quiet = ~|out_cnt, which is high exactly when no transaction is outstanding.

Inputs:
- clk, rst.
- en: idle/enable input. When en is low, all state holds.
- issue: a request is accepted by the port.
- ret: a response comes back.

State registers:
- out_cnt[15:0]: outstanding transactions.
- iss_cnt[15:0]: total issues, wrapping.
- ret_cnt[15:0]: total returns, wrapping.
- armed (1 bit): sticky scope register.

Behaviour (only when en=1; reset clears everything to 0):
- iss_ok = issue && (out_cnt != 16'hFFFF).
- ret_ok = ret && (out_cnt != 0).
- out_cnt <= out_cnt + iss_ok - ret_ok.
- iss_cnt <= iss_cnt + iss_ok.
- ret_cnt <= ret_cnt + ret_ok.
- armed <= armed | iss_ok. Q is the first accepted issue; armed is never cleared afterwards.
- Output: bus_quiet = ~(out_cnt[0] | out_cnt[1] | ... | out_cnt[15]), i.e. the NOR gate.

Relation R (holds by construction, modulo 2^16): out_cnt == iss_cnt - ret_cnt. Every increment or decrement of out_cnt is matched by exactly one increment of iss_cnt or ret_cnt, and all three update together under the same en.

Property P (precedence, after Q). If the bus is observed quiet now, then every issued transaction must already have returned. The shadow registers iss_cnt and ret_cnt record that history.
  always @(posedge clk) assert (!(armed && bus_quiet) || (ret_cnt == iss_cnt));

Why k-induction fails without R. Consider the state armed=1, iss_cnt=2, ret_cnt=0, out_cnt=1.
- R is violated: it requires out_cnt == 2.
- P holds, because out_cnt=1 makes bus_quiet=0.
- The state can be held indefinitely with en=0, so the inductive prefix can be arbitrarily long.
- Then step with en=1, ret=1, issue=0. ret_ok fires because out_cnt != 0. The next state is out_cnt=0, ret_cnt=1, iss_cnt=2, armed=1.
- Now bus_quiet=1 and ret_cnt != iss_cnt, so P is violated.

Adding R as a lemma makes P inductive. R gives out_cnt==0 implies iss_cnt==ret_cnt, and R is itself inductive. Note that the saturation guard on out_cnt keeps the counter from wrapping, while iss_cnt and ret_cnt wrap consistently, so R holds modulo 2^16.

What it is: Clock failover switch controller: Automatically moves the system clock from a primary to a backup source when the primary is reported failed, keeping a selected-source register, a switch-in-progress flag and a sticky failover status bit.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module ppu_clkfail_ctl: failover controller for an FPGA PPU replacement's pixel clock. It moves the PPU dot clock from the console's 21.477 MHz master crystal (primary) to an on-board backup oscillator when a loss-of-clock detector reports a failure, then holds the backup.

Ports:
- inputs clk, rst_n, en, prim_fail
- outputs use_backup, busy, fail_flag

When en is low, every register holds its value.

State registers:
- sel_src (1b): 0 = primary, 1 = backup.
- switching (1b): switch in progress.
- settle_cnt (8b): glitch-free handover delay.
- sticky_fail (1b): sticky failover status.
- fail_cnt (8b): saturating count of prim_fail pulses seen.
- fail_seen (1b): shadow register that records whether any prim_fail has ever been observed.

On reset, all registers are 0.

Behaviour when en=1:
- If prim_fail is high: fail_seen<=1, sticky_fail<=1, and fail_cnt increments, saturating at 255.
- If prim_fail && !sel_src && !switching: switching<=1 and settle_cnt<=8'd200, to wait out the PPU dot clock's phase.
- Else if switching: settle_cnt<=settle_cnt-1. When settle_cnt==1, also sel_src<=1 and switching<=0.
- Once sel_src=1, it stays at backup until reset.

Outputs: use_backup=sel_src, busy=switching, fail_flag=sticky_fail.

Relation R (holds by construction):
- (switching || sel_src) -> (fail_seen && sticky_fail)
- switching -> (settle_cnt != 0)

Property P (precedence, global, guarded): backup can only be selected if a primary failure was seen earlier.
  always @(posedge clk) if (sel_src) assert (fail_seen);

Counterexample to induction: sel_src=0, switching=1, settle_cnt=8'd1, fail_seen=0, sticky_fail=0, fail_cnt=0.
- P holds, because the guard sel_src is false.
- R is violated, because switching is set while fail_seen=0.
- Holding en=0 keeps this state unchanged for any number of cycles, so k-induction cannot rule it out at any depth k.
- One step with en=1 and prim_fail=0 gives settle_cnt==1, so sel_src<=1 while fail_seen stays 0. The guard is now true and fail_seen=0, so P is violated.

Giving R to the prover as a strengthening invariant removes this state, and P then becomes 1-inductive. R itself is inductive:
- switching and sel_src are only set on, or after, a prim_fail cycle, and that same cycle sets fail_seen and sticky_fail.
- settle_cnt is loaded with 200 and switching clears exactly when the count reaches 1.

What it is: Barrett reduction unit: Reduces a product modulo a fixed modulus by estimating the quotient with a precomputed scaled reciprocal and applying final correction subtractions, keeping modulus, reciprocal, quotient-estimate and residue registers.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Caribou-themed cuckoo-hash bucket indexer. A Barrett unit reduces a 64-bit key-hash product modulo the current table size, and a 32-bit countdown watchdog guards each request.

Inputs: clk, rst, en, req, a[31:0], b[31:0], rehash, new_mod[31:0]. When en is low, all state holds.

State registers:
- mod_r[31:0], the bucket count.
- mu_r[32:0] = floor(2^64/mod_r), the precomputed scaled reciprocal.
- prod_r[63:0], the product.
- q_r[31:0], the quotient estimate.
- res_r[32:0], the residue.
- stage[2:0], the pipeline step.
- cnt[31:0], the countdown.
- busy, done, expired (1 bit each).
- pre_rehash (1 bit). It resets to 1 and is cleared on the first enabled cycle with rehash high.

Operation, on enabled cycles only:
- Request accept (req && !busy): prod_r <= a*b, busy <= 1, stage <= 0, cnt <= 5, done <= 0.
- While busy, each step advances stage and decrements cnt:
  - stage0 to 1: q_r <= (prod_r*mu_r)>>64.
  - stage1 to 2: res_r <= prod_r - q_r*mod_r.
  - stage2 to 3: first correction, if res_r >= mod_r then subtract mod_r.
  - stage3 to 4: second correction, same rule.
  - At stage 4: done <= 1 and busy <= 0, with the bucket index in res_r.
- On every decrement, expired <= expired | (cnt==1 && stage!=4). This flags a countdown hitting zero while the request is still outstanding.
- When idle, rehash loads mod_r <= new_mod and the matching mu_r. In that case done <= 0.

Relation R (holds by construction): busy -> (stage <= 4 && stage + cnt == 5). Also expired == 0.

Property P (bounded response, safety form, before-R scope, $stable style). Antecedent list: pre_rehash, en.
assert property (pre_rehash && en && $stable(done) |-> $stable(expired));
In words: before any rehash has occurred, on an enabled cycle where done did not change, the expiry flag must not change either. Since expired starts 0, this means the countdown never runs out while the reduction is outstanding.

Why k-induction fails without R: the tool can start from an unreachable state that satisfies P but breaks R.
- The state: busy=1, stage=0, cnt=1, done=0, expired=0, pre_rehash=1.
- It satisfies P, because expired is 0 and unchanged.
- It violates R, because stage + cnt = 1, not 5.
- It can be held indefinitely with en=0, so every induction prefix stays in this state and stays P-consistent.
- Raising en with no req and no rehash takes one step. stage goes to 1 and cnt to 0, and since cnt==1 and stage!=4, expired rises to 1. done stays at 0, so $stable(done) is true while expired changes, violating P.

Given R, while busy cnt == 5 - stage. So cnt==1 occurs only at stage 4, which is exactly the completion cycle. The expiry term therefore never fires, and P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Gardner timing error detector: Computes a symbol-timing error from the current and previous symbol samples and the midpoint sample between them, storing those samples in a small history register set and a strobe phase flag.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module gardner_ted_lxp: a Gardner symbol-timing error detector with a 32-entry error log, themed after LXP32's small register file kept in a RAM block.

Inputs: clk, rst, en (when low, all state holds), sample_in[7:0] (signed, two samples per symbol).

State registers:
- phase (1 bit): the strobe phase flag. 0 means a midpoint sample, 1 means a symbol sample.
- prev_sym[7:0], mid[7:0], cur_sym[7:0]: the sample history.
- sym_cnt[7:0]: symbols completed in the current 32-symbol block.
- half_cnt[7:0]: half-symbol samples taken in the current block.
- err_mem[0:31][15:0]: log of timing errors.
- err_out[15:0]: the latest error.

Behavior when en=1 (reset sets every register to 0):
- phase toggles each cycle.
- When phase==0: mid <= sample_in.
- When phase==1 (strobe): prev_sym <= cur_sym, cur_sym <= sample_in, and err = (sample_in - cur_sym) * mid as a signed 16-bit value. err_out <= err and err_mem[sym_cnt[4:0]] <= err.
- Block wrap: if half_cnt==63, then half_cnt <= 0 and sym_cnt <= 0.
- Otherwise, half_cnt <= half_cnt+1, and sym_cnt <= sym_cnt+1 when phase==1.

The wrap is deliberately decided by half_cnt alone, not by sym_cnt.

Relation R (holds by construction): half_cnt == 2*sym_cnt + phase, with half_cnt <= 63.
- After reset: 0 == 0 + 0.
- A midpoint step adds 1 to half_cnt and moves phase from 0 to 1.
- A strobe step adds 1 to half_cnt, adds 1 to sym_cnt, and moves phase from 1 to 0, so 2*sym_cnt + phase grows by 1.
- The wrap happens at half_cnt=63, i.e. sym_cnt=31 and phase=1, and returns everything to 0 together.

Property P (bounded existence, global scope): always @(*) assert (sym_cnt <= 8'd31);
The bound 31 is far below the 8-bit maximum of 255, so it is a real fact about reachable states, enforced only through half_cnt's wrap.

Why induction fails without R: take the state sym_cnt=31, phase=1, half_cnt=10, with any sample and memory contents.
- It satisfies P, since 31 <= 31.
- It violates R, since 2*31 + 1 = 63, not 10.
- With en=0, the state is frozen indefinitely, so any k-step P-satisfying prefix exists.
- With en=1 in that state: half_cnt != 63, so no wrap occurs. Phase is 1, so sym_cnt increments to 32 and P fails.

So P is not k-inductive for any k. Given R, the strobe step from sym_cnt=31 forces half_cnt=63, which triggers the wrap, and P becomes inductive.

The idle hold through en is essential: it lets the bad pre-state persist for k cycles.

What it is: AXI default slave: Terminates AXI transactions routed to unmapped regions with DECERR responses, storing the accepted ID, a burst-length countdown for returning read beats and a pending write-response flag.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
ft60x_axi_default_slave: AXI4 default slave behind an FT60x-to-AXI bridge. It terminates unmapped bursts with DECERR. Read bursts are clamped to the FT60x 16-beat packet size.

Inputs: clk, rst_n, en (idle when low: every register holds and all handshakes are gated off), arvalid, arid[7:0], arlen[7:0], rready, awvalid, awid[7:0], wvalid, wlast, bready.

Outputs: arready = en & ~busy; rvalid = en & busy; rresp = DECERR; rlast = (sent_q+1 == len_q); rid = rid_q; awready = en & ~bpend & ~wact; wready = en & wact; bvalid = en & bpend; bid = bid_q.

State registers:
- rid_q[7:0]: accepted read ID.
- len_q[7:0]: burst length, loaded as min(arlen,15)+1.
- sent_q[7:0]: count of R beats returned.
- busy (1): read burst in progress.
- rbeat_q (1): registered R handshake, rbeat_q <= rvalid & rready.
- win (1): window register.
- bid_q[7:0]: accepted write ID.
- wact (1): absorbing W beats.
- bpend (1): write response pending.

Behavior:
- An AR handshake loads rid_q and len_q, clears sent_q and sets busy.
- Each R handshake increments sent_q. On the rlast handshake, busy and sent_q clear.
- An AW handshake stores bid_q and sets wact. The wlast handshake clears wact and sets bpend. A B handshake clears bpend.
- Window: win sets on an AR handshake (Q) and clears on the rlast handshake (R). Every read burst reopens and recloses it, so the window opens and closes many times.

Relation R (by construction): len_q <= 16, and sent_q <= len_q, and (busy -> sent_q < len_q), and (~busy -> sent_q == 0).

Property P (bounded existence, at most 16, in edge style): assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff(!rst_n) (win && $rose(rbeat_q)) |-> sent_q <= 16);
sent_q is 8 bits wide (maximum 255), so the bound of 16 is a real fact about reachable states and not a width truism.

Why P alone is not k-inductive: consider the state busy=1, win=1, len_q=200, sent_q=16, rbeat_q=0, en=0. It satisfies P, since sent_q is 16 and there is no rising edge on rbeat_q. It violates R, since len_q exceeds 16. With en=0 this state is held for any number of cycles, and all frames satisfy P, so the k-step hypothesis is met for every k. Then raise en=1 with rready=1. rlast is 0 (because 17 != 200), so a non-last beat handshakes. On the next cycle sent_q=17, rbeat_q rises and win is still 1, so P fails.

With R supplied as a lemma, len_q <= 16 and sent_q < len_q while busy. Hence any beat leaves sent_q <= 16, and the last beat resets it to 0, so P becomes 1-inductive.

What it is: Scan-chain select demultiplexer: Directs the test scan-in stream to one of several internal scan chains chosen by a chain-select instruction register loaded through the test port.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module nyuzi_scan_demux: a test-port scan-chain select demultiplexer for a GPGPU core's 256 debug scan chains (one per thread-lane/register-slice). Inputs: clk, rst, en (test-clock enable; when low ALL state holds), ir_load, ir_data[7:0], shift, scan_in. Output: chain_si[255:0], where chain_si[i] = scan_in & shift & en & (chain_sel==i), plus frame_done pulse.

State registers:
- chain_sel [7:0]: instruction register selecting one of 256 chains.
- shift_cnt [15:0]: bits shifted into the current chain frame.
- remaining [15:0]: down-counter of bits left in the frame (frame length 1000).
- armed [0:0]: sticky, set the first time ir_load occurs with en high, never cleared except by rst.

Behavior (only when en=1): on ir_load, chain_sel<=ir_data, shift_cnt<=0, remaining<=999, armed<=1. Else on shift: if remaining==0 then shift_cnt<=0, remaining<=999, frame_done pulses; else shift_cnt<=shift_cnt+1, remaining<=remaining-1. Reset: chain_sel=0, shift_cnt=0, remaining=999, armed=0. When en=0 every register holds.

Relation R (by construction): shift_cnt + remaining == 999 (both updated in lockstep, reset/reloaded together). Wrap is decided only by remaining, never by shift_cnt.

Property P (Bounded Existence at most 999, after-Q scope, Q = first chain-select load):
always @(posedge clk) assert (!armed || shift_cnt <= 16'd999);
The bound 999 is far below the 16-bit limit 65535, so it is a real reachable-state fact.

Why k-induction fails without R: consider the state armed=1, shift_cnt=999, remaining=5, chain_sel arbitrary. It satisfies P (999<=999) but violates R (999+5 != 999). With en=0 it is held indefinitely, so any number of P-satisfying predecessor steps can be stacked. Then with en=1, shift=1, ir_load=0: remaining!=0 so shift_cnt becomes 1000, violating P. Given R, shift_cnt==999 implies remaining==0, forcing the wrap to 0, so P becomes inductive (P with R is 1-inductive).

What it is: Packet header parser: Extracts fixed-offset header fields from a streaming packet into field registers, keeping a byte-offset counter.
The designer's plan, written before the code:
Module sv2v_hdr_parser: a streaming header parser for a 'converted-construct' packet. The theme imagines sv2v emitting a stream of descriptor packets per lowered SystemVerilog construct.
